docs.title: datarecord
docs.text:
Dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema.

A record holds entities (named members of a type), groups of them — connections between entities and buses being the one every network has — attribute values over both, and the axes those values vary along. A schema declares what may exist; the data says what does.

Records stack: a layer is a partial record on top of a parent, resolved last-writer-wins, so a scenario variant costs the rows it changes rather than a copy of everything. On disk a record is a plain parquet directory that a tool knowing nothing about this package can read.

datarecord depends only on duckdb, narwhals and pydantic. It names no modelling framework — a framework consumes a record, a workflow engine produces one, and neither needs to know how the other works.

pip install datarecord           # core
pip install datarecord[pypsa]    # with the PyPSA tool

from datarecord import Workspace

ws = Workspace()
record = ws.at("s3://bucket/my-record/")

record.properties["entity"].collect()  # one row per entity, its properties
record.attributes["p_max_pu"].collect()  # long value rows
record.flags(component="Generator")  # which axes each attribute uses

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to datarecord are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Buses and carriers are dims in the PyPSA tool, carried by two core changes:
  • A property's name is its subject's, addressed as subject.name: set("bus.x", ...), a trait's on and bundled properties, and default_by keys ({"entity.component": {...}}). One name, one spec now holds across attributes and results only, so a property may share its name with an attribute, a dim or another subject's property; one named like its subject's key (the dim, a within parent, a group's struct column or into), or a group's property named like one of its coordinates, is refused. A plain name is an attribute or result, one only properties are called refused naming their dotted forms. Schema.resolve(name) replaces subject_of and property_spec, and Schema.column_type takes the property's subject. add(dim, labels, **properties), flags and properties[subject] keep plain names. A bare selector keyword of set names a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches, categorizing or not; one several reached dims declare is refused. Every manifest declaring a trait or default_by on a property is rewritten.
  • A property may be into a dim (PropertySpec.into): its values are that dim's labels and its dtype the dim's, declared on any subject. set and add refuse a value naming no label of the dim, NULL naming none; the writer refuses a layer storing one it removed, and remove(dim, labels) is refused while such a property still names one. It never categorizes. A group over one coordinate into a dim is now refused at load: declare the property into the dim instead.
  • The PyPSA tool: Bus and Carrier are no entity types, a bus being a label of bus and a carrier of a new carrier dim. bus.carrier, type, x, y, unit and location, and carrier.color and nice_name are properties; v_nom, v_mag_pu_*, co2_emissions, max_growth, max_relative_growth and custom bus or carrier columns attributes over their dim; marginal_price, v_mag_pu and v_ang results over bus, which build sets back. Bus.p, q, control, generator and sub_network are not written, nor the Line.v_nom and ShuntImpedance.v_nom PyPSA copies from the bus, so a solved network exports. entity.carrier and bus.carrier are into carrier: to_datarecord adds every carrier named but not listed and stores "" as NULL. entity_type is entity.component, and bus joins partial. A bus and a load may share a name; a custom column clashes only with an attribute over another dim. verify reports an entity attached to no bus. Every PyPSA record is re-exported.
  • Properties, metadata apart from data: a new properties section of the schema (PropertySpec) declares per dim or group the values describing one label, stored as columns of dims/<dim>.parquet or groups/<group>.parquet. An Enum property of a partial dim categorizes it; traits key on categories, and default_by gives a default per category (Schema.categorizing, attributes_for(dim, **categories), properties_for, default_for). This replaces the entity_type dim, its group over entity and the dims/entity_type/<Type>.parquet member files. entity is an ordinary dim: it broadcasts, and must be in partial to be patched per label or categorized; a NULL on a categorized dim reaches only the labels whose categories carry the attribute. Every attribute, whatever its dims, is stored in inputs/. On reading, dims[dim] holds key columns only, properties[subject] the stored property values, and attributes every attribute; entity_types is gone and flags takes categories (flags(component="Generator")). WorkingRecord edits any dim: add(dim, labels, **properties), remove(dim, labels) (cascading to group tuples), and set(name, value, **coords) writing attributes and properties alike, a property keyword selecting labels at call time; set loses indexed_by. The PyPSA tool declares component, carrier, sign and type as properties of entity and role of connection, with partial={"entity", "scenario", "connection"}. Every manifest and record is rewritten.
  • An attribute over a group carries it as one struct column named for the group, a field per key coordinate (connection STRUCT(entity, bus)), in place of the coordinates flat. This is an on-disk format change: inputs/ and outputs/ files over a group are rewritten. The dims a group draws on now broadcast, so a per-bus value with bus = NULL holds for every bus, and patching one bus at a time needs bus in partial. WorkingRecord.set still takes bus=; a long frame carries the struct, its coordinates flat being rejected. Naming a group beside a dim its key is named for (dims={"connection", "bus"}) is rejected.
  • A group is a broadcast coordinate like a dim, its axis the resolved group: a NULL struct means every tuple of the group, and a struct with some fields NULL is refused by set, add_group and the writer. The owner map's key is entity plus the partial dims and groups; partial may now name a group, and a group outside it is owned whole, so a layer patching one connection's value restates every connection's. The PyPSA tool declares partial={"scenario", "connection"}, keeping per-connection ownership. Schema.membership_keys is gone, and Schema.group_columns is every group but the entity-type group. Materialised owner maps are rebuilt.
  • A group file is keyed by one struct column named for the group, as an axis file is by its dim: groups/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role | deleted, an into label a plain column beside it. This is an on-disk format change. Record.groups[...] hands back that shape; add_group takes the struct column and rejects the coordinates flat; remove_group still takes a tuple per key. The PyPSA tool no longer declares bus as an attribute: a port's bus is the connection tuple. Schema.group_coordinates and Group.coordinates are gone.
  • WorkingRecord.set(..., entity=...) fills only a coordinate named entity. An attribute over a group with no such field, a contract (from, to), takes every party as a keyword and refuses entity=; it used to stage one duplicate row per entity of the type. add refuses a frame carrying a group's columns without its full key, which used to stage a half-keyed row. Likewise set on a group attribute without one of its key coordinates (set("efficiency", 0.9, entity=["dc"]), no bus=) is refused; it used to store a value no read reached.
  • A group may not share a dim's name, the entity-type group excepted: a group is carried as a column named for it. Rename a functional group for the relation, bus_country into country.
  • A Workspace holds the DuckDB connection and a Store one location; connect, layer_dir, DATARECORD_BASE_URI, Record.at and the process default connection are gone. A store's revisions live beside its layers as revisions/<id>.json, so a Revision serialises as its location and reads its ancestry back in a new process. ws.con is the calling thread's cursor, and a relation from another connection or thread is rejected at the write and edit boundary.
  • Writing is store.root(source), rev.child(source) and ws.write(source, uri); write_record, Revision.create and the source-less Revision.child() are gone. A WorkingRecord no longer commits: rev.child(w.edits) writes its edits as a child, ws.write(w, uri) the flattened record, and NewChild, Directory and commit are gone. A tree write writes its revision file last, so a failed write leaves no revision and never widens the manifest.
  • Tool.to_datarecord(model, con) and Tool.results(model, con) take the connection their frames are planned on, so PyPSA.results(n, w.con) sets straight onto w rather than failing on a relation from DuckDB's default connection; on_connection is gone.
  • Resolver.group_frame and Resolver.entity_type return an empty relation, rather than None, where every row written is tombstoned: telling the two apart ran the whole fold a second time on every read. None still means no layer wrote a row.
  • A schema declaring a dim, group, group coordinate, attribute or result whose name holds " or ., starts with _, or is a column datarecord writes itself (value, deleted, layer_uuid, ... ignoring case, and entity_type for an attribute), or that differs from another declared name only in case, is refused at load, naming each offender. Such a name used to collide silently: a dim named deleted read every label as a tombstone. A manifest declaring one no longer loads; rename it. Based on #26 by @FBumann.
  • The PyPSA tool stores per-port results on connections, like per-port inputs: p0, p1, p2, ... and a one-port type's p are one result p over the connection group, a row per (entity, bus) keeping each port's sign, and likewise q. Bus.p and Bus.q, the sum of those rows at a bus, are no longer written, and Link.p/Process.p are p_internal. A three-port Link's p2 is now a declared result.

  • The PyPSA tool stores a Process's rate0, rate1, rate2, ... as one input rate over the connection group, like efficiency, and build puts each row back in its port's column, static or per snapshot. rate declares no default, its ports defaulting to -1 and 1.

  • Removing an entity removes the group tuples naming it: WorkingRecord.remove tombstones every tuple with a field over entity naming it, in the same layer, and a value over a group goes with its tuple rather than with the entity. An add of the name revives the entity alone. A layer adding a tuple that names a dead label, or removing a label a tuple still names, is refused at write. A value over a dim or group outside partial naming a removed label is dropped at read, a removed bus label's per-bus values included. A materialised node caches the dead labels in resolved/dead/; one materialised before reads as having none.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • A store or standalone directory on s3://, through boto3 behind the datarecord[remote] extra and configured by the AWS environment alone. Revision files are written create-only and the manifest by compare-and-swap, so two writers widening one schema never silently lose a widening.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The PyPSA tool round-trips a network's snapshot and investment period weightings: to_datarecord writes them as snapshot_weighting_objective, _stores and _generators over snapshot and period_weighting_objective and _years over period, beside scenario_weight, and build sets them back rather than leaving PyPSA's defaults.
  • The PyPSA tool round-trips a multi-period network, which to_datarecord failed to write: its snapshot is one flat axis beside period, each snapshot carrying snapshot.period, a property into period, so period=2030 selects a period's snapshots. A snapshot is labelled by its timestep where no timestep repeats across periods, else by its position, the timestep then snapshot.timestep. Every input and result keeps the dims it has in a single-period network, whose schema is unchanged. build restores the snapshots, investment periods, time series and both weightings.
  • The PyPSA tool round-trips a network's shapes, which to_datarecord failed to write: a geometry is stored as WKT in inputs/geometry.parquet and the network's CRS as crs in the schema's meta, and build restores n.shapes as a GeoDataFrame in that CRS. srid is no longer written among the network attributes.
  • Removing an entity drops the values of every group row naming it, not only where it is the group's first entity coordinate: a contract over (from, to) loses its values when either party is removed, and flags(ctype) counts such a row towards the type of each party.
  • Writing a layer whose manifest.json write keeps losing, as it does with a credential that can write the manifest but not read it, gives up after ten attempts with an error naming s3:GetObject, rather than looping forever.
  • materialise() writes owner_map/inputs.parquet last, each file through a temporary name, so a node never reads as materialised from half its cache.
  • A fold cached before the manifest widened now reads under the wider schema.
  • Reading an attribute over a partial dim no longer slows with the square of that dim's length.
  • Folding the owner map no longer compares every row with every label of a partial dim's axis; the first read of a record with long series is linear again.
  • A record whose layers are all written scans its owner map once for the layers owning each attribute, rather than once per attribute read.
  • A pickled Revision unpickles through Workspace.process() and reads its ancestry back, rather than reading empty, and pickles after .record is read rather than failing on its DuckDB connection.
  • A standalone record's manifest.json carries an id that ws.write mints, and which keys its folds in the workspace in place of its URI. A record deleted and written again at one URI, or one relative path read from another working directory, no longer reads the folds of the record before it. ws.at resolves a local path as ws.store does, and refuses a manifest without an id: write such a record again.
  • ws.write to an existing empty directory raises its FileExistsError up front, saying a standalone record is written to a URI that does not exist yet, rather than passing the check and failing inside the write.
  • PyPSA.to_datarecord melts a time series whose component name holds a ", or is snapshot or period, rather than failing to parse or duplicating an id column: a name is no longer pasted into the UNPIVOT as an SQL identifier.
  • PyPSA.build keeps the time series of a component named snapshot, or period in a multi-period network, rather than dropping it from dynamic: the PIVOT is on each component's position, so no name becomes an SQL identifier there either.
  • PyPSA.to_datarecord accepts components whose names differ only by case, such as Gen and gen, rather than reporting them as one name: neither the melt nor the pivot folds case any more.
  • PyPSA.results and a network's outputs key exactly the results the PyPSA schema declares, so setting each one with kind="outputs" no longer raises KeyError: Bus.control and SubNetwork.carrier, which PyPSA also registers as inputs, are no longer emitted as results.
  • PyPSA.build turns a per-connection input back into PyPSA's port columns: efficiency on a Link's bus2 connection is efficiency2 again, static or per snapshot, rather than every port's value landing in efficiency and efficiency2 reading as its default.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contribution rules and conventions for datarecord. We welcome all contributors — a good place to start is the issues tagged "help wanted" and "good first issue".

By opening a pull request you represent that your contribution is your own original work and that you agree to license it under the project's MIT license.

docs.title: Reporting issues
docs.text:
Open a GitHub issue to report a bug or request a feature:

  • Report a bug — include a full traceback where there is one.
  • Request a feature.
  • Report a documentation problem.
  • Anything else.

docs.title: Development workflow
docs.text:
• Manage the environment with pixi and run every command inside it: pixi run <command> (e.g. pixi run pytest).
  • Run the test suite with pixi run test, and lint, format and type-check with pixi run lint before every commit — it runs the full lefthook hook set (ruff, prettier, taplo, typos, zizmor, reuse and mypy).
  • Lockfiles must stay consistent with package metadata: after any change to pixi.toml, run pixi lock.
  • The per-python environments (py311 … py314) mirror CI.

docs.title: Project conventions
docs.text:
• Branch off main for every change and open pull requests via the GitHub CLI (gh). A one-line commit message is fine for a small change; a larger one gets a summary line of at most 50 characters, a blank line, then a body describing what changed and why. Before opening a pull request, check you have updated CHANGELOG.md, added or updated documentation, and added tests for new functionality; give the pull request a clear summary of the change.
  • Write tests for new features and bug fixes under tests/ as test_*.py, reusing the shared fixtures in tests/fixtures.py and tests/conftest.py where useful. Run the tests after making changes and make sure they pass.
  • The design pages are the authoritative design. Cite them from a docstring's numpydoc Notes section rather than restating the argument — a comment that re-argues the design is a defect. When behaviour changes, update the page, not just the code. (Notes, not References: numpydoc discourages web links under References and expects entries there to augment a docstring rather than be required to understand it, which these are.)
  • Documentation is mkdocs: pixi run -e docs docs serves it locally, and pixi run -e docs docs-build is the strict build CI runs, which fails on a broken cross-reference. Every pull request publishes a rendered preview to https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/pr-<N>/, linked from a comment on the pull request itself; it is removed when the pull request closes, and a weekly job sweeps any that outlive it. Both live in .github/workflows/docs.yml.
  • No tool import may leak into core datarecord (module layout): everything framework-specific lives under datarecord/tools/ behind an optional extra.

docs.title: Design enhancement proposals
docs.text:
A change to the design starts as a design enhancement proposal (DEP): the argument for it, the design it lands, and usage examples.

  • Start from the template: copy it to docs/design/proposals/dep-NNNN-slug.md, where NNNN is the next free four-digit number, and append it to the end of the Enhancement proposals nav in mkdocs.yml. A number is never reused or reassigned.
  • Its header carries Status — Draft, Accepted, Implemented or Superseded, with the date — and Version, the release it ships in: Unreleased until the release that sets it.
  • Implementing it moves the design into the design pages and the usage examples into the usage pages, with as much of the argument as they need to stand on their own, and what it leaves open into open questions. The DEP stays as the record of the argument, and is not revised after: a change is a new DEP that replaces it.
  • Nothing outside the DEPs links to one — not a design or usage page, a docstring, a test or an error message — except open questions and the template. A DEP that is not yet implemented is not the design, and one that is has been superseded by the pages it landed in. pixi run lint fails on such a link.

docs.title: Architecture in one paragraph
docs.text: datarecord stores dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema: entities (named members of a type, unique record-wide), groups of them — a connection over (entity, bus) being the one every network has — attribute values over both, and the axes those values vary along. A record is defined by the RecordLike protocol — what it answers, not how it is stored — and a parquet directory is its on-disk form. The concrete Record folds a tree of layers resolved last-writer-wins, degenerating to a scan over a single directory (Record.at(uri)), so a consumer cannot tell how many layers it holds. Queries are built with narwhals and executed by duckdb, staying lazy until collected. Beyond those and pydantic, core depends on nothing. Keep new features consistent with this schema-declared, backend-agnostic, lazily-evaluated design.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
The version lives in [project].version in pyproject.toml; there is no VCS-derived versioning. CHANGELOG.md tracks user-facing changes under an [Unreleased] heading between releases.

To cut vX.Y.Z:

  1. Confirm pixi run test and pixi run -e docs docs-build pass — best done on a release pull request.
  2. Rename the [Unreleased] heading in CHANGELOG.md to vX.Y.Z with the release date, set version in pyproject.toml, and set Version to vX.Y.Z in every DEP header reading Unreleased.
  3. Merge the release pull request, then tag the merge commit vX.Y.Z and create the GitHub release from that tag.
  4. Open a follow-up adding a fresh [Unreleased] heading to CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: AI-assisted contributions
docs.text: If you use AI tools when contributing, please read AGENTS.md for how AI-generated content must be marked and what we expect you to write by hand.

docs.title: Installing a user environment
docs.text:
Hint

If it is your first time using Python, we recommend pixi, conda, or uv as easy-to-use package managers. They are available for Windows, macOS, and GNU/Linux. It is always helpful to use dedicated environments.

You can install datarecord via all common package managers:

pixiuvcondapip 
pixi add --pypi datarecord

uv add datarecord

conda create -n datarecord "python>=3.12" "pip"
conda activate datarecord
pip install datarecord

pip install datarecord

datarecord is written and tested to be compatible with Python 3.12 and above. We recommend to use the latest version with active support (see endoflife.date).

docs.title: Installing a development environment
docs.text:
The install instructions are slightly different to create a development environment compared to a user environment:

git clone https://github.com/energy-models/datarecord
cd datarecord

pixi run test    # the test suite
pixi run lint    # ruff, prettier, taplo, typos, zizmor, reuse, mypy

For more detailed instructions specific to developing the datarecord codebase, see the contributing guide.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
Workspace(database: str = ':memory:')

A DuckDB database and the files it reaches, shared by every store on it.

con is the calling thread's cursor: one workspace serves every thread, and their work shares one database - its tables, never its relations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default database str

DuckDB database, :memory: by default. What lives there is a workspace and never the record: deleting it loses at most uncommitted edits.

':memory:' Notes
  • the store
  • a cursor per thread
Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def __init__(self, database: str = ":memory:") -> None:
    self._db = duckdb.connect(database)
    self._db.execute(_REVISIONS)
    self._cursors = _Cursors(self._db)
    self._stores: dict[str, Store] = {}
    self._local = LocalFiles()
    self._remote: Files | None = None
    self._remote_lock = threading.Lock()

docs.title: con property
docs.text:
con: DuckDBPyConnection

The calling thread's cursor, made on its first use in that thread.

docs.title: process classmethod
docs.text:
process() -> Workspace

The process's workspace, created on first use on :memory:.

What a deserialised Revision attaches to, having no workspace passed; nothing else reaches it unless named.

Notes
  • crossing a process boundary
Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
@classmethod
def process(cls) -> Workspace:
    """The process's workspace, created on first use on `:memory:`.

    What a deserialised `Revision` attaches to, having no workspace passed;
    nothing else reaches it unless named.

    Notes
    -----
    - [crossing a process boundary](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/layers/#crossing-a-process-boundary)
    """
    global _process
    with _process_lock:
        if _process is None:
            _process = cls()
        return _process

docs.title: files
docs.text:
files(uri: str) -> Files

The Files for uri's scheme: local without ://, remote for s3://.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

For any other scheme.

Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def files(self, uri: str) -> Files:
    """The `Files` for `uri`'s scheme: local without `://`, remote for `s3://`.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For any other scheme.
    """
    if "://" not in uri:
        return self._local
    if not uri.startswith("s3://"):
        msg = f"{uri}: a location is a local path or an s3:// URI"
        raise ValueError(msg)
    with self._remote_lock:
        if self._remote is None:
            self._remote = self._connect_remote()
        return self._remote

docs.title: store
docs.text:
store(uri: str) -> Store

This workspace's store at uri, one object per normalised location.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

For an empty uri.

Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def store(self, uri: str) -> Store:
    """This workspace's store at `uri`, one object per normalised location.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        For an empty `uri`.
    """
    if not uri:
        msg = (
            "a store needs a location; an empty one would be the working directory"
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)
    location = _absolute(uri)
    self.files(location)
    return self._stores.setdefault(location, Store(location, self))

docs.title: at
docs.text:
at(uri: str) -> Record

The standalone record at uri, read under its own manifest.json.

A local uri is resolved, as store resolves one, so a later chdir cannot point it at another record.

Raises:

Type Description FileNotFoundError

If uri has no manifest: a directory without one is a tree layer, read under its store's schema through Store.layer.

ValueError

If the manifest carries no record id.

Notes
  • the record format
  • one schema per record
Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def at(self, uri: str) -> Record:
    """The standalone record at `uri`, read under its own `manifest.json`.

    A local `uri` is resolved, as `store` resolves one, so a later `chdir`
    cannot point it at another record.

    Raises
    ------
    FileNotFoundError
        If `uri` has no manifest: a directory without one is a tree layer,
        read under its store's schema through `Store.layer`.
    ValueError
        If the manifest carries no record id.

    Notes
    -----
    - [the record format](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/format/)
    - [one schema per record](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#one-schema-per-record)
    """
    base = _absolute(uri) + "/"
    found = self.files(base).read_text(base + "manifest.json")
    if found is None:
        msg = (
            f"{base} has no manifest.json; a layer of a tree is read through "
            f"its store's `layer(id)`"
        )
        raise FileNotFoundError(msg)
    id = json.loads(found[0]).get("id")
    if id is None:
        msg = (
            f"{base}manifest.json carries no record id; a standalone "
            f"record's id is minted by `Workspace.write`, so write it again "
            f"through that"
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)
    schema = Schema.model_validate_json(found[0])
    return _record(DirectorySource(base, schema, self, UUID(id)), workspace=self)

docs.title: write
docs.text:
write(source: LayerData | RecordLike, uri: str) -> Record

Write source as a standalone record at uri, and read it back.

A standalone record is written to a URI that does not exist yet. The directory carries its own manifest, written last, so one whose write failed reads as no record. The manifest carries a fresh id, so a record written again at uri is never read as the one before it.

Raises:

Type Description FileExistsError

If anything exists at uri: locally the path, even an empty directory; remotely any key under it.

Notes
  • writing a whole record
  • a standalone directory
Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def write(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike, uri: str) -> Record:
    """Write `source` as a standalone record at `uri`, and read it back.

    A standalone record is written to a URI that does not exist yet. The
    directory carries its own manifest, written last, so one whose write
    failed reads as no record. The manifest carries a fresh id, so a
    record written again at `uri` is never read as the one before it.

    Raises
    ------
    FileExistsError
        If anything exists at `uri`: locally the path, even an empty
        directory; remotely any key under it.

    Notes
    -----
    - [writing a whole record](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/writing/)
    - [a standalone directory](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/writing/#a-standalone-directory)
    """
    base = _absolute(uri) + "/"
    if self.files(base).exists(base):
        msg = (
            f"{base} already exists; a standalone record is written to a URI "
            f"that does not exist yet"
        )
        raise FileExistsError(msg)
    data = layer_data(source, self.con)
    write_layer(data, base, self, manifest=_manifest(data.schema, uuid4()))
    return self.at(base)

Look one revision up, reading its file and any parents not yet held.

Source code in src/datarecord/store.py 
def revision(self, id: UUID) -> Revision:
    """Look one revision up, reading its file and any parents not yet held.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If this store has no revision `id`.

    Notes
    -----
    - [the tree beside the layers](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/layers/#the-tree-beside-the-layers)
    """
    from datarecord.layered.revision import Revision

    row = self._held(id)
    if row is None:
        read = []
        next_id: UUID | None = id
        while next_id is not None and self._held(next_id) is None:
            found = self._read_revision(next_id)
            if found is None:
                msg = f"No revision {next_id} in {self.uri}"
                raise KeyError(msg)
            read.append(found)
            next_id = found[1]
        self._cache(read)
        row = read[0]
    return Revision(id=row[0], parent=row[1], store=self)

def revisions(self) -> list[Revision]:
    """Every revision in this store, unordered.

    One listing of `revisions/`, reading only the files the workspace does
    not already hold.

    Notes
    -----
    - [the tree beside the layers](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/layers/#the-tree-beside-the-layers)
    """
    from datarecord.layered.revision import Revision

    held = {
        row[0]
        for row in self.workspace.con.execute(
            "SELECT id FROM revisions WHERE location = ?", [self.uri]
        ).fetchall()
    }
    listed = {
        UUID(name.removesuffix(".json"))
        for name in self.files.list(f"{self.uri}/revisions/")
        if name.endswith(".json")
    }
    self._cache(
        [
            row
            for id in listed - held
            if (row := self._read_revision(id)) is not None
        ]
    )
    rows = self.workspace.con.execute(
        "SELECT id, parent FROM revisions WHERE location = ?", [self.uri]
    ).fetchall()
    return [Revision(id=id, parent=parent, store=self) for id, parent in rows]

def child(self, source: LayerData | RecordLike) -> Revision:
    """A new child of this revision, with `source` as its layer.

    Any node may be a parent: a layer is write-once, so a base cannot shift
    under its descendants. A `WorkingRecord`'s `edits` are a delta against
    the revision it was built over, so they are written only under that
    one; the `WorkingRecord` itself writes its whole resolved record.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If `source` is staged edits built over another revision, whose delta
        would read back wrong here.

    Notes
    -----
    - [a layer's data is write-once](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/layers/#a-layers-data-is-write-once)
    - [writing a whole record](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/writing/)
    - [edits](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#edits)
    """
    from datarecord.mutable import StagedSource

    if isinstance(source, StagedSource) and source.base != self.id:
        msg = (
            f"these edits were staged over revision {source.base}, so they "
            f"are a delta against it and not against {self.id}; write them "
            f"as a child of the revision the `WorkingRecord` was built over"
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)
    return self.store._write(source, self.id)

docs.title: WorkingRecord
docs.text:
WorkingRecord(base: RecordLike)

Bases: Record

A Record whose last source is a staging area, plus the edit surface.

A Record in the type as well as in the fold: what it reads is the data with its pending edits applied, and it reads it by being one layer deeper than its base rather than by overlaying anything of its own. Every read member is inherited unchanged - outputs alone is overridden, results not overlaying - so an edit reads back through the same code path a committed layer would.

Staged rows live in connection-scoped DuckDB tables, the only place a staged row exists: the reads fold them rather than holding a copy, so what is staged is asked of the reads themselves.

The Resolver is fixed at construction and the source list never changes; a set changes what the last source's tables hold, not which sources there are. That is what lets the inherited members stay correct - they cache a key set only where the fold is stable, which a staged source makes it not.

Notes
  • WorkingRecord
  • staging
  • reading with pending edits
Source code in src/datarecord/mutable.py 
def __init__(self, base: RecordLike) -> None:
    # `object.__setattr__` throughout: the base is a frozen dataclass, and
    # these are set before `super().__init__` because the `StagedSource`
    # below reads them off `self`.
    object.__setattr__(self, "_layer_id", uuid4())
    object.__setattr__(self, "_staged", {})
    base_cache = _base_resolver(base)
    object.__setattr__(self, "_base", base_cache)
    # This record *is* the fold one layer deeper, and that layer is the
    # staging area - so the field the base class holds is that fold, whose
    # last source is the staged layer, `edits`.
    super().__init__(base_cache.with_source(StagedSource(self, self._layer_id)))

Staged results, keyed by attribute - what a tool handed back.

Results reach a record through set(..., kind="outputs"), so a tool can solve against this record's pending inputs and attach what it computed without committing first. The base's results are not included: they were computed from inputs these edits may have changed, and results do not overlay, so what is staged is the whole answer.

Keeping them coherent with the inputs is the caller's business - editing an input after attaching results leaves results describing a record that no longer exists, and nothing here silently discards them.

docs.text:
set(
    attribute: str,
    value: Any,
    *,
    kind: Literal["inputs", "outputs"] = "inputs",
    **coords: Any,
) -> None

Stage values of one attribute.

Every coordinate is a keyword - entity=, snapshot=, a group's field such as bus= or a corridor's from= - since which exist is declared rather than fixed. A keyword holds one label, fixing that coordinate, or a list of labels the value is staged at each of. A coordinate no keyword names is NULL, which by the broadcast rule is every label of it.

value takes six forms:

  • a scalar, staged at every combination of the listed labels;
  • a sequence, aligned positionally to the one list keyword;
  • a mapping or a one-dimensional labelled series, keyed by labels of the series' index.name where that names a coordinate, else of the one coordinate no keyword names;
  • a long frame supplying its own keys, which keywords may complete with single labels;
  • a narwhals expression, a function of the current value: it reads the rows the keywords select before it stages, so two such calls compose.

An attribute's values are long rows, whatever its dims. A property - a category included - patches one column of existing axis rows: a mapping or series from label to value, a dim= keyword naming the labels, or a scalar for every label the axis has. A group's property takes a scalar, its fields as keywords selecting the tuples, none selecting every tuple.

A property is named subject.name - set("entity.carrier", ...) - and a plain name is an attribute or result.

A keyword naming no coordinate of attribute is a property of a dim it reaches - component="Generator", or a list of values - and selects the labels of that dim matching it on the record as staged, the keywords combining as an intersection; set writes one row per label, and stores nothing of the filter, so a label added later is not reached.

kind="outputs" stages into outputs/ instead of inputs/, which is how a tool hands results back. Results use the same long schema; they do not overlay, and their labels are not checked, a solve producing rows for labels it derived rather than read.

Raises:

Type Description KeyError

On an undeclared attribute, result or keyword, a partial dim's label the record does not resolve, a property's label no layer wrote, a value of a property into a dim naming no label of it, or a label whose categories do not carry attribute.

ValueError

On a property with kind="outputs" or an nw.Expr value, a keyword the attribute does not vary over, a sequence with no single list keyword to align to, keys whose coordinate is ambiguous, a value an Enum property does not list, or a property keyword whose dim the attribute does not reach through exactly one coordinate, or that is given beside that coordinate's own keyword.

Notes
  • outputs
  • the shape of an edit
  • set
  • a derived value
  • validation

def set(
    self,
    attribute: str,
    value: Any,
    *,
    kind: Literal["inputs", "outputs"] = "inputs",
    **coords: Any,
) -> None:
    """Stage values of one attribute.

    Every coordinate is a keyword - `entity=`, `snapshot=`, a group's field
    such as `bus=` or a corridor's `from=` - since which exist is declared
    rather than fixed. A keyword holds one label, fixing that coordinate, or
    a list of labels the value is staged at each of. A coordinate no keyword
    names is NULL, which by the broadcast rule is every label of it.

    `value` takes six forms:

    - a scalar, staged at every combination of the listed labels;
    - a sequence, aligned positionally to the one list keyword;
    - a mapping or a one-dimensional labelled series, keyed by labels of
      the series' `index.name` where that names a coordinate, else of the
      one coordinate no keyword names;
    - a long frame supplying its own keys, which keywords may complete with
      single labels;
    - a narwhals expression, a *function of the current value*: it reads the
      rows the keywords select before it stages, so two such calls compose.

    An attribute's values are long rows, whatever its `dims`. A property -
    a category included - patches one column of existing axis rows: a
    mapping or series from label to value, a `dim=` keyword naming the
    labels, or a scalar for every label the axis has. A group's property
    takes a scalar, its fields as keywords selecting the tuples, none
    selecting every tuple.

    A property is named `subject.name` - `set("entity.carrier", ...)` -
    and a plain name is an attribute or result.

    A keyword naming no coordinate of `attribute` is a property of a dim it
    reaches - `component="Generator"`, or a list of values - and selects
    the labels of that dim matching it on the record as staged, the
    keywords combining as an intersection; `set` writes one row per label,
    and stores nothing of the filter, so a label added later is not reached.

    `kind="outputs"` stages into `outputs/` instead of `inputs/`, which is
    how a tool hands results back. Results use the same long schema; they do
    not overlay, and their labels are not checked, a solve producing rows
    for labels it derived rather than read.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        On an undeclared attribute, result or keyword, a `partial` dim's
        label the record does not resolve, a property's label no layer
        wrote, a value of a property `into` a dim naming no label of it, or
        a label whose categories do not carry `attribute`.
    ValueError
        On a property with `kind="outputs"` or an `nw.Expr` value, a
        keyword the attribute does not vary over, a sequence with no
        single list keyword to align to, keys whose coordinate is
        ambiguous, a value an `Enum` property does not list, or a property
        keyword whose dim the attribute does not reach through exactly one
        coordinate, or that is given beside that coordinate's own keyword.

    Notes
    -----
    - [outputs](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/read-path/#outputs)
    - [the shape of an edit](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#the-shape-of-an-edit)
    - [set](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#set)
    - [a derived value](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#an-nwexpr-value-derived-from-the-current-one)
    - [validation](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#validation)
    """
    keyed = isinstance(value, Mapping) or _series_index(value) is not None
    if isinstance(self.schema.resolve(attribute), tuple):
        self._set_dotted(attribute, value, kind, coords)
        return
    coords = self._select(attribute, coords)
    listed = {c: list(v) for c, v in coords.items() if _is_labels(v)}

    if _is_frame(value) and not keyed:
        if listed:
            msg = (
                f"`set({attribute!r}, <frame>)` supplies its own keys, so "
                f"keywords {sorted(listed)} may give one label each, not a list"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)
        lazy = _incoming(value, self.con)
        self.schema.check_group_columns(
            self.schema.groups_of(attribute),
            lazy,
            carrier=f"`set({attribute!r}, <frame>)`",
        )
        if kind == "inputs":
            self._validate_frame(lazy, attribute, coords)
        else:
            self._validate_result(attribute, coords)
        self._stage_long(attribute, lazy, kind, coords)
        return

    if kind == "inputs":
        self._validate_input(attribute, coords)
    else:
        self._validate_result(attribute, coords)

    if isinstance(value, nw.Expr):
        self._stage_derived(attribute, value, kind, coords)
        return

    if keyed:
        key = self._key_coordinate(attribute, value, coords)
        keys, values = normalise_value(value)
        if kind == "inputs":
            self._require_labels(
                attribute,
                _flat_coordinates(self.schema, attribute)[key],
                cast("list[Any]", keys),
            )
        column: dict[str, Sequence[Any]] = {key: cast("list[Any]", keys)}
    elif _is_labels(value):
        if len(listed) != 1:
            msg = (
                f"`set({attribute!r}, <sequence>)` aligns to exactly one list "
                f"keyword, and was given {sorted(listed) or 'none'}"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)
        ((key, labels),) = listed.items()
        del listed[key]
        _, values = normalise_value(value, labels)
        column = {key: labels}
    else:
        values = [value]
        column = {}
    rel = self._values_relation(
        {**column, "value": values},
        {
            **{c: self._coordinate_type(attribute, c) for c in column},
            "value": None,
        },
    )
    for c, labels in listed.items():
        rel = rel.cross(
            self._values_relation(
                {c: labels}, {c: self._coordinate_type(attribute, c)}
            )
        )
    fixed = {c: v for c, v in coords.items() if not _is_labels(v)}
    self._insert_long(
        rel, self._ensure(kind, attribute), attribute, set(rel.columns), fixed
    )

def add(self, dim: str, labels: Sequence[Any], **columns: Any) -> None:
    """Stage labels of `dim`, each as one whole row of its axis file.

    `columns` are that file's other columns - `dim`'s properties and a
    nested dim's parent keys - each a scalar for every label or a sequence
    aligned to `labels`. A column
    no keyword names is NULL on these rows: `add` restates a label's row
    whole, replacing any this record staged for it, a `remove`'s tombstone
    included.

    Not a sequence of `set` calls: a label exists by virtue of its axis row,
    so adding one with no columns at all is an edit. An attribute's value,
    whatever its `dims`, goes through `set`, a group's row through
    `add_group`.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If the schema declares no `dim`, or on a value of a property `into`
        a dim naming no label of it.
    ValueError
        On an attribute, a column the axis file has no place for, a nested
        dim's missing parent key, a sequence of the wrong length, or a
        value an `Enum` property does not list.

    Notes
    -----
    - [add / remove](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#add-remove)
    - [where a value lives](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/format/#where-a-value-lives)
    """
    if dim not in self.schema.dimensions:
        msg = f"the schema declares no dim {dim!r}"
        raise KeyError(msg)
    call = f"add({dim!r}, ...)"
    table = self._ensure(f"{_AXIS_PREFIX}{dim}")
    self._reject_undeclared(call, table, [*columns])
    missing = [
        c for c in self.schema.axis_key(dim) if c != dim and c not in columns
    ]
    if missing:
        msg = (
            f"`{call}` gives no {missing}; {dim!r} is `within` them, so a "
            f"label names a point only with its parents' keys "
            f"(https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#within-an-axis-inside-an-axis)"
        )
        raise ValueError(msg)
    names = list(labels)
    data: dict[str, list[Any]] = {dim: names}
    for c, given in columns.items():
        data[c] = list(given) if _is_labels(given) else [given] * len(names)
        if len(data[c]) != len(names):
            msg = (
                f"`{call}` has {len(data[c])} {c!r} values for {len(names)} labels"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)
    self.schema.require_listed(dim, data, f"`{call}`")
    self._require_live(dim, data)

And one tombstone per tuple, of any group, with a field over dim naming one of labels, read from the record as it currently resolves: a group attribute's value goes with its tuple. Only for a dim keyed by its label alone, a nested dim's label naming no point without its parents, which a tuple does not carry.

def remove(self, dim: str, labels: Sequence[Any]) -> None:
    """Stage a tombstone per label of `dim`.

    Need not enumerate what it deletes: one axis row per label, and the fold
    drops every value keyed by the label where `dim` is `partial`. A nested
    dim's label is a tuple in `Schema.axis_key` order. No labels stage
    nothing.

    And one tombstone per tuple, of any group, with a field over `dim`
    naming one of `labels`, read from the record as it currently resolves:
    a group attribute's value goes with its tuple. Only for a dim keyed by
    its label alone, a nested dim's label naming no point without its
    parents, which a tuple does not carry.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        While a property `into` `dim` stores one of `labels`, the record
        as staged read.

    Notes
    -----
    - [add / remove](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/working-record/#add-remove)
    - [deletion](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/layers/#deletion)
    """
    if not labels:
        return
    key = self.schema.axis_key(dim)
    if len(key) == 1:
        self._require_unnamed(dim, labels)
    rows = [label if len(key) > 1 else (label,) for label in labels]
    rel = self._values_relation(
        {c: [row[i] for row in rows] for i, c in enumerate(key)},
        {c: self._column_type(c) for c in key},
    )
    self._insert(
        rel,
        self._ensure(f"{_AXIS_PREFIX}{dim}"),
        {"deleted": lit(True)},  # noqa: FBT003
        key=key,
    )
    if len(key) > 1:
        return
    groups = self.resolver.dims.groups
    for g in self.schema.group_columns:
        fields = [f for f, d in self.schema.groups[g].over.items() if d == dim]
        if not fields or g not in groups:
            continue
        naming = reduce(
            operator.or_,
            (
                fn.struct_extract(col(g), lit(f)).isin(*(lit(r[0]) for r in rows))
                for f in fields
            ),
        )
        self._insert_snapshot(
            groups[g].filter(naming).project(col(g)),
            self._ensure(g),
            {"deleted": lit(True)},  # noqa: FBT003
            key=(g,),
        )

def add_group(self, group: str, frame: Any) -> None:
    """Stage rows of one declared group from a frame keyed by its struct column.

    The frame carries the group as one struct column named for it, its
    `into` label and the group's properties as plain columns - the shape of
    `groups/<group>.parquet`. The one path every group is added
    through, a record's `connection` group included.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        On a missing group or `into` column, an attribute column, and as
        `Schema.check_group_columns` does.

    Notes
    -----
    - [groups](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#groups)
    """
    call = f"`add_group({group!r}, ...)`"
    lazy = _incoming(frame, self.con)
    columns = lazy.collect_schema()
    self.schema.check_group_columns([group], lazy, carrier=call)
    into = self.schema.groups[group].into
    for required in (group, *([into] if into else [])):
        if required not in columns:
            msg = f"{call} needs a {required!r} column"
            raise ValueError(msg)
    table = self._ensure(group)
    self._reject_undeclared(call, table, list(columns))
    self._insert(
        as_relation(lazy, self.con),
        table,
        {"deleted": lit(False)},  # noqa: FBT003
        key=(group,),
    )

def remove_group(self, group: str, keys: Sequence[tuple[Any, ...]]) -> None:
    """Stage a tombstone per tuple, each in `Schema.group_key` order.

    Each tuple is packed into the group's struct column. An `into` label is
    no part of a key: the tuple is removed, whatever label it carried.

    Notes
    -----
    - [groups](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#groups)
    """
    key = self.schema.group_key(group)
    over = self.schema.groups[group].over
    types = {c: self.schema.dimensions[d].dtype for c, d in over.items()}
    flat = self._values_relation(
        {c: [k[i] for k in keys] for i, c in enumerate(key)}, types
    )
    packed = _packed(self.schema, group, key, {}, DuckTypes(flat))
    self._insert(
        flat.project(packed.alias(group)),
        self._ensure(group),
        {"deleted": lit(True)},  # noqa: FBT003
        key=(group,),
    )

def check_group_columns(
    self,
    groups: Iterable[str],
    frame: nw.LazyFrame[Any],
    *,
    carrier: str,
) -> None:
    """Reject each of `groups` carried other than as one struct column of exactly its key, whole or NULL.

    A carrier without a group's column passes.

    Parameters
    ----------
    carrier
        What carries the columns, named in the message.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        On a key coordinate as a column of its own, a group column not a
        struct of exactly the key, naming the struct to pass instead, or a
        struct with some fields NULL and not all.

    Notes
    -----
    - [groups](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#groups)
    - [the broadcast rule](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/record/#the-broadcast-rule)
    """
    columns = frame.collect_schema()
    for group in groups:
        key = self.group_key(group)
        flat = [c for c in key if c in columns]
        dtype = columns.get(group)
        fields = (
            key
            if dtype is None
            else [f.name for f in dtype.fields]
            if isinstance(dtype, nw.Struct)
            else None
        )
        if flat or fields is None or set(fields) != set(key):
            carried = f"{flat} flat" if flat else f"{group!r} as {dtype}"
            msg = (
                f"{carrier} carries {carried}; pass {group!r} as one struct "
                f"column with a field per key coordinate, {list(key)} (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#groups)"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)
        if dtype is None:
            continue
        struct = nw.col(group)
        partly = ~struct.is_null() & nw.any_horizontal(
            *(struct.struct.field(c).is_null() for c in key), ignore_nulls=True
        )
        if not frame.filter(partly).head(1).collect().is_empty():
            msg = (
                f"{carrier} carries a {group!r} with some fields NULL; a "
                f"group value is a whole tuple, or NULL for every tuple (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/record/#the-broadcast-rule)"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)

            f"properties are {list(allowed)}"

def require_listed(
    self, subject: str, data: Mapping[str, Iterable[Any]], what: str
) -> None:
    """Refuse a value of an `Enum` property of `subject` its categories do not list.

    `data` maps names to values; a name that is no `Enum` property of
    `subject` is skipped, as is a NULL.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        Naming `what`, the property, the unlisted values and its categories.
    """
    specs = self.properties.get(subject, {})
    for name, values in data.items():
        dtype = specs[name].dtype if name in specs else None
        if not isinstance(dtype, nw.Enum):
            continue
        unknown = sorted(
            {str(v) for v in values if v is not None} - {*dtype.categories}
        )
        if unknown:
            msg = (
                f"{what} gives {name!r} values {unknown}, which are not "
                f"categories of {name!r}; it declares {list(dtype.categories)}"
            )
            raise ValueError(msg)

def default_for(self, name: str, **categories: str) -> Any:
    """The default of attribute, result or `subject.name` property `name` for a label of `categories`.

    `categories` are keyed by each categorizing property's own name. The
    first `default_by` key listing the label's category decides, else
    `default`; a category left out matches none.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        As `resolve` does.

    Notes
    -----
    - [AttributeSpec](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#attributespec)
    - [default_by](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#default_by-a-default-per-category)
    """
    resolved = self.resolve(name)
    spec = resolved[1] if isinstance(resolved, tuple) else resolved
    for key, by in spec.default_by.items():
        category = categories.get(key.partition(".")[2])
        if category in by:
            return by[category]
    return spec.default

def resolve(self, name: str) -> AttributeSpec | tuple[str, PropertySpec]:
    """What `name` addresses: an attribute or result, or a property as `subject.name`.

    Read off the name alone: a plain name is never a property.

    Returns
    -------
    AttributeSpec or tuple of str and PropertySpec
        The attribute's or result's spec, or a property's subject and spec.

    Raises
    ------
    KeyError
        If `name` addresses nothing; for a plain name some subject's
        property is called, naming each dotted form.

    Notes
    -----
    - [properties](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#properties)
    """
    subject, dot, prop = name.partition(".")
    if dot:
        spec = self.properties.get(subject, {}).get(prop)
        if spec is None:
            msg = f"the schema declares no property {name!r}"
            raise KeyError(msg)
        return subject, spec
    attribute = self.spec_for(name)
    if attribute is not None:
        return attribute
    dotted = sorted(
        f"`{s}.{name}`" for s, specs in self.properties.items() if name in specs
    )
    hint = f"; did you mean {' or '.join(dotted)}" if dotted else ""
    msg = f"the schema declares no attribute or result {name!r}{hint}"
    raise KeyError(msg)

def field_over(self, group: str, dim: str) -> str | None:
    """The one field of `group` over `dim`, if any.

    Raises

    ValueError

    fields = [f for f, d in self.groups[group].over.items() if d == dim]

            f"label of it decides what a tuple carries"
        )

def owned_per(self, attribute: str) -> frozenset[str]:
    """Which dims a layer owns `attribute` per.

    Derived rather than declared: `AttributeSpec.dims` says which axes the
    attribute may vary over, `partial_dims` the fold key (group columns
    plus the `partial` dims), and ownership is their intersection. A
    dim in `dims` but not the fold key - a non-`partial` value axis like
    `timestep` - is owned whole, so a patch to one of its values restates the
    attribute's entire extent along it (`_owned_whole`).

    Notes
    -----
    - [partial](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#partial-the-granularity-of-an-override)
    - [one fold for every axis](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/read-path/#one-fold-for-every-axis)
    """
    spec = self.attributes.get(attribute)
    if spec is None:
        return frozenset()
    return spec.dims & set(self.partial_dims)

The declared type for one column, or None if the schema declares none.

Covers the structural columns the format fixes, the declared dims and groups, the properties of subject - columns of its axis or group file, read first - and the owner map's two flag structs, whose fields follow the schema's dims. A narwhals dtype, translated to DuckDB (duck.DuckTypes) only where a caller builds a column of it.

No dim is structural: each is declared, and typed from that declaration. So an Enum property pins its vocabulary everywhere the column is built. An attribute is no column but a long row's value, typed by value_type.

A schema declaring no dims at all is "no manifest yet" rather than a record to fold, and DuckDB has no empty struct - so the flag columns are undeclared there, and a caller building an empty relation falls back to VARCHAR for a map that will never hold a row.

def column_type(
    self, column: str, subject: str | None = None
) -> nw.dtypes.DType | None:
    """The declared type for one column, or None if the schema declares none.

    Covers the structural columns the format fixes, the declared dims and
    groups, the properties of `subject` - columns of its axis or group
    file, read first - and the owner map's two flag structs, whose fields
    follow the schema's dims. A narwhals dtype, translated to DuckDB
    (`duck.DuckTypes`) only where a caller builds a column of it.

    No dim is structural: each is declared, and typed from that
    declaration. So an `Enum` property pins its vocabulary everywhere the
    column is built. An attribute is no column but a long row's value,
    typed by `value_type`.

    A schema declaring no dims at all is "no manifest yet" rather
    than a record to fold, and DuckDB has no empty struct - so the flag
    columns are undeclared there, and a caller building an empty relation
    falls back to `VARCHAR` for a map that will never hold a row.

    Notes
    -----
    - [one schema per record](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#one-schema-per-record)
    - [the owner map](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/read-path/#owner-map)
    """
    own = self.properties.get(subject or "", {})
    if column in own:
        return own[column].dtype
    if column in STRUCTURAL_TYPES:
        return STRUCTURAL_TYPES[column]
    if column in self.dimensions:
        return self.dimensions[column].dtype
    if column in self.groups:
        return self.group_type(column)
    if column in ("varies", "broadcast"):
        return flag_type(self.broadcast_dims) if self.broadcast_dims else None
    return None

def compatible_with(self, other: Schema) -> list[str]:
    """Why layers written under `other` would not read under `self`.

    Empty when the change is compatible: old layers stay readable and only
    `version` moves. The compatible changes are those where NULL already
    means what the new schema needs it to mean, so the broadcast rule absorbs
    them without touching a row.

    Returns
    -------
    list of str
        One reason per incompatibility, empty if there are none.

    Notes
    -----
    - [the broadcast rule](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/record/#the-broadcast-rule)
    - [versioning](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/schema/#versioning)
    """
    problems = []

    for dim, was in other.dimensions.items():
        now = self.dimensions.get(dim)
        if now is None:
            problems.append(f"dim {dim!r} removed")
            continue
        if now.dtype != was.dtype:
            problems.append(f"dim {dim!r} dtype {was.dtype} -> {now.dtype}")
        if now.within != was.within:
            problems.append(
                f"dim {dim!r} nesting changed; the axis key changes shape"
            )

    # Results version like inputs: a layer's `outputs/<attr>.parquet` is
    # unreadable for the same reasons its `inputs/` counterpart would be.
    for kind, mine, theirs in (
        ("attribute", self.attributes, other.attributes),
        ("result", self.results, other.results),
    ):
        for attr, was_spec in theirs.items():
            now_spec = mine.get(attr)
            if now_spec is None:
                problems.append(f"{kind} {attr!r} removed")
                continue
            if now_spec.dtype != was_spec.dtype:
                problems.append(
                    f"{kind} {attr!r} dtype {was_spec.dtype} -> {now_spec.dtype}"
                )
            narrowed = was_spec.dims - now_spec.dims
            if narrowed:
                problems.append(
                    f"{kind} {attr!r} no longer varies over {sorted(narrowed)}; "
                    f"rows setting those dims have no valid reading"
                )

    for dim, specs in other.properties.items():
        for name, was_prop in specs.items():
            now_prop = self.properties.get(dim, {}).get(name)
            if now_prop is None:
                problems.append(f"property {name!r} of {dim!r} removed")
            elif now_prop.dtype != was_prop.dtype:
                problems.append(
                    f"property {name!r} of {dim!r} dtype {was_prop.dtype} "
                    f"-> {now_prop.dtype}"
                )

    problems.extend(self._dropped_by_category(other))

    if other.partial is not None and self.partial is not None:
        lost = other.partial - self.partial
        if lost:
            problems.append(
                f"{sorted(lost)} no longer `partial`; a layer that patched one "
                f"value along such an axis is now a partial override of an axis "
                f"owned whole"
            )
    return problems

Categories the tool requires the record to define labels of, or, in a verify result, ones it has no counterpart for.

(key, dim) pairs the schema declares that this tool cannot honour; key is "input_key", the fold's unit of ownership. The record layer trusts every declared key, so this is a tool's verdict on the record it was handed, not a schema rejection.

(category, attribute) pairs whose stored shape this tool cannot represent, as opposed to a value it is missing - a piecewise-linear attribute where the tool takes a scalar.

Labels the framework scopes per category and two of its categories claim, where a record has one axis row per label.

A one-line summary, for an error message or a log line.

def describe(self) -> str:
    """A one-line summary, for an error message or a log line."""
    parts = []
    if self.dims:
        parts.append(f"dims {sorted(self.dims)}")
    if self.categories:
        parts.append(f"categories {sorted(self.categories)}")
    if self.attributes:
        parts.append(f"attributes {sorted(self.attributes)}")
    if self.unsupported_keys:
        unsupported = ", ".join(
            f"{dim} as {key}" for key, dim in sorted(self.unsupported_keys)
        )
        parts.append(f"unsupported keys ({unsupported})")
    if self.unsupported_values:
        parts.append(
            f"piecewise-linear attributes {sorted(self.unsupported_values)}"
        )
    if self.names:
        parts.append(
            f"labels claimed by more than one category "
            f"{sorted(self.names)} (https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/format/#entity-is-unique-across-types)"
        )
    if self.columns:
        parts.append(
            f"columns whose name is declared with another shape "
            f"{sorted(self.columns)}"
        )
    return ", ".join(parts) if parts else "nothing"

def resolve(self, record: RecordLike) -> DuckDBPyRelation:
    """This attribute's long relation, read through the `Record` interface.

    The record rather than the record, so a tool builds from any backing.

    Notes
    -----
    - [the Record protocol](https://energy-models.github.io/datarecord/design/record/)
    """
    rels = [to_relation(record.attributes[s]) for s in self.source]
    if self.compute is None:
        return rels[0]
    return self.compute(*rels)

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Status: Draft · Owner: Jonas Hörsch · Date: 2026-08-05

The authoritative design for datarecord. Usage is how to use the package; these pages are what it is and why it is that way. The docstrings in the source cite them by link rather than restating the argument — a comment that re-argues the design is a defect.

docs.title: What a data record is
docs.text:
Dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema.

A record holds entities (named labels, classified by their categories), groups of them — the connection group over (entity, bus) being the one every network has — attribute values over both, and the axes those values vary along. A schema declares what may exist; the data says what does.

A record exposes seven things:

record.schema                   what may exist: the axes, properties, attributes
record.dims                     the axes themselves, keyed by dim
record.properties               what describes each label, keyed by dim or group
record.groups                   which tuples exist, keyed by group
record.attributes               the values, keyed by attribute name
record.outputs                  results, keyed by attribute name
record.flags(**cats)            which axes an attribute actually uses

That is the Record protocol, and The Record protocol gives it precisely.

An entity's entity identifies it across every category: names are unique record-wide, not per type (entity is unique across types). That is why the values are keyed by attribute and not by type — an attribute row names an entity and nothing more, and an entity's type is a property the record knows about it rather than part of its address.

Record is the one class that answers all of this, and it is the narwhals interface over a fold across layers:

  • A tree of layers, each adding a partial record on top of its parent, resolved last-writer-wins. No single directory is the record; the answer is the fold across them. Revision.record gives one.
  • One parquet directory, via Workspace.at(uri) — folded over the single layer it is, which degenerates to a scan of it. Not a second implementation.
  • WorkingRecord — a Record whose last layer is a staging area, so pending edits read back before anything is written.

RecordLike is the protocol all of these satisfy, and so does a framework's own object — a PyPSA Network presenting itself as a record, without depending on this package at all.

A consumer cannot tell which it holds, so a framework reads a hundred-layer overlay through the same call it would use for a single directory.

Neither the concept nor this package names a modelling framework. A framework consumes a record, a workflow engine produces one, and neither needs to know how the other works. datarecord depends only on duckdb, narwhals and pydantic; its one optional dependency, datarecord[remote], adds boto3 for a location on S3 (files, local and remote).

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• In scope: the Record protocol (the definition) and WorkingRecord; the parquet format that stores it; the schema; overlay resolution and its owner map; the write path; why one directory needs no second implementation.
  • Out of scope: a non-DuckDB implementation (the protocol permits one, see the protocol names no engine, but only DuckDB-backed ones are provided); concurrent writers to one record; unmaterialised/meta layers.

docs.title: The record format
docs.text:
A record's on-disk form is a parquet directory: a write produces it, Workspace.at(uri) reads it, and a foreign tool can consume it knowing nothing about this package. A record that is never written has no directory, and answers the protocol all the same.

record/
├── manifest.json                   # the schema, and the record's id
├── dims/<dim>.parquet              # one axis table per declared dim: labels and properties
├── groups/<group>.parquet          # which tuples of the group exist, and their properties
├── inputs/<attr>.parquet           # one input attribute per file
└── outputs/<attr>.parquet          # one result attribute per file

Every file under dims/ and groups/ is named for what it holds, singular: dims/scenario.parquet for the scenario axis, as inputs/p_nom.parquet is for p_nom. A dim's file is its name and nothing else — no pluralisation, which would be English grammar applied to a declared identifier and would spell a dim named bus as buss.parquet.

docs.title: The entity axis
docs.text:
dims/entity.parquet is what an entity's identity is: which entities the layer names, what describes each, and which are tombstoned.

entity | <entity key dims> | deleted | <property> ...

It is an axis file like any other, with nothing about it particular to entity: a Record hands it over as dims["entity"], the writer writes it, and every other dims/<dim>.parquet has the same shape.

  • Membership. An entity exists because it has a row here.
  • Its tombstone. Deleting an entity is a deleted row here, and the fold reads its tombstones from the file it folds membership from: membership from one source and deletions from another would resolve a deletion the fold never saw.
  • Its properties, one column each — component, carrier, sign in PyPSA's schema — NULL on a row whose categories do not carry it.

One layout, categories or none. A record whose entities have categories and one whose entities have none differ by a column: there is no per-category member file. Per-type files existed because every type had a different column set; the schema now says which properties each category carries (properties_for), so a category's frame is a filter on its property and a projection to those columns — recoverable from one file, where per-category files would state each entity's category twice, once in a column and once in a filename. Parquet stores an all-NULL column chunk for almost nothing and DuckDB reads only what it projects. Only a per-category dtype would need per-category files, and a subject's property has one spec.

docs.title: Where a value lives
docs.text:
Decided by the section a name is declared in, not by how many coordinates address it. One name is one spec across attributes and results, each one file; a property's name is its subject's, a column of that subject's file alone, so bus.x and an attribute x are two places:

declared as lands in property of a dim dims/<dim>.parquet — a column of the axis file property of a group groups/<group>.parquet — a column of the group file attribute, any dims inputs/<attr>.parquet — long rows result, any dims outputs/<attr>.parquet — long rows

inputs/p_nom.parquet is entity | attribute | breakpoint | value, one row per entity, and widening p_nom over scenario adds a column to the same file — NULL in every row written before, which is what the broadcast rule needs to read them unchanged. A scenario weight over scenario alone is long rows too: an attribute with one coordinate is still data.

An axis or group file then carries only its key, its within keys, its tombstones and its subject's properties — no data. A framework's constant frame per category is the category's properties joined with the coordinate-only rows of its attributes; the tool builds it.

A group's rows are in groups/<group>.parquet, keyed by that group's tuple and carrying their own tombstones — groups/connection.parquet for the connection group over (entity, bus). The file is keyed by one struct column named for the group, connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role | deleted, role being a property of connection, exactly as dims/<dim>.parquet is keyed by the column named for the dim: the column an attribute row carries the group as is the one the group's own file is keyed by, so no read or write converts between two shapes. A record with no such file has no rows of that group.

One file per group, never split by category. A group's rows are keyed by its coordinates and component is not one of them: splitting put connection rows for a Link and a Line in different files despite identical keys, forcing a union on every read and privileging entity among the coordinates. A corridor between two buses has no type to split on at all, and a contract between two entities has two — one per coordinate, neither of them the row's — so the split never generalised beyond the case it was written for.

A functional group's into label is a plain column of the group's file beside the key, so groups/bus_country.parquet is bus_country STRUCT(bus, scenario) | country. A classification of one coordinate is a property into the dim instead, bus.country a column of dims/bus.parquet like any property. Either way into decides nothing about storage, so nothing in the layout branches on it.

docs.title: The long schema
docs.text:
Every inputs/ and outputs/ file carries its attribute's own coordinates, then the columns every row has:

<coordinate> ... | attribute | breakpoint | value

The coordinates are what the attribute's dims declare, groups first, with a group carried as one struct column named for it, a field per key coordinate — so inputs/efficiency.parquet over the connection group carries connection STRUCT(entity, bus), and inputs/p_max_pu.parquet over entity and snapshot carries entity | snapshot and no bus. The writer rejects a group column that is not a struct of exactly the group's key: DuckDB casts a struct by field name, so a missing field would turn NULL and an extra one be dropped, silently re-keying every row.

Per attribute rather than schema-wide. One attribute is one file, so one column set per file; a fixed prefix of entity | bus would put an all-NULL entity on a record-level weighting, claiming an entity the value has none of, and would privilege one group's spelling of bus over every other group's coordinates.

That the shapes differ costs nothing, because UNION ALL BY NAME supplies NULL for a column a file does not carry — which is also what lets a file written before a dim was declared still read back correctly (resolving a relation). The fold's key is uniform even though the files are not: it is partial_dims plus attribute, one fixed tuple over every attribute, and a coordinate an attribute does not carry reads as NULL there.

One attribute per file, so value carries that attribute's dtype. There is no category column: entity is unique across every category (below), so inputs/p_max_pu.parquet holds every type's p_max_pu keyed by entity alone, and a reader wanting one type's rows joins the entity axis.

docs.title: entity is unique across types
docs.text:
A label identifies one member of its dim across the whole record — an entity one entity, whatever its categories. A Generator and a Load both called north are a collision, not two entities; a bus north beside them is a label of another dim, and no collision.

That is what removes component from every attribute key. An inputs/ row addresses (entity, …, attribute), a group in place of entity where the attribute is over one, and the category it belongs to is recoverable but not part of the address. The alternative — carrying the category in the key — makes it an entity's identity in one place and a row's in another, and every join then has to agree about which.

The axis carries the categories. component is a column of dims/entity.parquet, carried on its resolved row, never of the attribute rows — so entity -> component is one read of one file, and a consumer wanting one type's p_max_pu joins the resolved attribute frame to the resolved entity axis on entity. That join is against a relation the read path already builds.

Two things follow, and they are the reason to want this. An attribute row is addressed the way an entity is, so set("p_nom", 150.0, entity="wind1") needs no category: the entity determines it (set). And the inputs key carries no category, so the fold's key is (*partial dims and groups, attribute) — one less column to compare NULL-safely in every join in the read path.

Structural, not checked. One axis row per label is the uniqueness: an entity's categories are columns of its one row, so there is no second table for a name to recur in, and add of a label already there restates its row (add / remove).

A modelling framework that scopes names per type must therefore reconcile before it writes. Its tool's verify is where that is reported, rather than something the record layer mangles a name to paper over: a record's entity is the framework's own name, and a record that renamed them would hand back entities a framework cannot find.

docs.title: Layered resolution
docs.text:
A Record resolves a tree of layers. Each node adds one layer; a node's data is its layer resolved over its ancestors', last-writer-wins.

class Revision(BaseModel):
    id: UUID
    parent: UUID | None  # None for a root
    store: Store  # serialised as its location

Each revision has one layer at <location>/layers/<id>/; the path derives from the UUID and its store rather than being stored. Caches derived from the ancestry rather than from layer data live in a resolved/ subdirectory of it, so the layer's own top level stays exactly what that layer wrote.
