Nodes form a tree: branching is several children sharing a parent, and they share the parent's layer and all further ancestry by pointing at it, not by duplication. Resolution order along a root→node path is ancestry order; a node's own layer is last and wins.

The node metadata — (id, parent) — is persisted beside the layers, one file per revision, so a revision id resolves to its ancestry, and thus its layer set, from the location alone.

Two of the protocol's columns take their meaning from the overlay key.

A group partial names is part of the inputs key, (*partial dims, attribute) — the connection column, NULL for an entity-level attribute and NULL-safe-compared so that case is unaffected. That is what makes a per-connection attribute owned per connection: without it, a patch changing one connection's efficiency owns — and so restates — every connection's, which is what a group outside partial costs. It is also why a connection is keyed by its bus rather than by position: a patch layer would otherwise have to know a connection's current index, so an ancestor inserting one earlier would silently redirect that patch to a different bus.

breakpoint (wide and long rows), by contrast, is deliberately not part of the overlay key. A layer owns a whole curve, the same rule a non-partial dim follows (partial), so a parent's breakpoints and a descendant's can never resolve into one curve with a hole.

docs.title: A layer's data is write-once
docs.text:
A node has no mutable state.

A layer's data is created by one act — store.root or rev.child, the latter also how a WorkingRecord's edits are written — which refuses an existing directory and stages into a sibling path, so a layer is complete when it first becomes visible and never changes afterwards; and its revision file, written last, is what makes it reachable at all. Editing needs no mutable layer: edits accumulate in the staging area and become a layer when written as a child.

The one thing written into a layer directory after that act is its resolved/ cache, which is why the invariant is stated over the layer's data rather than over the directory. That is not a loosening that costs anything: a cache is derived from immutable layers, so writing one cannot change an answer, and nothing downstream reads it as data.

Two properties follow. Any node may be a parent, since an immutable base cannot shift under its descendants. And a cache never needs invalidating, since one derived from immutable layers cannot go stale.

docs.title: Materialised node caches
docs.text:
A node's owner map and resolved dims may be materialised under layers/<id>/resolved/. Not the schema: there is one for the whole record, so there is nothing per node to resolve.

Where a materialised map exists, a read stops there: the map is already folded over everything above it, so a read walks the ancestry only back to the nearest materialised node rather than to the root. That truncation is what keeps a deep chain cheap. The same rule decides where resolved dims come from — a node's own resolved/dims/ where materialised, its raw dims/ otherwise — answered by the cache's presence rather than by any recorded state. The two are distinct paths within one directory, so a record read as an ancestor and the same record read as itself never alias.

Beside the resolved dims and groups, resolved/dead/<coord>.parquet holds the dead labels of each coordinate outside partial and each dim a group draws on, written only where there are any. A read above the node seeds its dead labels from these, the resolved relations themselves holding no tombstones.

Materialising is a policy: every N layers, at a branch point, on demand. It is purely additive, writing files under resolved/ and changing no answer, only how many layers a read touches to reach it.

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text:
A deleted = true row in dims/<dim>.parquet — the entity axis like any other — tombstones a label from every attribute, and from every value of every other dim — existence does not vary along one, so there is nothing to scope a deletion by. A deleted = true row in groups/<group>.parquet tombstones one row of that group — the row itself, and its inputs/ rows where the group is partial — leaving the labels it names and their other rows intact, so a connection is removed without touching the entity it attached.

A tombstone is honoured by the one fold that resolves every axis: the deepest statement of a key wins, and where it is a tombstone the key leaves the resolved relation (a deeper restatement reviving it). An attribute's orphaned rows stop surfacing the same way, for every key column: an attribute row is keyed by the partial dims and groups its dims name, and fold_inputs anti-joins the map against each one's deleted rows as it folds — so a key whose entity, connection tuple or dim coordinate was deleted is absent from the resolved map. A label of a dim or group outside partial is in no key, so its rows are dropped at read against that coordinate's dead labels instead. Each axis and group honours only its own tombstones, read from the same file it folds from, and nothing is inferred from a dead label a row refers to. So removing a label is written as a cascade, the same for every dim: remove(dim, labels) tombstones the labels and every live group tuple with a field over dim naming one, in one layer, and the tuples' values go with them. A layer adding a tuple, or storing a property into a dim, that names a dead label, or removing a label either still names, is refused by the writer, which folds the parent's axes and groups to tell; a property naming a label is cleared before the label goes, remove refusing it until then. A reference an ancestor left dangling fails no later write, the check being of what the layer does. A nested dim's labels are not checked, a reference carrying no parents to place them by. Re-adding the label does not revive its tuples. Re-adding a tuple outside partial revives its values, which are owned per attribute rather than per tuple. A tombstone only affects the branch that carries it; sibling branches keep the label.

The fold treats an absent deleted column as "tombstones nothing", so a layer may be any standard parquet directory, not only one this package wrote. Every derived cache lives under resolved/ for the same reason: every glob the read path issues into a layer is single-level — inputs/*.parquet, dims/*.parquet, groups/*.parquet — so nothing under resolved/ is reachable by one. A reader pointed at a layer directory therefore sees exactly what that layer wrote, and materialising a node's caches never changes what it sees.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
What a process holds is two objects' state. A Workspace holds the DuckDB database and the means to reach files, local or remote, which is all a standalone directory needs. A Store holds one store location — its manifest, its revision tree, its layers — and works through a workspace, which several stores share so that records from them join.

ws = Workspace()  # ":memory:" by default
store = ws.store("/data/a")  # one Store per normalised location
rev = store.revision(rid)  # look one up
record = ws.at("out/")  # a standalone directory, read under its own manifest
layer = store.layer(rid)  # one layer read alone, under the store's manifest

A call reaches the workspace explicitly only where nothing in hand carries one: ws.store, ws.at, and the con a tool converting a framework object is handed. Everything built from something takes it from that: a revision from its store, a Record from its Resolver, a WorkingRecord from its base record.

The location is required and absolute. ws.store("") raises, and a local path is resolved, so neither a later chdir nor a process with another cwd moves it — there is no default location left to fall back to. layer_dir, resolved_dir and the manifest's location derive from it and nothing else.

The location is authoritative, the database is disposable. What lives in a workspace's database is never the record: deleting it loses at most uncommitted edits. A file-backed one keeps staged edits across a crash, the revisions cache across runs, and gives DuckDB room to spill. A location is not reused: every cache keyed by id assumes what an id names never changes, which a fresh UUID over write-once files guarantees and a location wiped and written again does not.

docs.title: The tree beside the layers
docs.text:
<location>/
├── manifest.json
├── revisions/<id>.json        # {"id": ..., "parent": ...}
└── layers/<id>/

Beside layers/ rather than inside a layer, so a layer directory stays exactly what the layer wrote and listing the tree is one listing over small files. One file per revision because a file named by a fresh UUID is write-once like a layer, so two processes creating revisions in one location never write the same object; it is written create-only through files, so that is enforced rather than assumed.

The workspace's revisions table is a cache of those files for every store on it, keyed by (location, id). It cannot go stale, only incomplete, since a revision's parent never changes, so it is only ever added to: revisions() lists revisions/ once and reads only the files the table lacks, and revision(id) that misses reads the file and each parent not yet held, raising KeyError where the first is absent. Two cursors adding one row at once conflict, and the row is the same whoever wins, so the loser moves on.

docs.title: Files, local and remote
docs.text:
Tables go through DuckDB. Everything else — the manifest, the revision files, listing them — goes through the workspace's Files, picked by the URI's scheme: a URI without :// is local, and any scheme but s3:// raises.

class Files(Protocol):
    def read_text(self, uri: str) -> tuple[str, Version] | None: ...  # None on a miss
    def write_text(
        self, uri: str, text: str, *, expect: Version | Absent | None
    ) -> Version: ...
    def list(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]: ...  # names directly under prefix
    def exists(self, uri: str) -> bool: ...

expect is the precondition: Absent writes only if nothing is there, a Version only if the object is unchanged since it was read, None unconditionally. Locally every write lands under a temporary name and is moved into place, so a reader meets a whole file or none: Absent is a hard link, which the OS refuses over an existing file, and a Version — the content's SHA-256 — is checked and replaced while holding a lock on a sibling <name>.lock, which is what makes the check and the write one step.

Remotely, Files is on boto3, behind the optional extra datarecord[remote]. expect maps to put_object's conditional headers — IfNoneMatch="*" for Absent, IfMatch for a Version, which is the object's ETag — and a refused write (412, or 409 for a racing one) raises PreconditionFailedError. They guard the revision files, create-only by the server's guarantee, and the manifest's compare-and-swap; not the layer's parquet, which DuckDB's httpfs writes unconditionally under a fresh UUID. They hold only as far as the server honours them: SeaweedFS checks them atomically from 4.18, AWS S3 since November 2024.

The configuration is the AWS environment and config files, and nothing datarecord-specific. boto3 reads it itself; DuckDB gets CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, PROVIDER credential_chain), to which a set AWS_ENDPOINT_URL adds its ENDPOINT, URL_STYLE 'path', USE_SSL per its scheme and CHAIN 'env;config', since a self-hosted server has no bucket-subdomain DNS and no instance-metadata service to probe. Both are set up on the first s3:// URI a workspace is handed, so a purely local one never pays for either.

docs.title: Crossing a process boundary
docs.text:
Revision serialises its store as its location, {"id": …, "parent": …, "store": "/data/a"}, and validates back through Workspace.process().store(uri).revision(id), reading the revision file and each parent the process lacks — so ancestry() answers in a fresh process. Store pickles the same way.

That is the one default that survives, and nothing reaches it implicitly but deserialisation: Workspace.process() is created on first use, on :memory:, and code wanting its own records joinable with deserialised ones names it.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
The target, once the split below is done:

datarecord/                     # the standalone concept
├── schema.py                   # Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec, Schema
├── record.py                   # RecordLike, LayerData, Frames, LazyFrames, Flags
├── store.py                    # Workspace, Store
├── files.py                    # Files: manifests and revision files, local or remote
├── mutable.py                  # WorkingRecord, the edit path
├── layered/                    # Record and its resolution
│   ├── record.py               # Record, the narwhals face of a Resolver
│   ├── revision.py             # Revision, the node tree
│   ├── resolve.py              # owner-map fold
│   ├── categories.py           # which labels a NULL reaches on a categorized dim
│   ├── sources.py              # LayerSource: where a layer's files are
│   └── write.py                # the writer root, child and ws.write share
└── duck.py                     # relation helpers

Record lives beside its backing, the Resolver, rather than in the top-level record.py, which holds the vocabulary a record speaks — the protocols and the value types their members use. Its own module rather than resolve.py, so that file stays the DuckDB fold alone; the dependency runs one way, layered/record.py importing Resolver and nothing importing back. Where a connection and a location come from is store.py's, so duck.py holds no state.

"Depends on duckdb, narwhals and pydantic, and on nothing else" is achieved at this layer — datarecord/tools/ is where a framework-specific tool lives instead (below), and nothing under it is imported by the package's own __init__.py.

The protocols live with their implementations rather than with any one consumer, because there are several: a tool both implements and consumes RecordLike, WorkingRecord satisfies it, and the writer takes a LayerData — the write-side protocol a source and a resolver share — wrapping a RecordLike in an adapter where a tool hands one over instead.

A tool lives outside this core, under datarecord/tools/<name>.py — one module per modelling framework, imported explicitly (from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA) rather than through datarecord.tools itself, which imports none of them. What decides the side is one question: does it name a modelling framework? Nothing in datarecord's core may. The dependency runs strictly one way, so importing the record layer pulls in no framework, and importing one tool pulls in no other.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• May an entity's existence depend on a dim? Dimension.keys said yes — a generator present in scenario high and absent from low — and is now deleted, with nothing in its place. An entity exists or it does not.

What it cost to keep was a second question with no good answer: what an entity tombstone means for a connection keyed by fewer dims. Deleting an entity in one scenario removed a connection that was not scenario-scoped, even though the entity survived elsewhere, and no projection recovers the difference — the connection row has no scenario column to write it into. The conservative reading was implemented and pinned by an xfail.

What it cost to drop is narrower than it looks. A value may still vary along any axis; it is the thing that may not. A stochastic network with a different capital_cost per scenario is an attribute over {entity, scenario}, which the file split already places in inputs/. Only membership itself is unrepresentable.

Reopening it means deciding all three: whether it is needed at all, whether an entity table and a group may disagree about which dims scope them, and what the coarser one's rows mean if they may.

  • Whether partial should ever be per attribute. The schema puts it on the axis because it is true of every attribute varying over that axis. A counter-example would be an attribute whose series a consumer can accept in pieces while others cannot — none known, and permitting it would make the fold's key vary per attribute, which the fixed inputs key assumes it does not.

  • Whether a broadcast survives materialisation. A materialised ancestor's owner map stores a NULL row already expanded to the labels that existed then, and seeds a child's fold without re-expanding. So set("p_max_pu", 0.9) reaches a generator added — or re-categorized — in a child only while the ancestor is unmaterialised; plain NULLs behave the same. One level down, a WorkingRecord folds its committed prefix once, so a label staged or re-categorized there is not reached by a parent's NULL even while the parent is unmaterialised.

  • Whether staged results should be invalidated by a later input edit. Results attached through set(..., kind="outputs") were computed from the inputs pending at that moment, so editing an input afterwards leaves them describing a record that no longer exists. Dropping them on the next input edit was considered and rejected: it silently discards work the caller may have wanted, and a record that guesses which of the two the caller meant to keep is worse than one that keeps both and says so. Coherence is the caller's business, and writing edits writes whatever is staged. If this bites in practice, a pending-level warning is the cheap next step rather than a silent truncation.

  • Whether a WorkingRecord over an open record stages against a snapshot. Writing into an open record invalidates its owner-map cache. A mutable record would need the same invalidation per edit, or to stage against a snapshot taken at construction. The second is simpler and arguably more correct — an edit sequence should not see another writer's changes mid-flight — but it means a record can go stale.

  • Registering a record's relations as named views. A frontend issuing ad-hoc SQL needs names in a catalog rather than Python objects, which CREATE VIEW against a file-backed catalog provides — each view's definition being the resolved overlay, materialising nothing. Creating a view binds its schema, so registering N attributes costs N footer reads; and catalog reopen cost is linear in view count, which argues for one catalog per record rather than one shared.

  • What else a Record should answer about its labels without handing over a frame. flags sets the shape — cheap derived metadata a consumer plans against without opening a file — but answers only per attribute. entity -> component is now a column of the resolved axis, names being unique record-wide, so it is one frame rather than one per type; "which categories have live labels" and "how many labels a category has" are still frames to collect. What is open is the granularity: those are the same kind of question, and a protocol growing one method per question is worse than the frames it replaces. Whatever is chosen, it has to be answerable off the fold, which is where a record's membership already lives.

  • What a NULL group struct reaches when two of its fields are categorized. A NULL connection reaches the tuples whose entity field names a label carrying the attribute. A group with two fields over categorized dims — a contract between two entities — has no single label to ask, and its NULL reaches every tuple; requiring both, or either, would each be a reading the schema does not state.

  • Whether a property into a partial dim may categorize it. entity.carrier names labels of carrier, and a trait keyed on it would make a vocabulary that is data: a category a layer adds and removes rather than an Enum the schema declares.

  • Whether a default must name a live label. bus.carrier defaults to AC in PyPSA's schema, and a default is never stored, so nothing checks that AC is a label of carrier.

  • Whether a property into a nested dim should be checked. Its values name labels of a dim keyed by its parents too, which one column does not carry, so remove and the writer skip the live-label check for one, as they do for a group field over a nested dim; set and add check the label alone, under any parent.

  • Whether bus earns its place in the fold key. PyPSA's partial gains bus so a layer patches one bus's v_nom, and every partial coordinate is paid for by every read (keep it small). Measuring it on a pypsa-eur-sized record would settle it.

  • Whether a custom bus column can be a property. It is an attribute over bus today, so custom Bus.country beside custom Generator.country is one attribute over two dims and refused. Placing it as bus.country would dissolve the one remaining custom-column clash, but needs a rule telling a custom property from a custom attribute.

  • Whether selector keywords need a qualified form. A bare selector naming a property of two dims one attribute reaches is refused, with no way to say which is meant short of setting per dim.

  • What PyPSA#1474 lands as. Upstream making buses and carriers indices may turn an unlisted carrier into an error, or stop "" meaning none; the tool adds the one and stores the other as NULL today (tools).

docs.title: Settled
docs.text:
• Whether flags needs a record-level counterpart — it is one. flags() answers per record, every attribute included, and flags(**categories) per category, restricted to what those categories carry (properties). An attribute over an axis alone or a group outside partial is reachable through the first.

  • What a NULL group struct reaches across entity types — the tuples whose field over the categorized dim names a label carrying the attribute, as a NULL on the dim itself reaches its carrying labels (the owner map). A constant link efficiency no longer lands on generators' connections.

  • What a connection value staged without its bus should mean — nothing; the call is rejected. {entity: dc, bus: NULL} is no group value, a group value being a whole tuple or NULL, so it is refused wherever a row comes in. The alternative, "every connection of this entity", would broadcast over part of a tuple — a group column broadcasts only whole, a NULL struct meaning every tuple.

  • Whether within should subsume bus — no; groups do it. The recorded blocker was that bus inverts the rule NULL follows for a dim: a NULL declared dim means "all values" and the fold expands it against the axis, while a NULL bus is compared NULL-safely and never expanded. That premise did not survive. Expansion is governed by whether a coordinate is in the fold's key set, and a non-partial dim is never expanded either — so the behaviour that "makes a dim a dim" was never uniform, and bus was not an exception to it. A group states the rule instead of carrying an exception: a group coordinate addresses a sparse subset with no axis to expand against, which is the broadcast rule rather than a special case in it. Since a group is one struct column, a connection's bus is a field of connection rather than the dim's column, so the dim bus broadcasts like any other and the exception is gone from the dim entirely. Since a group is a dim it is gone from the group too: a NULL struct expands against the resolved group, as a NULL dim does against its axis.

docs.title: Owner map
docs.text:
The owner map answers, for a node, which layer owns each key. One map: inputs. It is the only relation whose winning key and winning row's values live in different files — an attribute's ownership spans every inputs/<attr>.parquet, so the map names the owning layer per key and a read then goes to that layer's file for the value. Every axis — a dim's coordinates, the entity axis among them, and a group — is a single keyed file whose winning row is the whole row, so none needs a map; each folds to a resolved relation read inline.

The inputs map's columns, keys first:

# inputs
<partial dims>          -- the fold key: exactly the partial dims and groups
  <owned_per coordinates> -- e.g. entity, scenario; a partial group as one STRUCT: connection STRUCT(entity, bus)
attribute
layer_uuid              -- the owning layer
varies      STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)   -- a field per broadcast dim and group
broadcast   STRUCT(<coordinate>: BOOLEAN, ...)
breakpoints BOOLEAN

It maps each key to the owning layer_uuid, with deletions already applied. It carries no value, no varying dim's value, and no breakpoint, so it stays small regardless of the series data or the size of a curve.

The inputs key is schema-derived, not spelled: it is partial_dims plus attribute. partial_dims is exactly the broadcast coordinates — dims and groups alike — a layer may patch per value (partial); no dim is in it by name, entity included. A coordinate an attribute's own file does not carry reads as NULL, which is what keeps the key one fixed tuple across attributes whose columns differ. A group is one column, so which columns name a connection is legible from the map itself, with no schema to say which belong together.

A group outside partial is not in the key, as a dim outside it is not: a layer touching one connection's value owns the attribute's whole extent along the group. An attribute over such a group and no other partial coordinate has the key (attribute) alone, the grain of a record-level weighting.

No category is on inputs: an attribute row is addressed by entity alone (entity is unique across types), and the resolved entity axis is what says which categories an entity has. That axis is what every category-scoped question goes through — per-category flags join it, as does a consumer wanting one type's frame — and it carries each categorizing property as a column, functionally determined by the label rather than keyed alongside it, so a re-categorized label is one row with a new value.

The map is built by folding along the root→node path: parent map minus deletions and overrides, union the layer's own keys. A node whose caches are materialised persists it (and the resolved axes beside it), so a read needs only the ancestry back to the nearest materialised node — the key scalability property. Every key column's tombstones reach this map in the fold: fold_inputs anti-joins the parent against the deleted rows of each partial dim and group — read from the same file that axis or group folds from — so a key whose entity, connection tuple or dim coordinate was deleted is absent from the resolved map rather than filtered at read. A group's tombstones are one NULL-safe anti-join on its struct column, the group file's own key — the same shape as a dim's. A layer's tombstones apply to its parents' keys, not to its own rows. A dim's anti-join matches its top-level column only. A label inside a struct is reached through its tuple: removing a label tombstones the live tuples naming it in the same layer, and each group honours its own tombstones. A row leaving a key column NULL is not addressed by it, and its NULL-safe anti-join never takes it; only a row naming a dead entity, tuple or label is dropped.

On a categorized dim a NULL reaches the labels carrying the attribute. Where the fold expands a NULL against the axis, an attribute some trait narrows on that dim joins a carriers relation — (label, attribute), built through attributes_for once per category combination the resolved axis holds — so set("p_max_pu", 0.9) reaches every generator and never a bus; a label with a NULL category carries none of the narrowed attributes. An attribute no trait narrows expands over every label, as before. A materialised ancestor's map is seeded already expanded, so its NULL rows do not reach labels a descendant adds or re-categorizes (open).

docs.title: One fold for every axis
docs.text:
A dim's coordinates, the entity axis, and a group are one construct: a keyed relation a layer patches per key — a group's key being its one struct column, as a dim's is the column named for it. They fold by one path — last-writer-wins per key, deleted honoured, its other columns carried on the winning row (component on the entity axis, role and into on a group) — producing one resolved relation with no deleted column and no layer_uuid.

The resolved relation is returned in first-introduced member order — root first, then file order within a layer — and a node's caches persist it in that order, so a reader recovers member order from the resolved file's own row number. There is no persisted order_key column: member order is the file's row order. A consumer wanting positional ports numbers an entity's connections by this order, so a patch layer adding a connection appends rather than renumbering — the positional-keying failure that order exists to prevent. Across a materialised parent it still holds: the resolved seed is read in its own row order and a descendant's new rows number after it.

Every property is a column of its subject's file, so the resolved axis or group is the whole of what a per-category read needs: properties[dim] filtered on categorizing columns and projected to properties_for, with no second file to gate against.

The fold runs live over an unmaterialised tail, cached in the workspace's database as shared tables; since layers are write-once, such a cache never needs invalidating.

The flags are folded in alongside the ownership group-by, so they cost nothing beyond it. They are computed per key, so per entity: whether this entity's p_max_pu sets timestep is a different question from whether any does.

The structs have a field per broadcast coordinate: every declared dim, entity included, and every group. A group broadcasts and has its field, as does a dim a group draws on, so a constant-over-buses marginal_price reports bus as broadcast.

Two structs rather than a varies_<dim> column per dim, because which dims exist is declared and a flat layout would make the map's column set depend on the schema. Versioning calls adding a dim compatible; that has to hold for a map already persisted at a materialised node, not only for the layers. With a struct the difference is a missing field, which UNION ALL BY NAME fills with NULL exactly as it would a missing column, and the new dim reads as unset — which it is, since no row mentions it. The map's columns are then fixed, and only the fields move.

breakpoints stays outside both structs, being no dim (wide and long rows). That also means the dim namespace lives entirely inside varies/broadcast, so a dim named breakpoints would collide with nothing.

Record.flags() unions them over the record, and flags(**categories) over the labels of those categories, restricted to what they carry — the granularity a consumer works at, where what the union means is argued.

docs.title: Resolving a relation
docs.text:
A resolved relation joins the owning layers' files to the inputs map, keeping only owned rows:

SELECT u.timestep,
       COALESCE(u.scenario, o.__owned_scenario) AS scenario,   -- one per owned_per coordinate, entity likewise
       u.attribute, u.breakpoint, u.value
FROM ( -- one arm per distinct layer the map names for this attribute
  SELECT ?::UUID AS layer_uuid, * FROM read_parquet(<layer>/inputs/<attr>.parquet)
  UNION ALL BY NAME
  ...
) u
JOIN ( -- the map keyed as its owning layer stored each key
  SELECT * EXCLUDE (scenario), scenario AS __owned_scenario,
         UNNEST(list_concat(
           CASE WHEN COALESCE(varies.scenario, false)   THEN [scenario] END,
           CASE WHEN COALESCE(broadcast.scenario, true) THEN [NULL] END
         )) AS scenario
  FROM inputs
) o
  ON o.attribute  = u.attribute
 AND o.layer_uuid = u.layer_uuid
 AND o.scenario   IS NOT DISTINCT FROM u.scenario  -- owned-per coordinates: as stored, NULL included

The projected coordinates are the attribute's own, not a fixed prefix: connection for a connection attribute, corridor for one over a corridor, entity for a per-entity one, none of them for a record-level weighting (the long schema). The join's arms follow from the same place — the key columns the attribute's file carries — so the query shape is derived from the schema rather than spelling entity and connection as literals, which is what lets a second group resolve through the identical code. A coordinate outside the key, timestep here or a group outside partial, is in no arm and passes straight through.

The map already names the winning layer per key, so resolution reads only the owning layers' files. There is no per-read MAX/group-by, and the only tombstone filter is for what the map cannot see — see below.

Each owned-per coordinate's arm is NULL-aware: a stored NULL means "all values", and the map may own it for only some of them, so the row joins every entry naming its layer and takes that value in the output. The arm cannot be the obvious condition: u.scenario IS NULL OR u.scenario IS NOT DISTINCT FROM o.scenario is no hash key, so DuckDB joins on the other columns and filters the dim afterwards, which costs the square of the dim's length per key. So the map is keyed the way its owning layer stored each key, which its flags record: a map row keeps its value where the layer's row set the dim (varies) and holds NULL where the row left it NULL (broadcast), with the owned value carried beside it. A layer row then finds its owned keys by its stored values, NULLs included, on NULL-safe equality — one hash join, scanning the layers and the map once each; the keyed map holds one row per owned key, two for a key its layer wrote both ways. A map row NULL in the dim itself, broadcast over an empty axis, has varies false, so only its NULL form exists and it matches once. A flag field missing from a map folded before the dim was declared counts as broadcast here, unlike in the flags a consumer reads: the layers' rows hold NULL there.

A partial group column like connection joins NULL-aware exactly as scenario does, broadcasting over the resolved group; DuckDB hash-joins IS NOT DISTINCT FROM on a STRUCT key directly. A dim the group draws on, bus beside it on a per-bus attribute, is a broadcast dim of its own and joins NULL-aware where it is partial.

breakpoint is projected but not joined on, being no part of the key: a curve is owned whole (wide and long rows), so every breakpoint of a key comes from the winning layer.

Non-key dims pass through unchanged, because within one key-dim combination the rows come from one layer.

An attribute no layer wrote is absent from the map; its relation is empty, and the consumer applies the schema's default.

docs.title: A label outside the key
docs.text: Every coordinate in the key is tombstone-pruned in the fold, so a row whose entity, partial connection tuple or partial dim label was deleted is already gone from the map. A dim or group outside partial is not in the key, so the fold cannot see its labels: with connection owned whole, a connection attribute's map row is (attribute) alone, and owns every tuple's value. The read drops those rows instead, anti-joining each such coordinate against its dead labels — those whose winning row in the fold is a tombstone, a group's being its dead tuples — so a removed tuple's values go whichever way the group is keyed. The fold keeps them beside the resolved axes and groups, and a materialised node caches them, since its resolved relations hold no tombstones and a read above it would otherwise not see a label removed below. The set is usually empty, and the join against it cheap.

docs.title: One record over one fold
docs.text:
There is one Record, and it is the narwhals interface over a Resolver. A plain parquet directory is not a second implementation of it: Workspace.at(uri) folds over a single DirectorySource, and over one source the fold degenerates to a scan of it — there is one layer, so every key is owned by it and the anti-join has nothing to evict.

So a directory takes the same properties as a tree node, rather than its own column of exceptions:

  • flags are computed in the ownership GROUP BY, one scan rather than the second one a separate aggregate would cost. They need a real aggregate either way: parquet's footer statistics are per row group, not per category, so a file mixing one type's series rows with another's constant says nothing about either.
  • Member order is order_key, which over one source is (0, file order) — file order, arrived at by the general rule.
  • schema.partial is the granularity of a patch, and one layer patches nothing, so it is inert rather than absent.

Being a node in a layer tree is not what the fold requires; being a layer layout is, and that is what a record directory is. A directory copied out of any tree, with no revision file, reads identically.

docs.title: A cursor per thread
docs.text:
A DuckDB connection is not safe to use from two threads at once. DuckDB's answer is a cursor per thread, so the workspace's con is the calling thread's cursor on its one database, made on first use in that thread by a threading.local subclass — which reruns its __init__ in each new thread, so there is no existence check and no lock, and a thread's cursor is dropped with the thread. A dict keyed by thread id would reuse ids; a ContextVar is copied into a task runner's workers, which would share the parent's cursor.

Tables are shared between cursors — the revisions cache, the staging tables, the folded caches. A DuckDBPyRelation is not: it is bound to the cursor that built it. So the line runs around relations alone:

  • Nothing but a relation holds a cursor. A store, a revision, a Resolver and a layer source hold their workspace and look up workspace.con per call, so every relation they build lands on the calling thread's cursor, and a Record is usable from any thread. What they cache besides is plain data any thread computes the same.
  • A relation, a narwhals frame over one, and a WorkingRecord belong to the thread that built them. One reaching another thread's write path is rejected as a relation from another connection is.

What a fold caches is shared, not held. The frozen prefix's folded axes and groups are tables, dims_<dim>_<id> and group_<name>_<id>, beside the owner_map_<kind>_<id> owner map; a last coords_<id> table lists them and is created after them, so a reader finding it finds them all. A dim or group name is hashed into the table name, being a caller's string. <id> is the node whose frozen layers were folded: a revision's id, the base's for a WorkingRecord, the id its manifest carries for a standalone directory. The schema is not in the key, so a fold made before the manifest widened is read as it is under the wider one. A compatible widening changes no column a table already has and only adds; the one addition a table can lack is the new dim's field in the flag structs, and each reader of a flag takes a missing field as unset, decided from the struct's type when the query is built rather than per row. Nor are they cast to the declared types as a materialised map is: each holds what the same fold would return uncached.

A fold one thread builds serves every thread. Two threads missing at once both fold and both create, and DuckDB fails the second with a write-write conflict rather than a name clash; the miss path catches that and reads the winner's table. The duplicate fold is wasted, not wrong.

docs.title: A relation from another connection is rejected
docs.text: Copying a relation onto the target connection would collect it on its own — a full materialisation the caller never asked for, which fails anyway if that connection has been closed. So as_relation, the boundary every frame handed to a write or an edit crosses, binds it to the target cursor first, which costs no read and fails for a relation from another connection or another thread's cursor, and re-raises that as a ValueError naming the fix: build the frame on record.con in this thread, or hand over a non-DuckDB frame to land.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: outputs/<attr>.parquet does not overlay. An output relation reads the node's own layer only: if that layer has no outputs/, the record has no results, and an ancestor's are not inherited.

docs.title: The Record protocol
docs.text:
The definition sketched in what a data record is, in full. This is the contract a consumer codes against; the record format is how it is stored. It is read-only: writing is store.root(source), rev.child(source) or ws.write(source, uri).

Two names, one shape. RecordLike is the protocol below — what a signature annotates against, and what a framework object satisfies structurally without depending on this package. Record is the class this package provides: the narwhals interface over one fold, which is what Revision.record and Workspace.at(uri) both give you. The concrete thing gets the short name because it is what a caller constructs and holds.

@runtime_checkable
class RecordLike(Protocol):
    """Dimensioned attribute data with a declared schema."""

    @property
    def schema(self) -> Schema: ...  # dims, properties, attributes, partial

    @property
    def dims(self) -> Frames: ...  # axis key columns, keyed by dim
    @property
    def properties(self) -> Frames: ...  # stored property values, keyed by subject
    @property
    def groups(self) -> Frames: ...  # each group's rows, keyed by group
    @property
    def attributes(self) -> Frames: ...  # long input frames, keyed by attribute

    @property
    def outputs(self) -> Frames: ...  # long result frames, keyed by attribute

    def flags(self, **categories: str | Sequence[str]) -> dict[str, Flags]: ...

Each accessor holds one section of the schema: dims the labels, properties the metadata of those labels, attributes the data. Where a value is read follows from what it is declared as, never from how many coordinates address it.

docs.title: LayerData
docs.text:
RecordLike is what a caller reads; the writer writes a different, narrower protocol — LayerData, "the rows of one thing, enumerated and read":

@runtime_checkable
class LayerData(Protocol):
    @property
    def schema(self) -> Schema: ...
    @property
    def frozen(self) -> bool: ...

    def axes(self) -> Iterable[str]: ...
    def axis(self, dim: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...
    def groups(self) -> Iterable[str]: ...
    def group(self, name: str) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...
    def attributes(self, kind: Kind = "inputs") -> Iterable[str]: ...
    def attribute(
        self, name: str, kind: Kind = "inputs"
    ) -> DuckDBPyRelation | None: ...

Each pair is an enumerator — the keys of that kind — and a read for one key. The enumerators return Iterable[str] rather than set[str] so a Resolver, whose keys carry a stable order a Record over it relies on, can return a list where a source returns a set; the meaning is the same set of keys either way.

An axis is the rows of its file: the labels, their within keys, their tombstones and the dim's properties. A group is its tuples, its into label and the group's properties.

One object, two meanings: a LayerSource answers axis/group/attribute for its own layer's rows; a Resolver answers the same names for everything folded into it. The writer cannot tell which it holds and does not need to — a staged layer's own rows (w.edits) and a resolved whole record are both a LayerData, so a WorkingRecord hands over either without a third shape adapting one to the other.

schema governs which of the other pairs are populated, rather than standing beside them as a peer: groups/group answer only for the groups it declares. An enumerator answers the empty set, never a phantom key, where the schema declares nothing of that kind.

Rows are raw DuckDBPyRelations, not narwhals frames — the write path stays one engine throughout. A framework object satisfying RecordLike instead (narwhals Frames, as Tool.to_datarecord returns) is not itself a LayerData; the writer wraps it in a thin adapter that reads its Frames mappings through the same enumerate-and-read pairs, so a tool stays narwhals-facing without the writer growing a second code path.

docs.title: Wide and long rows
docs.text:
schema is the declaration: which axes exist, which properties describe their labels, which attributes each label may carry, and over which axes each may vary. The rest is data, and comes in two shapes.

dims, properties and groups are wide — one row per label or tuple:

dims["entity"]                     entity                              key columns only
properties["entity"]               entity | component | carrier | ... stored values
groups["connection"]               connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role | ...

dims[dim] is the axis's key — the label and its within parents — in axis order, and nothing else. Properties and categories are covered below.

groups is keyed by the group alone, one frame each: groups/connection.parquet holds every attachment whatever the categories of its entities (where the rows live). A group's own frame is keyed by the one struct column named for it, as an axis's is by the column named for the dim, its into label and its properties beside it.

attributes and outputs are long — one row per value, keyed by the attribute's name:

attributes["p_nom"]        entity | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes["p_max_pu"]     entity | <one column per coordinate> | attribute | breakpoint | value
attributes["efficiency"]   connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | <...> | attribute | breakpoint | value

attributes holds every attribute, whatever its dims: p_nom over entity alone is long rows like p_max_pu, so widening it over scenario adds a column to the same frame rather than moving it. A row names what the value belongs to, the coordinate it sits at, and the value there.

The columns are the attribute's own, not a fixed set every file carries: an attribute's coordinates are what its dims declare, with a group carried as one struct column named for it. So efficiency over the connection group carries connection, flow over a corridor carries corridor, and objective_weighting over snapshot alone carries no entity column at all — an all-NULL entity would be a column claiming an entity the value has none of. A consumer wanting a group's coordinates flat takes nw.col("connection").struct.field("bus"), or unnests; a numpy-backed pandas frame has no struct dtype, so a pandas consumer unnests on the DuckDB side first. union_by_name is what lets the fold union files of differing shape, supplying NULL for a coordinate a given file does not carry.

No property is a column of an attribute row: attributes["p_max_pu"] holds every entity's p_max_pu together, whatever its category, since an entity identifies one label on its own. A consumer wanting one category's rows joins properties["entity"], filtered on the category, on entity.

breakpoint is NULL for the ordinary case. It carries the abscissa of a piecewise-linear value: a curve is one row per breakpoint, value the ordinate at each. Convexity is never checked or recorded — that is a framework's judgement.

properties and attributes answer stored values only; no default is applied, so a NULL property is one no layer wrote, and a coordinate no row covers is absent. A default, a property's or an attribute's, is the consumer's to apply, through Schema.default_for.

docs.title: Properties and categories
docs.text:
A property is one value per label of its subject — a dim or a group — and is stored as a column of that subject's file.

properties[subject] is the subject's key with every property declared for it, as stored: a record-wide view, NULL wherever no layer wrote a value. It is keyed by each subject declaring properties, and its columns are the properties' plain names — the frame already names the subject.

An Enum property of a dim in partial categorizes that dim. One category's labels are properties[dim] filtered on it; which properties they carry is Schema.properties_for, and a property's default — default_by per category, else default — is Schema.default_for. A framework's static frame, PyPSA's n.generators, is that frame, defaulted, joined with the entity-only rows of its attributes. A per-category read applying the defaults itself is deferred until a caller needs it.

Which properties and attributes a label carries is decided by its categories at read time, against the traits. A label whose category changes keeps what it held for attributes it no longer carries — attributes shows what was written — but those values fall outside every per-category read and every broadcast.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Some attributes belong not to an entity but to one of its connections to a bus.

A connection is one row of the connection group — Group(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}) — rather than a structural category of its own. groups["connection"] lists the attachments themselves, one row per (entity, bus), whatever their entities' categories; role — which end of the entity it is — describes the connection and identifies nothing, so it is a property a tool declares on the group (PyPSA does) rather than a column the format fixes.

A connection is identified by the bus it attaches to, never by position. An attribute is a connection attribute because its dims name the group, so a per-connection value is otherwise an ordinary long row: efficiency may vary by timestep and scenario like any other attribute, and decodes by the same rules with no special case.

A connection attribute is keyed by the connection, not the entity. Its row carries no top-level entity; the entity's tombstone reaches it by the entity inside the struct, in the fold where the group is partial and at read where it is not. Removing an entity also tombstones its connections, so their values go with them.

A record declaring no such group has no connections, and one declaring it with no rows answers groups["connection"] empty. Nothing about the mechanism is particular to buses — corridor over (from, to) is the same machinery, which is why bus is a field name here rather than a word the read path knows.

docs.title: The broadcast rule
docs.text:
A row's value applies to every combination of its NULL dim columns, enumerated from the axis frames in dims. A NULL dim means "all values of that dim", not that the attribute lacks the axis: a constant p_max_pu is one row with timestep = NULL, a varying one is a row per timestep.

Every declared dim broadcasts, entity included, and the dims a group draws on too: a connection's bus is a field of the connection column, not the dim bus, so a per-bus marginal_price with bus = NULL holds one value for every bus.

On a categorized dim, "every" is narrowed by the schema. A NULL reaches only the labels whose categories carry the attribute, judged at read time: set("p_max_pu", 0.9) is one row with entity = NULL, reaching every generator — one added in a later layer included — and never a load. A label with a NULL category carries only what no trait narrows.

A group's column broadcasts too, its axis the resolved group: a NULL connection means every connection, expanded against groups/connection.parquet as a NULL timestep is against dims/timestep.parquet. A group value is therefore a whole tuple or NULL. A struct with some fields NULL, {entity: dc, bus: NULL}, names a tuple no group row matches, so it is refused wherever a row comes in rather than stored.

Rows never overlap, so at most one covers any coordinate. A coordinate no row covers — including an attribute with no rows at all — takes that attribute's default from the schema: its default_by entry for the label's category where one lists it, else default.

Broadcast form is preserved: a value held once is answered once, so a consumer can reconstruct the constant-versus-varying split from the shape it gets back.

docs.title: Axis order
docs.text:
An axis's order is the row order of its frame in dims.

Labels and a group's rows are in the order they were first introduced across layers (the owner map). Order is never a stored column: a file's row order is the input, and the fold derives first-introduced order from it.

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Frames = Mapping[str, nw.LazyFrame]

narwhals is the boundary type because it is a protocol over dataframes rather than a dataframe: a record may hand back a DuckDB relation, a polars plan or a pandas frame and the consumer's code is the same.

LazyFrames is the lazily-building implementation, used where constructing a frame is itself I/O: read_parquet reads the parquet footer to bind the schema, so it opens the file. Locally that is a page-cache hit; against a remote record it is a round trip per attribute, so a consumer wanting three of forty attributes pays three rather than forty, and listing the keys pays none.

Laziness here saves I/O, not memory: an unmaterialised relation is a query plan, so holding every attribute's frame at once costs little. The expense is collect, which is the consumer's call either way.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Which axes an attribute's rows actually use — so a consumer can plan its reads without opening a file.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Flags:
    varies: frozenset[str]  # dims some row of this attribute sets
    broadcast: frozenset[str]  # dims some row leaves NULL, i.e. "all values"
    breakpoints: bool  # any row carries a breakpoint

flags() answers for the whole record in one query, keyed by attribute. Only attributes with rows are present, so set(record.flags()) also answers which attributes the record has at all.

flags(**categories) answers for one category: the keywords are categorizing properties of one dim by their plain names, component="Generator" rather than the subject.name a schema addresses one by, each one category or a list (categories). Only rows reaching a matching label count — on the dim's own column, or through a group's single field over it — and only attributes those labels carry are present. Keywords categorizing several dims, or a group reaching the dim through two fields, are refused: there is no one label a row would count towards.

The sets name dims, so a consumer asks about a named axis: "timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].varies. breakpoints is a boolean rather than a set because a breakpoint is not a dim (wide and long rows) — it is an abscissa within one row's value, not an axis the value is indexed by.

The two sets are not complements. An attribute may have per-timestep rows for one entity and a single NULL-timestep row for another, so timestep lands in both. That is an instruction to use both containers: timestep in broadcast selects the NULL-timestep rows into a constant frame, timestep in varies selects the rest into a series frame. Per label they would be complements; the aggregation over many labels is what makes the pair carry information. That is also why a framework asks per category: a Generator's per-timestep rows and a Link's single row, unioned, describe neither.

varies | broadcast is the test for whether an attribute touches a dim at all. Both sets empty for a dim means the attribute has no values along it, so the consumer builds no container there.

Both sets are scoped to what the attribute is addressed by. A dim outside its dims is in neither, never in broadcast. The two are easy to conflate because whatever the flags are aggregated from — the owner map, a scan of inputs/, a staging table — is one relation over every attribute, so a dim one attribute uses reads NULL for the rows of one that does not; but that NULL means "no such axis", not "every value of it". Reporting it as broadcast would answer the question above wrongly for every attribute in the record: a consumer would build a constant container along an axis the attribute has no values on.

entity is a dim like the others here: p_nom set per entity reports entity in varies, and a single entity = NULL row puts it in broadcast. An attribute with no rows at all is absent from the mapping entirely.

flags says nothing about properties, which are columns of their subject's file and read from properties.

docs.title: The protocol names no engine
docs.text:
The protocol names no engine — nw.LazyFrame is all a consumer sees, so a pure-Python, polars or Ibis-backed record would satisfy it without change.

The implementations provided are DuckDB-backed, both of them, and the resolution engine is not abstracted behind an interface. The owner-map fold is relational algebra of real complexity, and an engine abstraction with one implementation behind it is a cost paid for a second that does not exist. Adding one later means writing a second Record, which the protocol already permits.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
One schema per record, and manifest.json is how it is written down — the two words name the same thing, the file and the object.

class Dimension(BaseModel):
    """One axis attribute data may vary over."""

    dtype: str  # the axis labels' type
    within: frozenset[str] = frozenset()  # labels unique only within these dims
    unit: str | None = None  # what the labels measure, if anything
    description: str | None = None  # what the axis is, in prose


class AttributeSpec(BaseModel):
    """What shape one attribute's data may take."""

    dtype: str  # value column type
    dims: frozenset[str] = frozenset()  # what addresses it: dims and groups
    default: Any | None = None
    default_by: dict[
        str, dict[str, Any]
    ] = {}  # categorizing property, as subject.name -> category -> default
    breakpoints: bool = False  # may carry a piecewise-linear curve
    unit: str | None = None  # what the values measure
    description: str | None = None  # what the attribute is, in prose


class PropertySpec(BaseModel):
    """One value per label of its subject, describing the label."""

    dtype: str | None = None  # the `into` dim's where omitted
    into: str | None = None  # a dim whose labels its values are
    default: Any | None = None
    default_by: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    unit: str | None = None
    description: str | None = None


class Group(BaseModel):
    """Which tuples over several dims exist: a sparse subset of a dim product."""

    over: dict[str, str]  # coordinate name -> the dim it draws labels from
    into: str | None = None  # each `over` tuple carries exactly one label of it
    description: str | None = None


class Trait(BaseModel):
    """A bundle of attributes, and which categories and labels carry it."""

    attributes: frozenset[str] = frozenset()
    on: dict[str, frozenset[str]] = {}  # one categorizing subject.name -> categories
    switch: str | None = None  # attribute deciding it per label; joins `attributes`
    description: str | None = None


class Schema(BaseModel):
    version: int  # bumped by any change to the declarations

    dimensions: dict[str, Dimension]
    attributes: dict[str, AttributeSpec]  # flat: one attribute, one spec
    results: dict[str, AttributeSpec]  # what a solve computes, governed apart
    properties: dict[
        str, dict[str, PropertySpec]
    ]  # subject dim or group -> name -> spec
    groups: dict[str, Group]
    traits: dict[str, Trait]  # the only thing that narrows a name to some categories

    # Which dims a layer may patch value by value; absent for a record with no
    # layers, since nothing overrides anything.
    partial: frozenset[str] | None = None

    meta: dict[str, Any] = {}  # opaque; the package never interprets it

partial is the only layering-specific part, and so the only optional one. Everything else describes the data and is always present.

attribute is VARCHAR, and no dim or property name means anything to this package: those vocabularies belong to a modelling framework, and this package knows none. A category is typed as the schema declares it, which is a record's own statement rather than a framework's — so a category the schema declares but no tool recognises reads back fine and is reported by the tool that cannot build it, not rejected inside the fold.

meta is where a framework's own top-level data goes — network attributes, coordinate reference system, free-form metadata. It is stored and never interpreted, since none of it describes the dimensioned data.

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.text:
Every dim is declared: a record with region, technology or vintage needs no code change, and dtype is the axis's own property.

A Dimension declares the axis's shape — its type and its nesting. It does not declare which dims an attribute varies over (that is per attribute), nor the patch granularity, nor order, nor what describes or classifies its labels — its properties say that, and a group into it from the relation's side.

docs.title: AttributeSpec
docs.text:
What one attribute may do over those axes:

attributes = {
    # a capacity to build: one decision, evaluated against every scenario
    "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="float64", dims={"entity"}),
    # an availability profile: varies over time, and per scenario
    "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(dtype="float64", dims={"entity", "scenario", "timestep"}),
    "marginal_cost": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="float64", dims={"entity", "scenario"}, breakpoints=True
    ),
    # addressed by a group rather than by the entity axis
    "efficiency": AttributeSpec(dtype="float64", dims={"connection", "timestep"}),
    # addressed by an axis alone: a weighting belongs to no entity
    "objective_weighting": AttributeSpec(dtype="float64", dims={"snapshot"}),
}

Flat, one spec per attribute, with categories subscribing rather than owning. The nesting this replaces said an attribute belongs to an entity type, which is false in both directions: objective_weighting has no type, and p_max_pu was three identical specs under Generator, Link and StorageUnit.

The storage already disagreed with the nesting. inputs/p_max_pu.parquet holds every type's rows in one file with one value dtype, so two types declaring one attribute with different dtypes was expressible in the schema and unrepresentable on disk — a silent wrong read that nothing rejected. Flat declaration makes it unrepresentable instead, which is the stronger form of the same guarantee: one attribute, one spec, one file, one dtype.

dims is the only addressing mechanism, and it names dims and groups alike, resolved by one rule: a name is the dim of that name if one is declared, and otherwise the group of that name, carried as one column. Whether a coordinate is the entity axis, a group or a plain axis changes where the labels come from, not how the attribute is declared or stored. There is no bus field: an attribute is a connection attribute because its dims name the connection group, which is what lets a second group exist without a second field.

dims is also what makes a scenario-varying p_nom a schema violation: a capacity is a first-stage decision, one value taken before the scenario is known, which is the point of stochastic scenarios differing only in dispatch.

dims says only which coordinates address a value, not what kind of value it is: p_nom over entity alone is data an optimiser decides, where carrier describes the entity — so carrier is a property, and dims may name one coordinate without making an attribute one.

breakpoints answers what a bare column set cannot: whether it may carry a piecewise-linear curve, so a curve on an attribute that takes one value is rejected on write rather than reported unbuildable later (wide and long rows).

Every attribute is long rows in inputs/<attr>.parquet, whatever its dims — where a value lives is decided by the section a name is declared in, not by how many coordinates address it, so widening dims adds a column to the same file rather than moving it.

default_by is a default per category, beside default (below).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
results is a second mapping of AttributeSpec, keyed and shaped exactly like attributes. What a solve computes is declared, not discovered: a result has a dtype, coordinates and a description like any other attribute, and reading one back needs its dtype as much as an input does — a string-valued result cast as a number is lost to TRY_CAST with nothing raised.

It is a separate mapping rather than a flag because the two are governed differently at every point a caller touches them. A result is written to outputs/<attr>.parquet, never overlays a parent's, and may name an entity the record does not declare. An input meets attributes_for, which is the per-category vocabulary that validates a set; a result meets none of that, and keeping it out of attributes is what makes that structural rather than a condition repeated at each site. A name in both is rejected: one name is one file with one value column, so it is an input or a result and not both.

The questions the long schema asks of a stored attribute — its dtype, its coordinates — span both, since outputs/ and inputs/ share a layout. Those go through one lookup that consults each in turn.

A tool declares its results from the same registry it declares its inputs from. PyPSA marks them with status starting "Output", so the vocabulary is read rather than kept as a list, and an upgrade that adds a result is picked up. That is what keeps declaration from becoming a maintenance burden on the tool: the alternative — a tool attaching whatever its registry produced, unchecked — buys nothing a caller can rely on, since a consumer reading outputs/ still needs a dtype to read it at.

Results version like inputs (versioning): removing one, changing its dtype, or narrowing its dims makes existing layers unreadable for the same reasons.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
What describes one label of a dim — its type, its carrier, a coordinate on a map — is metadata rather than data, and is declared apart from it, keyed by its subject:

properties = {
    "entity": {
        "component": PropertySpec(dtype=Enum(["Generator", "Line", "Load"])),
        "carrier": PropertySpec(into="carrier"),
        "sign": PropertySpec(
            dtype="float64", default=1, default_by={"entity.component": {"Load": -1}}
        ),
    },
    "bus": {
        "carrier": PropertySpec(into="carrier", default="AC"),
        "x": PropertySpec(dtype="float64", unit="°"),
        "country": PropertySpec(into="country"),
    },
    "carrier": {"color": PropertySpec(dtype="str", default="")},
    "connection": {"role": PropertySpec(dtype="str")},
}

A property is one value per label of its subject, a dim or a group, and so has no dims: it never varies along another axis. It is a column of the subject's own file — dims/<dim>.parquet, or groups/<group>.parquet for a group (where a value lives) — so component is a column of dims/entity.parquet because every property of entity is, and the schema attaches no meaning to the name.

An attribute is data: what a model reads as part of its problem and what a layer would vary. Which a name is, is the author's declaration rather than derived from its shape; a tool reads it from its registry where it can (PyPSA).

A property's name is its subject's. One name is one spec for attributes and results, each one file with one value dtype (flat attributes). A property is a column of its subject's file, so its name is unique there only: x on bus beside an attribute x — a line's reactance — and carrier on entity, on bus and as a dim. Refused at load are a property named like a column of its subject's key — the dim, a within parent, a group's struct column or its into — and a group's property named like one of its coordinates, the keywords a tuple is addressed by. Two spellings differing only in case stay refused record-wide (names).

A property is addressed as subject.name — entity.component, bus.x, connection.role — wherever a caller names one: set, a trait's on and bundle, a default_by key, default_for. A plain name is an attribute or result, never a property, however few subjects declare it, so its meaning does not change when another subject declares it later. Schema.resolve(name) returns the AttributeSpec, or the subject and the PropertySpec, and refuses an unknown plain name naming the dotted forms of the properties so called. A column keeps its plain name: the frames of properties[subject] and the categories flags and attributes_for take are each read against one subject already, and a selector keyword is bare — a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches.

A property may be into a dim: its values are that dim's labels and its dtype is the dim's, so entity.carrier and bus.carrier above name labels of carrier, bus.country one of country, and any subject may declare one. A stored value that is not NULL must name a live label, checked where a group's field is: set and add refuse one the record as staged lacks, the writer a layer storing one it removed, and remove a label one still names. NULL names none. Refused at load are into an undeclared dim and a dtype other than the dim's. It does not categorize: a category is a declared Enum, a label is data a layer adds and removes. One coordinate classified into a dim is such a property, never a group.

Why the split. Without it, where a value is stored follows how many coordinates address it rather than what it is: p_nom, data a model optimises against, and carrier, a label describing a generator, would both be columns of the entity axis, and widening p_nom to dims: [entity, scenario] — a compatible change — would move it to inputs/p_nom.parquet, away from the rows earlier layers wrote.

docs.title: Categories — an Enum property of a partial dim
docs.text:
Any Enum-typed property of a dim listed in partial categorizes it: its values are that dim's categories along it, which a trait's on and a default_by key on. Schema.categorizing(dim) lists them in declaration order. There is no flag declaring the role and no limit of one per dim — an Enum technology would categorize entity beside component. Keying on any other property — a str one, one into a dim, one of a dim outside partial, or one of a group — is refused, naming the property and why.

The two conditions are what a category needs: an Enum, so a category a trait or a default names is checked against a declared vocabulary; and the dim in partial, because only there is a dim owned and checked per label. A schema whose entities have no kinds declares no Enum property of entity, and nothing else about it differs.

Category, because label already names an axis value — what add(dim, labels) takes. What a label carries is asked by its categories, the label's value of each categorizing property:

  • attributes_for(dim, **categories) — the attributes reaching dim such a label carries, narrowed by traits, each category keyed by its property's plain name;
  • properties_for(subject, **categories) — the same for its properties, narrowed by the same traits; every tuple of a group carries all of its group's;
  • default_for(name, **categories) — the default of an attribute, result or property for such a label.

A category may change. It is a property like any other, patched by set. Values a label holds for attributes its new category does not carry stay stored, but fall outside every per-category read and every broadcast, which are judged against its current categories.

docs.title: default_by — a default per category
docs.text:
default stays the fallback; default_by maps a categorizing property, as subject.name, to per-category overrides, on attributes and properties alike:

"p_min_pu": AttributeSpec(
    dtype="float64", dims={"entity", "snapshot"}, default=0,
    default_by={"entity.component": {"StorageUnit": -1}},
)

A value read unset takes the first default_by key, in declaration order, whose map lists the label's category; else default.

  • Each key reachable from the value's address. A key must categorize a dim the value reaches — entity directly, or through connection's entity field for a value over the group — and a category outside its property's Enum is refused.
  • Never on a categorizing property. A category defaulted by a category is circular; such a property takes a plain default.
  • Only the default varies. dtype, unit and description are the spec's own, which is what keeps one name one column and one inputs/ file.

A default is never stored. record.properties and record.attributes hand over stored rows, so a consumer applies a default through default_for — the PyPSA tool does, building a component's static frame.

docs.title: Traits
docs.text:
A trait is a named bundle of attributes, and which categories carry them:

traits = {
    "investable": Trait(
        attributes={"capital_cost", "build_year", "lifetime", "capacity"},
        on={"entity.component": {"Generator", "Line", "Link", "Store"}},
    ),
    "dispatchable": Trait(
        attributes={"p_min_pu", "p_max_pu", "p_set"},
        on={"entity.component": {"Generator", "Link"}},
    ),
}

A trait narrows; it does not grant. An attribute the schema declares is carried by every label it can address, and a trait is the only thing that cuts that down. Writing entity in an attribute's dims is what says it is per entity; declining to bundle it says it is so for every category — the same thing dims={"scenario"} already means along the scenario axis, where no subscription mechanism exists and nobody finds it surprising.

That direction is why an attribute belonging to no type has somewhere to live at all. Under the previous shape a type subscribed and an attribute reached nothing until one did, which is what forced attributes to be nested under types and left snapshot weightings homeless.

Whichever property each trait keys on. An attribute no trait claims is carried by every label; a claimed one by every label some claiming trait matches. A trait on entity.component: [Generator] and one on entity.technology: [wind], both claiming p_max_pu, give it to every generator and every wind entity.

Schema.attributes_for(dim, **categories) and Schema.properties_for(subject, **categories) (categories) are what flags, a consumer's per-category frame and the validation of set read, so everything downstream asks one question and gets a resolved answer. A trait may bundle properties of the dim its on categorizes beside attributes, each as subject.name, and both are narrowed alike. An attribute addressed by an axis alone is carried by no category however few traits mention it: a snapshot weighting belongs to the record.

A trait rather than a bare list of attribute names, for two reasons. The deduplication is real: the boundaries are measured from a framework's registry rather than invented, and investable covers six types. And a trait is queryable — a consumer dispatching on "everything investable" asks the schema rather than enumerating types, which is what makes the vocabulary worth declaring at all.

Declared, not inferred. No framework ships a trait registry to read, so the mapping from its component registry to traits is authored and maintained. That cost is the price of the vocabulary being useful to something other than this schema.

Only a categorizing property may scope a trait, and one per trait. on names one categorizing property and categories of it; the schema rejects any other key, because a trait scoped to, say, country would make an attribute's vocabulary depend on a relation — which attributes an entity carries would follow from what its bus maps to, a join every caller of attributes_for treats as answerable from a label's own categories. A trait spanning two properties is two traits.

A trait with an empty on narrows nothing: it is a bundle for a consumer to dispatch on, and its attributes stay carried by every label.

A trait may only name an attribute or property the schema declares: it says which apply, never what they are, so a name with no spec is a typo rather than a shorthand declaration. Two traits bundling one attribute is fine — they resolve to a set — since one attribute has one spec and there is nothing left to conflict.

docs.title: switch — a trait an entity opts into
docs.text:
A trait narrows two ways: on says which categories carry it, switch names an attribute deciding it per label.

traits = {
    "committable": Trait(
        attributes={"start_up_cost", "min_up_time", "ramp_limit_start_up"},
        on={"entity.component": {"Generator", "Link"}},
        switch="committable",
    ),
}
attributes = {
    "committable": AttributeSpec(dtype="bool", dims={"entity"}, default=False),
}

The two never interact: on first, then switch. A trait with neither reaches every label; a switch needs an on, and is addressed by exactly the dim its on property categorizes — the dim it decides the trait per label of.

The switch is an ordinary attribute, with a dtype, a default and long rows in inputs/ like any other (where a value lives). bool is the only dtype admitted; an Enum switch selecting among several traits is deferred. Its default decides the unset case, and false keeps the bundle off every entity that predates the trait.

It joins the trait's attributes on its own, folded in at parse rather than listed by the author, so a consumer asking what committable bundles gets the switch with the rest. Being in the bundle it would otherwise be narrowed by its own trait, which nothing could then turn on — so it is in attributes for discovery and out of the narrowing.

attributes_for is unchanged by it. A switched trait's attributes are carried by the category, because the question it answers is which attributes a generator may have; the switch narrows which entities carry a value, which is a question about data. So the switch is a validation and query mechanism rather than a change to the vocabulary. What it is declared for — rejecting a value set on an entity whose switch is false, and asking which entities a trait reaches — reads the switch column, and neither is wired up yet: the declaration lands first, the checks that read data after. Whether attributes_for grows a per-label counterpart is open.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
A group declares which tuples over several dims exist: a sparse subset of a dim product, with its own order.

groups = {
    "connection": Group(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}),
    "corridor": Group(over={"from": "bus", "to": "bus"}),
    "bus_country": Group(
        over=["bus", "scenario"], into="country"
    ),  # functional: one country per bus and scenario
}

Not an axis of labels: a dim declares one, a group declares which combinations are there, which no axis can say because the product is sparse — an entity attaches to two buses out of a thousand. As a coordinate, though, a group is a dim whose axis is the resolved group: it broadcasts, and is partial or owned whole, by the rules a dim follows.

over maps coordinate name → dim rather than naming a bare set of dims, because two coordinates may draw on the same axis: a corridor between two nodes is (from, to), which a set could not spell. A list is sugar for the dict with identical keys and values, so over=["bus"] is over={"bus": "bus"}.

An attribute over a group carries the group as one struct column named for the group, a field per key coordinate in over order:

inputs/efficiency.parquet       connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
inputs/flow.parquet             corridor STRUCT("from", "to")  | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value
inputs/marginal_price.parquet   bus | timestep | attribute | breakpoint | value

The column's name says which group constrains the row, so two groups may share a coordinate set without ambiguity, and a group's coordinate never takes the column of the dim it draws on — bus inside connection is not the dim bus beside it.
