A group file is keyed by the same column: groups/connection.parquet is connection STRUCT(entity, bus) | role, as dims/bus.parquet is keyed by bus, so a row and the group it names meet on one column with nothing packed between them.

A group in dims resolves to itself, so dims={"connection", "timestep"} gives the columns connection | timestep, groups first — addressing states the full rule. The fold's key therefore does not vary per attribute: partial_dims is one fixed tuple, exactly the dims and groups partial names.

An attribute may not name a group beside a dim its key coordinate is named for. dims={"connection", "bus"} is rejected: the row would hold the bus twice, free to disagree — the same "keyed twice over" rule into states.

A group's file columns are not declared here. They are its properties, declared under the group's name — PyPSA's role on a connection is properties: {connection: {role: ...}}, declared by the tool whose vocabulary the word is — and an attribute over the group is long rows in inputs/ keyed by the struct (where a value lives). Declaring them a second time on the Group would be two ways to say one thing, disagreeing eventually. A group is never categorized: its tuples carry every property it declares.

A group column broadcasts, its axis the resolved group. A NULL struct means every tuple of the group, expanded against groups/<group>.parquet as a NULL dim is against dims/<dim>.parquet (the broadcast rule). A group value is a whole tuple or NULL. A struct with some fields NULL names a tuple no group row matches, so it is refused wherever a row comes in — set, add_group and the writer. A group is keyed where a dim is: in the fold key where partial names it, owned whole otherwise, so a layer touching one connection's value then restates the attribute's whole extent along the group. The dims a group draws on broadcast on their own: bus is an ordinary axis whose NULL means "every bus", so a per-bus marginal_price beside a connection group may hold one value for all of them. Every group is such a coordinate (Schema.group_columns).

Connections are one instance, not a structural category: Group(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"}), with role a property of it. bus is accordingly one coordinate of one group rather than a column the format fixes, and neither word appears in the record layer — connection is whatever a schema calls it, and role is a tool's declaration.

docs.title: into — a group that classifies
docs.text:
into names the dim a group is functional into: each tuple of over carries exactly one of its labels. bus_country over [bus, scenario] into country says every bus is in one country per scenario.

A group needs two coordinates or more. One over coordinate into a dim is refused at load, naming the property to declare instead: a bus in one country is bus.country into country, a column of the bus axis whose label is checked live, rather than a file of its own.

It is a declaration a bare group cannot make. A group can only happen to be single-valued, which leaves a duplicate row a data error the schema has no name for; into names it, so the constraint is declared and checkable on write. No existing system declares it — GAMS's map(b,c) is a set over a tuple of sets with single-valuedness left to convention, and a duplicated b silently double-counts — which is the argument for the field rather than against it, a schema whose purpose is making shape checkable having no reason to inherit that gap.

into must name a declared dim. That is what keeps the axis file, and the axis file is the whole of what a functional group has over a bare tuple set: dims/country.parquet gives country its order and somewhere for a per-country CO2 budget to live.

into is sugar, resolved once at parse. It is a plain column beside the key, so groups/bus_country.parquet is bus_country STRUCT(bus, scenario) | country and is keyed by its struct exactly as connection is, and no read path, file layout or fold key branches on whether a group has one. The field is retained for the three things that still need it: the uniqueness constraint (the key being the coordinates minus into), a consumer's aggregation, and round-tripping the manifest — writing back over: [bus, country] where the author wrote into: would silently rewrite their schema.

It may not key an attribute alongside what it maps from. dims={"bus", "country"} is rejected: into says the country follows from the bus and scenario, so the row would be keyed twice over and the two free to disagree.

docs.title: Addressing: dims: [X]
docs.text:
An attribute names a group in its dims exactly as it names a dim, and one rule resolves both:

X is the dim X if one is declared, and otherwise the group X, carried as one struct column of its name.

"efficiency": AttributeSpec(dims={"connection", "timestep"}),  # connection | timestep
"co2_budget": AttributeSpec(dims={"country"}),  # country: the dim

A group with no dim of its name has no other spelling, so naming it is the only way to declare an attribute over it; coordinates_of lists the attribute's groups first, then its dims in declaration order.

A group may not share a dim's name: a group is carried as a column named for it, so sharing a dim's name makes two columns one name. A functional group is named for the relation rather than the axis it classifies into — bus_country into country — and the schema's error says so.

docs.title: Existence does not vary along a dim
docs.text:
An entity exists or it does not. There is no declaration making membership vary per value of an axis — no generator present in scenario high and absent from low — so dims/entity.parquet holds one row per entity and a tombstone removes it whole.

That is a deliberate narrowing. An earlier Dimension.keys declared exactly this, putting the dim in an entity table's key so an entity existed per scenario; it is gone, with nothing in its place, because what it should mean is unsettled once connections are one group among several rather than a fixed second entity table.

What remains is the distinction that was doing the useful work: a value may vary along an axis where the thing may not. A stochastic network holding a different capital_cost per scenario is expressing exactly that, and it is an attribute with dims = {"entity", "scenario"} — long rows in inputs/, not an entity that exists twice. Where a value lives already places it.

docs.title: within — an axis inside an axis
docs.text:
A dim whose labels identify a point only within another dim's value. Multi-period time is the case: the axis is a (period, timestep) pair, so t1 alone names nothing and two periods may hold different timesteps.

dimensions = {
    "period": Dimension(dtype="int64"),
    "timestep": Dimension(dtype="datetime64[us]", within={"period"}),
}

within makes timestep.parquet carry a period column, and the axis key (period, timestep) rather than timestep. It is on Dimension because nesting is structural — true of the data however stored, so a directory record needs it exactly as much as a layered one.

A set, because two different things could each be one parent:

  • Chained — timestep in period in horizon. Each dim names its immediate parent and the chain is walked, giving (horizon, period, timestep).
  • Several direct parents — timestep identified only within a (period, stage) pair, where neither contains the other. This is what a multi-stage stochastic program with investment periods looks like.

So the axis key is (*parents, dim), parents in declaration order. Every name in within must be a declared dim, and the nesting graph must be acyclic.

Distinct from AttributeSpec.dims despite the similar shape: dims names independent coordinates — a value exists at each combination and the set never chains — whereas within qualifies a label and is transitive, so naming period pulls in period's own parents.

The inner dim is named for the thing it indexes (timestep) rather than for the pair (snapshot), because once nesting exists the pair needs its own name: a framework consuming the record calls (period, timestep) a snapshot.

docs.title: within is not into
docs.text:
Both are acyclic and both relate one dim to another. They mean opposite things:

  • within names a dim's parents: its label set is scoped per parent, so t1 in 2015 and t1 in 2020 are different points and the axis key is (period, timestep).
  • into names the dim a property or group classifies its subject by: one flat label set, each label or over tuple picking one of its labels. country is not scoped by bus; it is a partition of buses, and its axis key is country alone.

Nesting versus classification. within cannot express country, and into cannot express timestep. within stays on Dimension because nesting is a property of the axis itself; into is on a property or a Group because a classification is a relation: a column of the classified axis, or rows of a group.

A classification is single-valued by declaration rather than by construction, which is the whole of what into adds — a many-to-many classification is an ordinary group, and expressible as one.

A chain is not denormalised. bus→state→country is two properties, bus.state and state.country, never a country column on dims/bus.parquet. Two columns asserting bus→country would let a layer restating the states leave every bus's country stale with nothing to detect it, so the chain is a join over two axis files.

The record does not resolve across levels. An attribute over country is handed back keyed by country; projecting it down to buses is a join through the classification, and that is the consumer's work. The fold learns no new operation.

Membership could not vary along a classification either, if it varied along anything: whether an entity exists in Germany is already settled by its bus and that bus's country, so there would be no freedom for it to vary independently (existence does not vary).

docs.title: partial — the granularity of an override
docs.text:
Everything is overridable; a layer exists in order to override. The remaining question is at what granularity along each axis, and it splits from AttributeSpec's question because the two are properties of different things:

  • Which dims may this attribute vary over at all? — per attribute. p_max_pu varies over scenario and timestep; p_nom over neither. AttributeSpec.dims.
  • May a layer patch individual values along this axis, or must it restate the axis whole? — per dimension. scenario is patchable value by value; timestep is not, for any attribute. schema.partial.
partial = {"scenario"}  # timestep absent, so a patch restates the series

A dim outside partial is one a layer owns entirely once it touches it: overriding one timestep of p_max_pu means carrying that entity's entire series, because a partial series would resolve across two layers and produce a curve with a hole. The reason is a consumer's rather than the format's — a framework that splits constant from varying data cannot receive half a series — which is why it belongs to the axis: it is true of every attribute varying over it.

The dims a layer owns an attribute per follow from the declarations:

owned_per(attribute) = attribute.dims ∩ partial_dims
partial_dims         = broadcast coordinates ∩ schema.partial

partial_dims is the fold key: exactly the broadcast coordinates — dims and groups — declared partial. No dim is in it by name; a schema patching entity by entity lists entity, as PyPSA's {entity, bus, scenario, connection} does. A dim a group draws on is a broadcast dim like any other, so a layer patching a per-bus marginal_price one bus at a time needs bus in partial; a layer patching one connection's efficiency needs connection there, and the connection's bus is patched with it, inside the connection column. Neither is needed for the group itself: a dim a group draws on may stay out of partial, a removed label's tuples being tombstoned with it. So p_max_pu is owned per entity and per scenario — timestep is not partial, so a patch to one hour restates that entity-scenario's whole series; marginal_cost per entity and scenario; p_nom per entity, once across everything else.

Two things this buys. The schema can distinguish p_max_pu from p_nom, which a dim-level flag cannot: that would say every attribute is owned per scenario, including those a scenario must not change. And a p_nom row carrying a non-NULL scenario becomes a write-time violation rather than something the NULL-broadcast rule absorbs — a first-stage decision quietly turned into a per-scenario one is the error worth catching.

What the fold does with this is unchanged: the inputs key is one fixed tuple over all attributes, and an attribute not varying over a dim writes NULL there. So the declarations constrain and validate; they do not make the key vary per row.

An axis file is owned the same way, and the properties it carries do not argue for adding it — save one: a dim with a category must be in partial, since only there is it checked per label. Outside partial, a layer touching an axis restates it whole — every label, with the properties attached to them — because a layer holding one label is not saying the others are unchanged but that they are not there: the fold keys by the axis key, so what this layer carries is what the axis has here. That is the same "no half-owned extent" rule a series obeys, applied to a set of labels rather than a curve.

Keep it small. Every partial coordinate widens the fold key, and the key is paid for by every read of every attribute. The cost of leaving one out is paid once per edit and bounded by the axis or group; the cost of putting it in is paid by every read forever. So partial names only the dims and groups a layer genuinely patches value by value — entity, bus, scenario and connection, not timestep or carrier: a layer patches one bus's v_nom, but restates every carrier's co2_emissions, a few dozen rows.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
A declared dim, group, group coordinate, attribute, result or property name becomes a column, beside the columns datarecord writes itself. Schema refuses one at load that could not stand there, naming it and the reason:

  • " or .. A name reaches DuckDB as a column reference, which reads a.b as column b of table a and cannot spell a " at all. A space, mixed case, a keyword or a leading digit are fine: those quote.
  • A column the format writes. attribute, breakpoint and value on every long row, deleted as a tombstone, varies, broadcast, breakpoints and layer_uuid in the owner map, and order_key on a resolved frame. Ignoring case, as DuckDB resolves a column name. A collision is silent otherwise: a dim named value gives the long file two columns of one name, and one named deleted reads every label as a tombstone, dropping its rows with nothing reported.
  • A leading _. The prefix of every scratch column a fold adds and drops, so that set can grow without growing this list.
  • Two spellings differing only in case. DuckDB resolves Country and country to one column, so a schema declaring both would have one read the other's values. One spelling declared twice, as when a group's coordinate is named after the dim it ranges over, is a single column and fine.

Entity names and labels are data, never identifiers, so none of this constrains them.

No dim or property name is reserved — not entity, not component: a schema declares them like any other, so neither can be taken by surprise. What one name may not be twice over is a section's rule, not this list's.

docs.title: One schema per record
docs.text:
Not one per layer. A directory record's schema is manifest.json in the directory; a layered record's lives beside the layers, not inside any of them:

record-root/
├── manifest.json               # the schema — one, for the whole tree
└── layers/<uuid>/              # a layer: dims/, inputs/, outputs/ — no manifest
    └── resolved/               # caches (owner map, resolved dims)

A schema is not layered data. Folding it would let a layer change what p_nom means — its dtype, which dims it varies over — which is not a patch to data but a redefinition of the thing being patched, and it makes the schema unknowable without walking the ancestry. One schema makes it a property of the record, validatable before anything is read and stated once for a hundred-layer tree.

The cost is that adding an attribute amends the root schema rather than shipping inside the layer that introduces it. That is the right trade: a new attribute is a schema change, and one buried several layers deep is exactly what should be visible.

A layer directory therefore holds only data, which is what keeps it a plain parquet directory readable by a tool that knows nothing about layering.

Which of the two a directory is decides what it is read under. A standalone record carries its own manifest.json, so Workspace.at(uri) reads that file and the record answers the same through any workspace — it is one whole record, and may well be opened from somewhere that knows nothing about it; at refuses a directory without one. Its manifest also carries an id, a UUID ws.write mints, beside the schema's keys rather than wrapping them, so the file still parses as the schema. The id is the record's layer id, which keys the fold tables a workspace shares: derived from the URI instead, a record deleted and written again there, or a relative path read from another working directory, would be served the folds of the record before it. at refuses a manifest without one. A tree's manifest needs none, its revisions naming its layers. A single layer directory carries none, so it is read through its store, store.layer(id), under the manifest beside the tree it belongs to.

An edit changes neither. A WorkingRecord is one more layer over its base, and a layer declares nothing — so it reads under whatever its base's schema is, standalone or not. A staging area that could redeclare would be the layered-schema case above, arriving by a different door.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
One schema outlives many layers (above), so a change to it meets data written under the previous one. version records which schema a record's layers were written against, and what matters is which changes existing layers survive.

Compatible — old layers stay readable, version bumps and nothing else happens:

  • adding an attribute, a property, a category, a trait, or a group — none changes the owner map's key, which only partial widens
  • adding a dim no existing attribute varies over
  • a category carrying a further attribute, whether by a trait claiming it for that category or by no trait claiming it
  • widening an AttributeSpec.dims: rows that set fewer dims still decode, since an unset dim is NULL and NULL means "all values" (the broadcast rule)
  • adding to partial: ownership becomes finer, and an existing layer's rows are simply owned at the coarser granularity they were written with
  • changing a unit or description, which describe the data without deciding how any row decodes

Incompatible — existing rows would decode differently, or not at all:

  • narrowing dims, since a row setting a now-undeclared dim has no valid reading
  • changing a dtype, which includes dropping a category from an Enum
  • moving a name between properties and attributes, or between subjects: it moves the file the value is read from
  • removing from partial: a layer that patched one value along that axis is now a partial override of an axis owned whole, which is exactly the hole partial forbids
  • changing within, since the axis key changes shape
  • a category ceasing to carry an attribute, whether by dropping it or by a trait no longer claiming it for that category: its rows are still in the file, now with no valid reading for that category

Adding a functional group is compatible in the same sense adding any group is: the record gains a file, and until some layer writes it every coordinate reads as unclassified — no row, which is what "no country assigned" means anyway.

The compatible changes are those where NULL already means what the new schema needs it to mean, so the broadcast rule absorbs them without touching a row.

An incompatible change therefore needs the layers rewritten rather than the schema edited, which for a layered record means flattening it to a standalone directory under the new schema. A reader encountering a version it was not written for should refuse rather than guess, since every failure above is silent.

docs.title: unit and description
docs.text:
A Dimension, an AttributeSpec and a PropertySpec may each carry a unit and a description. Neither is interpreted: no conversion, no dimensional analysis, no validation that MW and kW are not being added. They are stored, read back, and handed to whatever displays or documents the record.

They belong in the schema rather than in meta because they describe the dimensioned data — which is exactly the line meta is on the other side of. A unit is a property of an attribute in the same way its dtype is, and a consumer asking "what is p_nom and what is it measured in" should not have to know a framework's own metadata layout to find out.

None means undeclared, not dimensionless. A quantity that genuinely has no unit is "" — the distinction matters to a renderer choosing between showing nothing and showing an empty unit, and to a later pass that wants to find what is still undocumented.

A dimension's unit describes what its labels measure, which is only sometimes meaningful: a vintage axis labelled in years or a distance axis in km has one, while scenario and timestep do not — a timestamp is not a quantity. description applies to any axis.

Neither field changes how a row decodes, so adding or editing one is a compatible change.

docs.title: Consuming a record
docs.text:
A tool is the framework-specific translation target built from a record. The call runs from the tool inward:

class Tool(Protocol):
    name: str
    schema: Schema  # attribute mapping

    def requires(self, record: Record) -> Requirements: ...
    def verify(self, record: Record) -> Requirements: ...  # falsy when usable
    def build(self, record: Record) -> Any: ...
    def to_datarecord(self, model: Any, con: DuckDBPyConnection) -> Record: ...
    def results(self, model: Any, con: DuckDBPyConnection) -> Frames: ...

to_datarecord is the inverse of build. It and results take the connection their frames are planned on, required; in practice ws.con of the workspace that writes them, or the con of the record they are set on. A tool is handed a connection, not a workspace or a store: it plans relations and has no business with directories, locations or the tree. A frame planned on another connection is rejected at the boundary, so a tool that picked its own would fail on the first write. build takes none: it reads record.con.

root = store.root(PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con))
w = WorkingRecord(root.record)
for attr, frame in PyPSA.results(n, w.con).items():
    w.set(attr, frame, kind="outputs")

results returns Frames — the same type Record.outputs presents, keyed by attribute, each frame in the long schema. So a tool's results go straight to a write, or one at a time to set(attr, frame, kind="outputs") with no key to unpack.

A framework holds its results per entity type, so reaching this shape means concatenating each attribute's types into one frame. That is free: the frames are lazy, so the union is a plan rather than a copy, and nothing materialises until a caller collects. The concatenation needs no category column to distinguish the arms, since entity is unique across them — which is what makes the union a plain one rather than a tagged one.

A framework's per-port results are stored on connections, like its per-port inputs.

Lazy is what the protocol asks for rather than what any implementation must do. A tool reshaping a solved model's in-memory containers has nothing to defer and wraps its eager frames with .lazy(); one that could fetch a result attribute from a solver on demand is free to, and a caller wanting three of forty then pays for three. That is the Frames argument, on the write side.

A record is the input to a translation, not the owner of one, so there is no registry and no name dispatch: a tool is a module-level singleton reached by importing it, build returns the framework's own type, and nothing in the record layer imports a tool.

build takes a Record rather than a record, so a tool builds from a directory as readily as from an overlay and has no reason to know layering exists.

A tool's verify catches what the record layer cannot: an entity type the framework has no registry entry for — the record checks a category against its Enum, not against the framework — a connection role it cannot place, a partial set that breaks the framework's constant-versus-varying split. It is also where a framework scoping names per type meets a record scoping them record-wide. PyPSA permits a Generator and a Load both called north, so to_datarecord reports such a network as unbuildable rather than writing a record whose two entities share one key. Collisions are within a dim: a bus is a label of bus, not an entity, so a Bus and a Load called north — every clustered pypsa-eur network — are no collision. Reported rather than repaired: renaming to Generator:north would hand back a network whose components the framework can no longer find by their own names, and the record layer does not own a framework's vocabulary. PyPSA is itself moving to record-wide unique names, so this is a constraint that resolves rather than one to design around. SubNetworks are the exception: PyPSA names them 0, 1, … on every topology pass, as it numbers Lines, so there is no caller to report to. The record keys them 0 SubNetwork, …, as a caller suffixes a clashing Load, the sub_network results pointing at them likewise, and build takes the suffix off, so the framework finds them by their own names again. It is also where bus-keyed connections are collapsed back to a framework's positional encoding, ordered by order_key, and where a curve is either translated or reported unbuildable. A per-connection input follows its connection's position: efficiency on a Link's bus2 connection is PyPSA's efficiency2, static or per snapshot. The PyPSA schema declares partial={"entity", "bus", "scenario", "connection"}, so a layer patches one link's efficiency series, or one bus's v_nom, without restating every other's (partial); entity is there also because component categorizes it. carrier is not: a layer restates every carrier's co2_emissions, a few dozen rows. remove("bus", …) is the cascade every dim has, and an entity it leaves attached to no bus is verify's to report, as its type's missing bus; remove("carrier", …) is refused while a stored carrier names the label. A Process's rate0, rate1, rate2, … are likewise the one input rate, numbered from 0 because PyPSA registers rate0 where it leaves port 1's efficiency unsuffixed. Its ports default differently, -1 at the input end and 1 at the others, so rate declares no default and a port with no row keeps PyPSA's own. Which stems are per-port is read off PyPSA's registry, a name ending in a port index plus a Link's unsuffixed efficiency, delay and cyclic_delay. Every per-port input, delay and cyclic_delay included, is long rows of inputs/ over connection: a number is an attribute whatever its dims.

Properties and attributes are read off the registry. The properties of entity are exactly component, carrier, sign and type, and role is a property of connection; every other input, every number among them, is an attribute, so p_nom is long rows of inputs/p_nom.parquet (where a value lives). component's Enum is the types exported as entities. A default that differs per component — sign, p_min_pu, p_set — is a default_by on entity.component, and build applies it when it builds a component's static frame from members and the entity-only rows of its attributes.

Buses and carriers are dims. Bus and Carrier are no entity types: a bus is a label of bus, a carrier a label of carrier, and what PyPSA stores on either is placed by the properties rule, every name PyPSA's:

PyPSA record Bus.type, Bus.carrier, Bus.x, Bus.y, Bus.unit, Bus.location properties of bus Bus.v_nom, Bus.v_mag_pu_min, Bus.v_mag_pu_max, Bus.v_mag_pu_set attributes over bus (and the varying dims) Bus.marginal_price, Bus.v_mag_pu, Bus.v_ang results over bus and the varying dims Bus.p, Bus.q, Bus.control, Bus.generator, Bus.sub_network not written: derived from the connections Line.v_nom, ShuntImpedance.v_nom not written: derived from the bus a custom Bus or Carrier column attribute over its dim, as a custom entity column is Carrier.color, Carrier.nice_name properties of carrier Carrier.co2_emissions, max_growth, max_relative_growth attributes over carrier a component's carrier entity.carrier, into carrier

So x is a line's reactance and bus.x a bus's coordinate, each addressed by its own name. entity.carrier and bus.carrier are into carrier, bus.carrier defaulting to AC. to_datarecord writes both axes in PyPSA's order, adds every carrier a component or bus names but n.carriers does not list, and stores PyPSA's "" carrier as NULL, naming none; build rebuilds n.buses and n.carriers from the axis, the properties with their defaults and the attribute rows, a series by its flags, and the bus results from outputs.

A custom column clashes only with an attribute. A static column PyPSA's registry lacks is an attribute over its type's dim, carried by that type alone where the dim is entity. One name being one spec among attributes and results, custom Bus.country beside custom Generator.country would be country with two dims, and Carrier.efficiency meets the per-port efficiency: to_datarecord reports either via Requirements.columns. A name a property has does not clash, so a custom Generator.location is an attribute beside bus.location. Line.v_nom and ShuntImpedance.v_nom, which PyPSA's calculate_dependent_values copies from the bus, are no custom column: they are not written, and build gets them back as PyPSA recomputes them.

A multi-period network's snapshots are one flat axis. PyPSA's (period, timestep) snapshots are the snapshot axis, each with its period as snapshot.period, a property into period; period is an axis of its own beside it. A snapshot is labelled by its timestep where no timestep repeats across periods, and otherwise by its position, 0 to n-1 across every period in the network's order, its timestep then the property snapshot.timestep; the pd.MultiIndex.from_product of set_investment_periods repeats every timestep, so its snapshots are positions. Every input and result over snapshot has the dims it has in a single-period network, and a single-period network's schema declares no property of snapshot. build rebuilds the (period, timestep) index from the axis order, snapshot.period and the label or snapshot.timestep. A period is selected like any property of a dim an attribute reaches, set("p_max_pu", 0.5, entity="wind", period=2030) staging the snapshots of 2030 alone (set).

A weighting is an attribute over its axis. PyPSA's weighting frames become scenario_weight over scenario, snapshot_weighting_objective, snapshot_weighting_stores and snapshot_weighting_generators over snapshot, and period_weighting_objective and period_weighting_years over period, written for each axis the network holds; a multi-period network's snapshot weightings are over its flat snapshot like any other. build sets them back, a label no row reaches keeping PyPSA's own default, an equal share for a scenario.

The tool's own Schema reconciles vocabularies: per entity type, which record attribute a tool's attribute is renamed from, or which several it is computed from. Since the schema makes a record's attribute names declared rather than conventional, this maps one declared vocabulary to another.

Frames are built and handed over one entity type at a time, so peak memory is one type's frames rather than the whole model.

docs.title: Results on connections
docs.text:
A per-port result is stored exactly like a per-port input: one attribute over the connection group, one row per (entity, bus), carried as the one connection struct column — to_datarecord packs it and build unpacks it back to entity and bus where it places ports. PyPSA's p0, p1, p2, … on a Line, Transformer, Link or Process and the one-port p on a Generator, Load, Store, StorageUnit or ShuntImpedance are all the result p, each row on the connection its port attaches to and keeping PyPSA's sign for that port; q0, q1 and the one-port q are q. So a third port needs no declaration of its own: a Link's p2 is p on its bus2 connection, which the schema built from the bare registry already declares.

Two results do not follow that rule, and the tool names both rather than inferring them:

  • Bus.p, Bus.q, Bus.control, Bus.generator and Bus.sub_network are not written. p and q are the signed sum of the connection p/q at that bus, so derivable, and a bus-level p would collide with the connection-level one; the other three follow from the connections and the topology.
  • Link.p and Process.p are p_internal. PyPSA's "internal power" is at no bus, so it is an entity-level result, renamed because one name holds one spec record-wide.

The schema's results and the frames results returns are read off one rule, so every frame is set with kind="outputs" under a name the schema declares. build reads no result but a bus's, so none is turned back into PyPSA's per-port columns.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
A geometry is text. PyPSA's Shape.geometry, the column its registry types geometry, is an attribute like idx and component beside it, its values WKT in inputs/geometry.parquet, declared String. The coordinate reference system is one per network rather than one per value, so it is not data but crs in the schema's meta, the CRS's authority string (EPSG:3035) where it has one. PyPSA's srid network attribute, that CRS's EPSG code, is not written beside it.

build sets the network's CRS from crs before adding any component, and parses each geometry back into a GeoSeries in it; a record without crs builds in PyPSA's default, EPSG:4326.

docs.title: WorkingRecord
docs.text:
Record is read-only, and the writers write a whole record from a source that already knows everything it will contain. Neither covers editing: adding labels, removing them, setting an attribute or a property.

class WorkingRecord:
    """A `Record` that accepts edits, and hands them over as a layer."""

    def __init__(self, base: Record) -> None: ...

    def set(
        self,
        attribute: str,  # an attribute, a result, or a property
        value: Any,  # scalar | sequence | mapping | series | frame | nw.Expr
        *,
        kind: Literal["inputs", "outputs"] = "inputs",
        **coords: Any,  # coordinates, a group's fields, properties of a dim reached
    ) -> None: ...

    def add(self, dim: str, labels: Sequence[Any], **columns: Any) -> None: ...
    def remove(self, dim: str, labels: Sequence[Any]) -> None: ...

    def add_group(self, group: str, frame: IntoFrame) -> None: ...
    def remove_group(self, group: str, keys: Sequence[tuple[Any, ...]]) -> None: ...

    @property
    def edits(self) -> LayerData: ...  # the staged layer alone
    def rollback(self) -> None: ...

Built over a base Record, WorkingRecord(revision.record), it stages on the base's connection, record.con.

A class, not a protocol. Record is a protocol because several things satisfy it — two backings, a framework object presenting itself as one, the two readings a write takes — and structural typing is what lets a consumer satisfy it without depending on this package. There is one way to edit a record, so a second name for it would be an interface over its only implementation. Where the staged rows live is this class's own business, which is why the name says what it is rather than how.

It satisfies Record, which is the load-bearing decision: a mutable record reads as a record, and what it reads is the data with its pending edits applied. So an edit can be read back, or the record handed to something that only knows Record, without writing it. Structurally, not by inheritance — the read members are implemented here over base-plus-staged.

Two properties follow from accumulate-then-write, and both are the point:

  • An edit costs a row in a staging table, not a rewrite. A hundred edits to one attribute are a hundred rows, collapsed once when written.
  • Nothing touches the record until edits is written as a child. A caller that fails halfway leaves no layer; one that changes its mind calls rollback().

docs.title: The shape of an edit
docs.text:
Each edit maps onto exactly one part of the format:

edit writes key it targets set an attribute inputs/<attr>.parquet rows the attribute's coordinates set a property one column of existing dims/<dim>.parquet rows the dim's axis key set a group's property one column of existing groups/<group>.parquet rows the group's struct add labels whole dims/<dim>.parquet rows the dim's axis key remove labels deleted = true axis rows, and the tuples naming them the dim's axis key, the group's key add_group / remove_group groups/<group>.parquet rows and tombstones the group's own key coordinates

Nothing names entity or a category: add and remove take any dim, and which coordinates an attribute's row carries is its dims. Nor is there a connect/disconnect pair beside add_group — connection is one group among however many the schema declares, and a call naming it would be the record layer holding one framework's vocabulary.

The crucial property: an edit is expressed in the format's own terms. Setting p_nom on twenty entities is twenty inputs/p_nom.parquet rows, which is what a patch layer would hold anyway. So a staged edit is already the row it will be written as, and writing edits is a concatenation rather than a translation.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # broadcast
w.set("p_nom", [150.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # per label
w.set("p_nom", {"wind1": 150.0, "wind2": 80.0})  # per label, keyed
w.set("p_max_pu", frame, entity=["wind1"])  # long frame
w.set("p_max_pu", series.rename_axis("snapshot"), entity=["wind1"])  # a series
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every label carrying it, now and later
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, component="Generator", carrier="wind")  # selected now
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="dc", bus="north")  # a connection
w.set("p_nom", 200.0, entity="wind1", scenario="high")  # scoped
w.set("p_nom", nw.col("value") * 1.1, entity=["wind1"])  # derived
w.set("entity.carrier", "solar", entity="g2")  # a property, by its subject
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # not `x`, an attribute of its own
w.set("p", solved, kind="outputs")  # a result

Every coordinate is a keyword, a group's fields included: entity=, snapshot=, bus="north" for one connection, from=/to= for one corridor. None has a parameter of its own, because which coordinates exist is declared rather than fixed. A keyword holds one label, fixing that coordinate, or a list of labels the value is staged at each of.

A coordinate no keyword names is NULL, which by the broadcast rule is every label of it — narrowed, on a categorized dim, to the labels whose categories carry the attribute. So set("p_max_pu", 0.9) is one row reaching every generator, one added in a later layer included, and never a load.

A group's fields are packed into the group's struct column, so entity="dc", bus="north" stages connection = {entity: dc, bus: north}. A group value is a whole tuple or NULL, so every field must be given or none: omitting bus alone is refused, since {entity: dc, bus: NULL} names no tuple, and naming no field stages the NULL struct, every tuple. A field is named by its own name: a contract (from, to) over entity is addressed as from="plant", to="mill", and entity= beside it is refused, since it would have to guess which party it names.

A property as a keyword selects labels when set is called. A keyword is bare: it names a coordinate of the attribute, else any property of a dim the attribute reaches, categorizing or not — coordinate first, so bus="north" on a connection attribute is the field even where entity has a property bus, and carrier="gas" on an attribute over the carrier dim is that dim, while on p_max_pu it is entity.carrier. A dotted keyword is refused, and so is a name several dims the attribute reaches declare a property of. component="Generator", carrier="wind" resolves to the labels matching every keyword on the record as staged, and set writes one row per label; nothing of the filter is stored. A label added later is not reached — a plain NULL and default_by are the two ways a value reaches labels not yet added. The property's dim must be one the attribute reaches through exactly one coordinate, and the keyword is refused beside that coordinate's own.

set writes a property too, a category included, when attribute names one as subject.name — a plain name is an attribute or result, never a property: a patch of one column of the axis rows of its subject, the other columns kept. Its value is a mapping or series from label to value, a scalar with a dim= keyword naming the labels, or a scalar for every label the axis has. A group's property takes a scalar, its fields as keywords selecting the tuples. A property is never a result and never derived, so kind="outputs" and an nw.Expr are refused for one. Changing a category is such a patch: set("entity.component", "Load", entity="g1"). What g1 holds for attributes a Load does not carry stays stored but falls outside every per-category read.

kind names the destination in the format's own terms — the shape of an edit is a mapping from edit to destination, and this makes that destination the parameter it was always implicitly carrying. "outputs" stages into outputs/ instead of inputs/, which is how a tool hands results back to a record before it is written.

value takes six forms, because assigning one value to many labels and assigning a different value to each are equally ordinary and neither should require building a frame:

value meaning keywords scalar staged at every listed combination an omitted coordinate broadcasts sequence aligned positionally exactly one list keyword, same length mapping keys are labels of one coordinate the one coordinate no keyword names series index is labels of one coordinate the index's own name, else the one coordinate no keyword names frame supplies its own keys single labels completing it nw.Expr a function of the current value selects what to derive from

A mapping's keys or a series' index are ambiguous: they may hold labels of any of the attribute's coordinates, an axis label being a string like any other. The caller says which by naming the series' index after a coordinate, or by naming every other coordinate as a keyword; where neither settles it, the call is refused. Never inferred from the labels themselves: testing them against the axis would make one call mean different things in two records — a scenario labelled wind1 would silently capture a series meant per entity — and a partial overlap would pick a reading without saying so.

A frame over a group carries it as the struct column, connection STRUCT(entity, bus). One carrying a field flat, entity or bus, is rejected with the struct to pass instead, and so is a struct whose fields are not exactly the group's key, which a cast would silently re-key. A struct with some fields NULL is rejected too; a NULL struct broadcasts over every tuple.

The first four normalise to a long frame before staging, so there is one staging path. A length mismatch between a sequence and its keyword is an error at the call, not a silently truncated edit.

Every form is checked against the labels the record resolves, the frame form included: "supplies its own keys" decides where the labels come from, not whether they have to exist.

docs.title: An nw.Expr value — derived from the current one
docs.text:
w.set("p_nom", nw.col("value") * 1.1)  # scale up every p_nom
w.set("p_max_pu", nw.col("value").clip(upper=0.9), entity=["wind1"])

A sixth value form rather than a second method. Nothing else a caller passes is an nw.Expr, so the dispatch is unambiguous — unlike the series-versus-mapping tie, which set has the caller settle rather than guessing at.

What it does differently is read before it stages:

  • What it derives from is the resolved value including earlier pending edits (reading with pending edits), so two such calls compose.
  • Where the other forms stage without touching parent data, this one must resolve the keys it targets first. On a layered record that is a fold, so a broad derived edit is the one edit whose cost scales with the ancestry rather than with the rows written.
  • What is staged is the result, not the expression. So a written layer holds ordinary rows, and nothing in the format records that a value was derived — replaying an edit sequence is not a thing the record supports.

The expression is evaluated by narwhals against the resolved long frame, so it names value rather than the attribute: the frame is long, and one attribute per call means the column is always value.

A named target must resolve to a row. If the caller names a coordinate, every one of those targets must produce a row to derive from, or the call raises. The caller asked for those rows to take a new value and there is nothing to compute one from, which is a failed change rather than a no-op — the same class of error as naming a label no layer declares.

With no keyword the instruction is "whatever resolves", so an empty result is an answer rather than a failure. That asymmetry is the whole of the rule: a broad derived edit where only some labels carry the attribute is ordinary, while a targeted one that hits nothing is a typo.

docs.title: Results through kind="outputs"
docs.text:
A tool solves against a record and hands back what it computed:

w = WorkingRecord(record)
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, entity=["wind1"])
model = PyPSA.build(w)  # solve the edited record
model.optimize()
for attr, frame in PyPSA.results(model, w.con).items():
    w.set(attr, frame, kind="outputs")
rev.child(w.edits)  # one layer, inputs and results together

In memory only: the results live in the staging area beside the input edits and become part of the same layer when edits is written, so a solve produces one new record rather than a record plus a separate results record. Nothing on disk is mutated, and write-once stands unchanged.

Two things differ from an input edit, both following from outputs:

  • The name is checked against results, not attributes. A result attribute is declared in its own vocabulary, so an unknown name is an error exactly as it is for an input — what differs is which mapping answers. A tool reads its result vocabulary off the same registry it reads its inputs from, so declaring them costs it no list of its own: PyPSA's status field marks them, and the tool forwards what it finds. The dim vocabulary is checked for both, and a result's coordinates are its own rather than every declared dim.
  • No label check. An input value for a label no layer declares is rejected, because it would resolve to nothing. A result may legitimately name a label the record never declared: PyPSA's SubNetwork exists only after a solve, so rejecting it would refuse a real result.
  • No extent completion when staged. Results are complete as produced rather than a partial override of a parent's, so there is nothing to carry forward from the base.

Keeping results coherent with the inputs they were computed from is the caller's business. Editing an input after attaching results leaves results describing a record that no longer exists, and nothing here silently discards them — a record that dropped them on the next set would be guessing at which of the two the caller meant to keep.

docs.title: add / remove
docs.text:
w.add("carrier", ["wind", "H2"])
w.add("bus", ["north", "south"])
w.add("bus", ["north H2"], carrier="H2", x=10.1)  # bare: the dim's own
w.add("entity", ["g1", "g2"], component="Generator", carrier="wind")
w.remove("entity", ["old_coal"])
w.remove("carrier", ["gas"])  # refused while a property `into` carrier names it

add(dim, labels, **columns) stages whole axis rows: columns are the other columns of dims/<dim>.parquet — the dim's properties, bare since the subject is dim, and a nested dim's parent keys — each a scalar for every label or a sequence aligned to labels. A column no keyword names is NULL on these rows, since add restates a label's row whole. An Enum property's value must be one of its categories. An attribute keyword is refused with a pointer to set: an attribute's values are long rows whatever its dims, never a column of the axis. A column the schema does not declare is rejected: a staging table is shaped like the file it becomes, so there is no dtype to give such a column. A tool that grows a column declares it first, which schema versioning accepts as a widening.

It is not a sequence of set calls. A label exists by virtue of its axis row, and validation rejects a value for a label no layer declares; adding a bus with no properties is an edit, with nothing to set. Uniqueness is structural: one axis row per label, so an add of a label the record already resolves restates its row rather than creating a second.

Adding a component with its connections and varying values is add, then add_group, then a set per attribute.

remove(dim, labels) stages one tombstone per label, and no dim scope: a label exists or it does not. It need not enumerate what it deletes: the fold drops every value keyed by the label where dim is partial, a group attribute's by the label inside its struct (the owner map). It also tombstones every tuple, of any group, with a field over dim naming one of labels, read from the record as it resolves with pending edits, so the writer never meets a dangling tuple. Only for a dim keyed by its label alone: a nested dim's label names no point without its parents, which a tuple does not carry. An add of the same label revives the label alone: its tuples are re-added through add_group. remove is refused while a property into dim names one of the labels, read from the record as staged: a tuple goes with its label, but a property's row is its subject's and outlives it, so the caller sets it to another label or None first. A nested dim is not checked, as above.

docs.title: add_group / remove_group
docs.text:
w.add_group("connection", frame)  # a `connection` struct column, `role` beside it
w.remove_group("connection", [("dc", "north")])

The one staging path every declared group writes through.

frame is shaped like the group's file: one struct column named for the group (connection STRUCT(entity, bus), corridor STRUCT("from", "to")), its into label where it declares one, and the group's properties, such as PyPSA's role. A field as a column of its own is rejected with the struct to pass instead, as set rejects it. keys is a tuple per row in the group's key order, packed into the struct for the caller.

A group's attributes are not columns of its file but long rows, set through set with the group's fields as keywords.

docs.title: Edits
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord does not write. What it holds are two things the writers take:

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("p_nom", 100.0, entity=["gen1"])
edited = rev.child(w.edits)  # the delta, as a child layer
ws.write(w, "out/")  # base plus edits, flattened
w.rollback()
  • w.edits — the staged layer alone, the LayerData it already is. Written as a child of the revision w was built over, it is only the edits — that is what a patch layer is, and the fold resolves the rest from the parent. The layer lands in the child, never in the node branched from, so it is child's return value that reads the edits back.
  • w itself — what is staged plus what the record already reads, the whole resolved record. Written as a standalone directory, there being no parent to resolve against.

The writer cannot tell which it was handed, which is the point: "enumerate what I hold, hand each over" is one contract whether "what I hold" is a single layer or a whole fold.

Each part of a write now has one owner. Which rows to write is the caller's choice of w.edits or w. Which parent is named by the caller, who built w from it. Clearing the staging area is rollback(), called or not: a WorkingRecord still holding its edits after a write reads exactly what it did before.

One mistake is caught. other.child(w.edits), with w built over a different revision, would write a delta computed against the wrong parent — an axis edit carries its base's sibling columns — and read back wrong, so child compares the edits' base revision with its own id and raises on a mismatch. Edits over a directory have no revision as their base and so are a child of none. One mistake is not caught: rev.child(w) writes the whole resolved record as a child layer rather than the delta. It reads back correctly, just larger, and a resolved record being a valid layer source too, edits is the name that has to carry it.

An edited axis follows partial, exactly as an attribute's rows do. A partial axis is patched label by label: the layer holds the labels the edit touched, and the fold resolves the rest from the parent, last-writer-wins per axis key. An axis outside partial is owned whole once touched, so the layer restates every label with its properties — one rule for what non-partial means, rather than an axis-shaped exception to it. The fold would resolve the narrower form correctly, since it keys per label and an omitted one keeps its parent's row; what ownership buys is that a layer's axis file says what the axis is there, rather than being readable only against its parent. A standalone write of w writes the resolved axis whole either way, and an axis nothing touched is written by neither.

Restating on edit is what an axis outside partial costs, and it is the cheaper side of that trade — which is the reason not to reach for partial when an axis merely gains a property.

Neither carries the base's results across. An edit changes the inputs a result was computed from, so a parent's outputs/ says nothing about the child — results belong to the node that was solved, and a node with different inputs is a different node.

What a write does carry is results staged into this record through set(..., kind="outputs"). Those were computed against these pending inputs, so they describe exactly the layer being written, and both readings write them: a child written from edits holds the edits and the results computed from them together.

An edit replaces the rows it names rather than appending beside them: it deletes the rows at the coordinate it writes and inserts the new ones, so a staging table holds one row per coordinate and no fold is needed to read it. The key it replaces on is the coordinate — the same one a read would have collapsed — so the delete removes exactly what a last-writer-wins fold would have discarded. An axis or group property is the exception in mechanism, not in effect: a row's columns are independently editable, so a property set patches its one column in place (UPDATE) rather than replacing the row, which is what keeps a sibling property a different set wrote.

Per coordinate, not per ownership key: the ownership key excludes the dims an attribute is not owned per, so replacing on it would drop a whole staged series to one row — two edits at different snapshots are two coordinates, not two writes to the same place. The same distinction governs the read overlay and the restate below, and it is the one thing easy to get wrong here.

Three interactions need stating, because each is where replacing by coordinate alone is not the whole story:

  • remove after set on the same label: the tombstone wins, since a deleted label has no values. A tombstone reaches another file's rows, so it stays an anti-join at read and write rather than a replace — the attribute rows are keyed by coordinate, the tombstone by label. A layer's tombstones apply only to its parents in the fold, so the staged collapse drops its own rows itself: a row naming a removed label, and a row whose group column names a tuple staged deleted, by remove_group or by remove's cascade.
  • add after remove of the same label: the label exists again. The axis replaces on its key, so the add row displaces the tombstone by construction. So do the parent's values for it, which only the displaced tombstone reached; its tuples stay removed.
  • set on a label this record also added: correct as-is, the attribute living in inputs/ and a property patching the staged row.

The non-partial rule is the subtle one. Overwriting one value along a non-partial axis means the layer must carry that label's whole extent along it, so such a set reads the resolved series for that key and stages the untouched coordinates alongside the edit. That is the one read of parent data an edit makes, and it happens as the rows are staged rather than at write: the staging table then already holds what the layer will hold, so a write of edits has no completion step of its own.

The scope is the key the edit named, never the attribute: a label no edit mentioned keeps its rows in the parent, and a layer carrying them would claim an extent it was never given. A group outside partial is owned whole the same way. A set on one connection's efficiency stages every other connection's resolved value beside it, and the scope is the attribute: a connection attribute's key names no label of a partial dim, so the key the edit named is (attribute) alone. A staged row that leaves the axis NULL is the exception, since the broadcast rule already makes it cover every label — there is nothing left to carry, and a carried row beside it would overlap. Carried rows go in only where no edit already holds the coordinate, so a later set on a carried coordinate replaces the fill rather than tying with it — the anti-join that keeps a fill off an occupied coordinate is the whole of what orders the two.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The writer validates structurally, so writing edits inherits that. What editing adds is edit-level, caught when the edit is staged, not at write — a caller should learn about a typo'd attribute at the line that typed it, not fifty edits later:

  • an undeclared attribute, result, property or keyword, or a keyword the attribute does not vary over; a plain name only properties are called is refused naming their dotted forms, set("carrier", …) suggesting bus.carrier and entity.carrier;
  • a label of a partial dim the record does not resolve, add them first;
  • a label whose categories do not carry the attribute (traits), judged by its current categories; a label with no category passes;
  • a value an Enum property does not list, in add or set;
  • a value of a property into a dim naming no label of it, as staged, in add or set — set("entity.carrier", "coal", entity="g1") with no carrier label coal; NULL names none;
  • an add missing a nested dim's parent key, or naming an attribute.

The label read these need is the one a property keyword already performs, so checking categories costs nothing beyond it. Two coordinates over one categorized dim — a contract's from and to — name no one label whose categories decide, so neither is checked against them.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
Staged rows live in DuckDB tables on the record's own connection:

CREATE TABLE staged_inputs_<attr>_<id>   (<that attribute's long columns>);
CREATE TABLE staged_outputs_<attr>_<id>  (<that attribute's long columns>);
CREATE TABLE staged_axis_<dim>_<id>      (<the axis key>, <the dim's properties>, deleted BOOLEAN);
CREATE TABLE staged_<group>_<id>         (<group struct>, <into>, <the group's properties>, deleted BOOLEAN);

Every table is shaped like the file it becomes, which is the rule the rest of this section is consequences of. So there is no table whose columns are a union over things the format keeps apart, and a column the schema does not declare has nowhere to go — add rejects one rather than widening a table to fit it, there being no declared dtype to give it.

One table per staged attribute, because that is the file it becomes: its columns are the attribute's own coordinates and value has the attribute's declared type. A shared table would have to widen value to text and carry every declared dim, which costs twice: the value needs casting back on the way out, and a NULL in a dim column becomes ambiguous between "this attribute has no such axis" and the broadcast rule's "every value of it". Per attribute both questions are answered by the table's shape, so neither is asked.

A result the schema never declares has no declared type to take; the table records the one its frame arrived with, settled once at creation rather than guessed per read.

One table per staged axis and per declared group, mirroring the maps the fold builds: its key, its properties and a tombstone column, so add writes one row per label and remove one tombstone. Both replace on the key, so re-adding or removing a label displaces its earlier row rather than stacking beside it, while a property set patches one column in place. entity is staged as any other dim, staged_axis_entity_<id>, and reaches the fold as axis("entity") with no special case.

These tables are the only place a staged row exists: the reads read them rather than holding a copy.

DuckDB rather than in-memory objects, for three reasons that all matter: the reads are already a fold, so staging elsewhere would mean marshalling every edit into a relation on every read; a large edit is a bulk insert rather than ten thousand Python objects; and a write of edits hands each table to the writer as the file it already is, no collapse in between.

Tables in the workspace's database, like the folded caches, so on :memory: they vanish with the workspace and never appear on disk. A record whose edits must survive a process boundary should be written as a child.

An edit replaces what it names rather than appending, so a table holds one row per key and reading it is a scan — no ordering column, and edit order is just which edit ran last.

docs.title: Reading with pending edits
docs.text:
The inherited Record members must reflect the edits; otherwise set then read gives the old value, which no caller would expect.

A set of pending edits is a layer — an unwritten one. So the reads compose the same way: the staged rows are the last layer, resolved over whatever the record was reading before.

resolved = fold(parent layers..., staged rows)

This is exactly one more fold step over the same owner-map machinery, with the staging tables standing in for a layer directory — over a layered base or a plain directory alike, a directory being a layer laid out like any other. It costs what one more layer costs, per read: a written layer is folded once and cached forever, and the staged one cannot be, being the only layer that can still change. So the fold is materialised up to the last layer that cannot change under the reader, and the staged step on top of it stays a relation — which is also why an edit needs no invalidation, there being nothing cached to invalidate.

flags follows for free, computed in the fold's own ownership GROUP BY as it is for any layer: a staged row setting a dim adds it to varies, one leaving it NULL adds it to broadcast, and a staged curve sets breakpoints. It says nothing about a property, which is a column of its subject's axis or group file and read from properties or members, staged edits included.

An axis overlays per column rather than per row: a staged label's edited columns win, and a label the edit did not name keeps the base's whole row. So two set calls for two properties of one label compose instead of the later one blanking the earlier's column.

docs.title: Writing a whole record
docs.text:
store.root(source) -> Revision  # a new root with this layer
rev.child(source) -> Revision  # a new child of rev with this layer
ws.write(source, uri) -> Record  # a standalone directory, read back

Three calls make something, one per place it can go, and each is named for what it returns. child lives on the parent rather than as a store call taking a parent, which would name the store twice, and not as rev.write, which would read as changing rev when layers are write-once. A call per destination rather than one taking a target, because a tree write needs the location and the tree, a directory write only a connection, and the two return different things.

Each writes source as a new layer. An existing layer directory is an error rather than an overwrite or a merge, so a whole-record write can never half-replace what a record holds.

outputs/ is written only for a source whose outputs mapping is non-empty, so a record with no results produces a layer with no outputs/ rather than an empty directory.

Keys are looked up one at a time and each file written before the next is built, so a lazily-building source does one read per file written rather than one per key up front. Locally, frames are staged into a sibling directory and renamed on success, so a frame the fold could not resolve leaves no layer rather than half of one.

Every column the schema declares a type for is cast to it on the way out, so a record's files carry the schema's types and a reader can trust them. Without that a source may hand over an all-NULL column its dataframe library typed as float, and every reader would re-cast defensively instead.

Validation is structural: a long frame carries its attribute's own coordinates, and an entity frame carries every dim it is keyed by. Which entity types are valid belongs to the schema's vocabulary, which the record layer does not interpret.

An input attribute the schema does not declare is rejected, unlike an entity type: its dims are what say which columns its file carries, so an undeclared one has no shape to write it in and would leave a file no reader could derive the columns of. A result is exempt — Tool.results derives which attributes count as results from a framework's own registry, so an unknown name is an error for an input and simply unknowable for a result.

A frame carrying a column its attribute is not addressed by is rejected too, rather than narrowed on the way out. The read path projects an attribute's own coordinates, so such a column would be written and never read — and a source emitting one means something different by the attribute than the schema does, which is worth reporting rather than absorbing. A result is exempt from both checks: its shape is a framework's business, and a name it shares with an input says nothing about which coordinates the result varies over.

The input is a LayerData: "the rows of one thing, enumerated and read" — the same interface a LayerSource answers for its own layer and a Resolver answers for a whole fold, so the writer cannot tell which it was handed and does not need to. A staged layer's own rows and a resolved record are both a LayerData, which is what lets a WorkingRecord hand over either.

A framework object exposing narwhals frames — Record rather than LayerData — is not itself one: the writer wraps it in a thin adapter that reads its Frames mappings as the enumerate-and-read pairs LayerData declares, so a tool stays narwhals-facing and the layered write path stays raw-relation throughout.

docs.title: A revision exists only by its file
docs.text:
The revision file is written last, and its existence is what makes the layer real. A tree write runs in three steps: the layer, then the manifest, then revisions/<id>.json. Without the revision file no revision(), revisions() or ancestry reaches the layer.

Locally a failed write leaves nothing, the layer being staged and renamed. Remotely there is no rename, so a failed write can leave part of a layer behind — but unreachable rather than half-read, which makes a remote write atomic in what any reader can see. Removing such leftovers is cleanup, a separate concern.

The manifest check comes after the layer, so a layer whose schema turns out incompatible, or whose write fails, leaves the manifest untouched as well as unreachable: the manifest is never widened for a layer that does not exist.

docs.title: The manifest's compare-and-swap
docs.text:
Two writers creating a location's first layers, or widening its schema, at once race on manifest.json. So the manifest is written through a conditional write: read with its version — Absent where there is none — checked for compatibility, and written only if still at that version. A writer that lost re-reads and checks again, so two writers widening at once end with both widenings, where the later one's schema includes the earlier's, or with the later one's incompatibility reported, never one silently lost. The retry is bounded: a writer that loses ten times, backing off with jitter in between, gives up with an error. That is also what a credential that can write manifest.json but not read it meets, since a remote read answered 403 counts as missing and every create-only write then fails.

materialise() follows the same rule. owner_map/inputs.parquet is what says a node is materialised, so it is written last, after the other maps, the resolved dims and groups. Locally each file is written under a temporary name and renamed, because a parquet file appears at its final path before it is complete and a reader meeting it mid-write fails rather than misses. Two writers materialising one node write the same content, so that race is harmless.

docs.title: A standalone directory
docs.text:
A standalone directory has no revision file, so there the manifest is written last: ws.at requires one, so a directory whose write failed reads as no record rather than part of one. ws.write writes to a URI that does not exist yet, refusing one that does — locally the path, even an empty directory, remotely any key under it — as a whole-record write refuses an existing layer: unlike a layer's UUID the caller picks this URI, and a write over an existing record would mix the two under the old manifest. The check and the write are two steps, so two writers racing to one new URI can still mix; a standalone directory has one writer.

Each write mints the record a fresh id, carried in its manifest, so a record deleted and written again at one URI is a new layer to every workspace rather than the old one's cached folds. ws.write and ws.at resolve a local path as ws.store does.

docs.title: DEP 1: Dims, mappings, groups and traits
DEP 1: dims, mappings, groups and traits
docs.text:
DEP 1 Title dims, mappings, groups and traits Author Jonas Hörsch Status Implemented 2026-08-16 Created 2026-08-15 Version v0.1.0a1

This page is the argument, not the design. What shipped is described by the schema — groups, traits — together with the record format and the read path, and those pages are authoritative where the two disagree. The on mapping this page landed has since been absorbed into groups as into, so its half of the argument describes a construct that no longer exists.

It is kept because the reasoning is not reproduced there: why keys was deleted rather than replaced, why bus stopped being structural, and what the worked example exposed about vocabulary collisions. Two things it raises stayed open and moved to open questions: whether existence may depend on a dim, and whether flags(ctype) needs a record-level counterpart.

Read below for why; read the design pages for what.

Two departures from the sketch below are worth naming, since the text still reads as though neither happened. shape() was not implemented — flags(ctype) stands alone, and the gap it leaves is the open question above. And set grew no bus= parameter: every coordinate but entity goes through **dims, which is what lets a two-coordinate group be addressed at all.

docs.title: What starts it
docs.text:
An attribute that belongs to no component type has nowhere to live.

Snapshot weightings are the case. A weighting is a number per snapshot — it varies over the time axis and over nothing else, and it is not a property of any generator, bus or line. Today Schema.attributes is component type -> attribute -> spec, so there is no key such a thing could be filed under. It is carried instead as an extra column on the axis frame, undeclared: dims/snapshots.parquet gains an objective column, and the PyPSA tool's import half recognises it by name.

That works and it is invisible. The column has no dtype, no default, no unit, no description; it appears in no flags; it does not resolve across layers; a reader that is not this tool cannot know it is an attribute at all. The same holds for the scenario weightings the fold already carries alongside the scenario axis.

The narrow fix is a place to declare axis payload columns. The wider observation is that name is not different in kind from snapshot: it is an axis, attribute values are addressed by it, and the reason it looks structural is that the schema is nested under it. Once that is seen, several other things in the design turn out to be the same mechanism written three ways.

docs.title: The four mechanisms
docs.text:
what it declares where it lives dimension an axis of labels dims/<dim>.parquet — labels and order, plus any attribute addressed by it alone mapping each label of the dim I am on has one label of mine a Dimension subclass; own axis file, plus a column on the classified dim's file group which tuples over several dims exist own table; subsumes connections trait which entities an attribute applies to a subscription on the component type

within is unchanged and stays a fifth thing, distinct from mapping — see mappings are not within.

The unifying claim is that AttributeSpec.dims becomes the only addressing mechanism. An attribute is addressed by the coordinates it declares; whether one of those is an entity axis, a group, a mapped classification or a plain axis changes where the labels come from, not how the attribute is declared or stored.

docs.title: entity — the component axis
docs.text:
name becomes a declared dim, called entity. It gets an axis file like any other dim, and that file is what a component's identity is:

dims/entity.parquet     entity | component_type | deleted

Four things move there, each of which is currently derived or enforced elsewhere:

Uniqueness becomes structural. One row per entity in one file, so the collision name uniqueness rejects at two call sites cannot be represented.

entity -> component_type is a column read. Today it is "the file a name's row is in", so building the components map means globbing every type's file and injecting the type per arm. The owner map already treats component_type as carried-not-keyed, functionally determined by the key — which is the shape of a payload column. This puts it where that shape says it belongs.

Tombstones get one home. Deleting a component is deleting its entity row, rather than a deleted flag globbed across per-type files.

Order is generated, not stored. order_key is a column of the owner map, never of a layer's parquet: the fold computes it as max(parent) + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY _row) per layer, from that file's own row order, and it persists only where a node's maps are materialised. Assigned before the union, because row_number() over what UNION ALL emits has no defined order to recover. Nothing sorts eagerly — a consumer wanting order applies ORDER BY order_key.

So dims/entity.parquet carries no order column, exactly as an axis file carries none: file order is the input, order_key is the derived answer. That is one rule for every table that folds, rather than a components-and-connections special case — and it is why the entity axis needs no more on disk than an ordinary dim's, despite being the one axis whose order is a fold product rather than a single file's.

The test for the rest is does this table gain rows across layers? A group does, and its map keeps order_key for the load-bearing reason the read path records: a framework reconstructing positional ports numbers them by this order, and a reshuffle silently moves an existing connection's attributes to a different port. An ordinary dim does not — an axis is not partial, so a layer restating it restates it whole and file order survives untouched.

What remains in dims/components/<Type>.parquet is then only what varies over nothing — the non-varying attribute values, partitioned by type. The partition is justified by the one thing that genuinely is per type: the attribute vocabulary, since every type has a different column set.

An attribute with no entity in its dims needs no owner and no special case:

"objective_weighting": AttributeSpec(dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"snapshot"})

That is the thing that started this, expressible — and the file-split rule puts it on dims/snapshot.parquet, which is where the undeclared column sits today.

docs.title: Attributes are top-level
docs.text:
Schema.attributes inverts: flat, one spec per attribute, and component types subscribe.

The current nesting says an attribute belongs to a component type. Once entity is one dim among several that is false in both directions — objective_weighting has no type, and p_max_pu is carried by Generator, Link and StorageUnit as three identical specs.

The storage already disagrees with the declaration: inputs/p_max_pu.parquet holds every type's rows in one file, keyed by name alone, with one value dtype. So the nesting is expressive where the storage is not — two types may declare the same attribute with different dtypes, and one column has to serve both. Nothing rejects that today; it is a silent wrong read waiting for a record that does it.

Flat declaration makes it unrepresentable, which is the stronger form of the same guarantee. The declaration then matches the file layout one-to-one: one attribute, one spec, one file, one dtype.

attributes = {
    "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"entity", "snapshot", "scenario"}, default=1.0
    ),
    "p_nom": AttributeSpec(dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"entity"}, default=0.0),
    "efficiency": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"connection", "snapshot"}, default=1.0
    ),
    "objective_weighting": AttributeSpec(
        dtype="DOUBLE", dims={"snapshot"}, default=1.0
    ),
}

AttributeSpec.bus is deleted: a connection attribute is one whose dims name the connection group.

docs.title: Where a value lives
docs.text:
Today the split is bool(spec.dims): varying over nothing puts an attribute in dims/components/<Type>.parquet as a column, anything else in inputs/<attr>.parquet as long rows. That test breaks the moment entity is a dim — capacity gains dims={"entity"}, bool says varying, and every non-varying attribute silently moves file.

The rule that replaces it: an attribute naming exactly one addressing coordinate and nothing else is a column on that thing's own table.

dims lands in {"entity"} dims/components/<Type>.parquet — one column per attribute, per type {"connection"} the connection group's table {"corridor"} dims/corridor.parquet {"scenario"} dims/scenario.parquet — the axis file {"entity", "snapshot"} inputs/<attr>.parquet {"connection", "snapshot"} inputs/<attr>.parquet

So varying is not "has dims" but "has dims beyond its address", and one rule now covers what were three unrelated stories: a component's constant columns, a connection's role, and an axis's payload.
