Every key has one meaning, and both tools know every key. mathspec stays strict: a key neither tool declares is refused. A key only one tool acts on is still validated for shape by both, so a typo in partial fails in mathspec and a typo in constraints fails in datarecord.

key datarecord reads it as mathspec reads it as dimensions the axes, the multi-dims and the enum dimensions the index sets properties properties, stored on the subject's table values per label, addressed subject.name parameters the inputs, in inputs/ the data a model reads variables the results, in outputs/ the decision variables constraints, expressions with result: true results too as today objective, conditions, macros, piecewise, sos, assumptions nothing; stored with the manifest as today partial, meta, within, traits as today nothing unit, description stored, not interpreted stored, not interpreted

traits keeps DEP 17's form until DEP 19 replaces it. attributes and results go as manifest keys; Schema.attributes and Schema.results stay as the read API, derived from the table above.

docs.title: Properties of a dimension
docs.text:
properties is a top-level section keyed by subject, as DEP 12 declares it. A subject is a dimension or a multi-dim, and under it each entry names one property:

properties:
  <subject>: # a key of `dimensions`
    <name>: # unique within the subject; addressed `<subject>.<name>`
      into: <dim> # its values are labels of <dim>; or
      dtype: <dtype> # a plain value: float, int, str, bool, date, datetime
      missing: <fill> # a value, refused or absent; or {by, cases, otherwise}
      unit: <str>
      description: <str>
  • Exactly one of into and dtype. into makes the property a reference: each value must be a live label of the named dim, checked as DEP 13 checks it. dtype makes it a plain value.
  • No dims. A property is one value per label of its subject and never varies along another axis. A value that does is a parameter.
  • missing: refused says every label must have a value; absent that a label may have none. A value is the fill, as default was.
  • missing: {by, cases, otherwise} is DEP 17's per-category default, renamed; any fill, refused or absent included, may stand in cases or otherwise. The same form applies to a parameter's missing.
  • A coordinate of a multi-dim is not declared here. connection.entity and connection.bus come from over, as DEP 15 declares.

Datarecord stores a property as a column of its subject's table, dims/<subject>.parquet, and hands it over through record.properties[subject], as today. mathspec reads it as a value per label of its subject:

property in a condition, where or holds in an expression into (link.bus0) link.bus0 != link.bus1 by=link.bus0, at(x, by=link.bus0), within=snapshot.period dtype (bus.x) bus.x > 0 a parameter over [bus]

A category is a label of an enum dimension, as DEP 16 declares, and #915, once merged, refuses at load a condition comparing a reference to that dimension with any other label. So a typo in a category fails at load in both tools: a constraint's where: "entity.component == 'Genrator'" is refused by mathspec, and cases: {Genrator: 1} under missing by both.

docs.title: Properties replace relations
docs.text:
A mathspec relation is a property of its key, or of a multi-dim naming its key:

mathspec today becomes Link_carrier: {key: link, values: carrier} properties.link.carrier: {into: carrier} ends: {key: line, values: {bus0: bus, bus1: bus}} properties.line.bus0: {into: bus}, .bus1: {into: bus} zone_of: {key: [plant, period], values: zone} multi-dim plant_period, property zone: {into: zone} connection: {key: [entity, bus]} (bare) multi-dim connection: {over: [entity, bus]} missing: refused \| absent on a relation missing on the property sum(x, over=link, by=Link_carrier[carrier]) sum(x, over=link, by=link.carrier) ends[bus0] != ends[bus1] in a where line.bus0 != line.bus1

A property that is not into a dim, such as bus.x, is a value per label of its subject. In math it reads as a parameter over [bus], addressed bus.x. Whether a value is a property or a parameter stays the author's declaration: it decides where datarecord stores it, not what the math can do with it.

docs.title: Shared spellings
docs.text:
Where the two differ after DEP 17, one spelling is picked:

concept datarecord after DEP 17 mathspec today both dtypes Float64, Int64, String, Boolean, Date, {Datetime: us} float, int, str, bool, datetime float, int, str, bool, date, datetime fill for an unset value default missing (a value, or refused, absent, neutral) missing fill per category default: {by, cases, otherwise} none missing: {by, cases, otherwise} inputs attributes parameters parameters outputs results variables variables, and result: true a multi-coordinate set dimensions, over relations, key dimensions, over a value per label properties, into relations, values properties, into a curve's axis AttributeSpec.breakpoints piecewise.over breakpoints: true on the dimension

neutral is on mathspec main; the open mathspec#894 removes it, and nothing here needs it.

Datarecord stores a breakpoint dim as the breakpoint column of a long row, not as a dim column, so a parameter over a breakpoints dim is the breakpoints=True attribute of today, read with that dim dropped from its dims.

docs.title: Traits stay datarecord's
docs.text: traits is a key only datarecord reads, as partial is; mathspec validates its shape and carries it. DEP 19 replaces it with mathspec's conditions.

docs.title: Who owns the language
docs.text:
mathspec owns the schema of the file; datarecord depends on it. mathspec.to_spec parses and validates a manifest, and Schema wraps the resulting mathspec.Spec and derives its views from it. Two pydantic models of one file would be the drift this DEP removes, one level down. mathspec needs only pydantic, pyparsing and pyyaml.

Schema.spec is the mathspec.Spec. A framework building a model from a record takes the spec from it rather than being handed one, and the record's inputs are by construction the spec's parameters.

A manifest is self-contained: it is one resolved file, fragments being combined with mathspec.merge before writing, and a spec with a non-empty given is refused.

docs.title: Changes in mathspec
docs.text:
Each of these is an issue to raise on mathspec, unless it names a pull request. Datarecord implements this DEP once they are released. Status is as of mathspec main on 2026-10-21. They assume mathspec#915, open, is merged as it stands: enum on a str dimension, carried on program.Dimension.enum, and a label compared to it checked at load.

  1. Multi-dims in dimensions. A dimension with over (a list, or a coordinate→dim map) and no dtype. It may appear in any dims, is iterated as tuples, and its coordinates are addressed connection.bus wherever a property may be. The datarecord side is DEP 15. Not proposed.
  2. properties replace relations. A per-subject section, where the subject is a dimension or multi-dim. An entry is into: <dim> (its values are that dim's labels) or a dtype, with missing, unit, description. relations is removed. Not proposed.
  3. Dotted addressing. subject.name reads a property or coordinate in by=, at, within=, where strings and expressions. . becomes reserved in names. The PyPSA example's prefixes (Link_bus0, Link_carrier) become link.bus0, link.carrier. Not proposed: mathspec#516 compared relation spellings, and its dotted proposal, #509, was closed.
  4. #915's label check reaches properties. It checks a RelationComparison in #915; entity.component == 'Generator' is the same comparison once the relation is a property into an enum dimension, as DEP 16 has it on the datarecord side. Also a date dtype. Builds on #915; the rest not proposed.
  5. A per-category missing. missing takes a value, a keyword, or {by, cases, otherwise} on parameters and properties. by is a property into an enum dimension of a dim the entry reaches; cases keys are checked against that enum at load; a reader fills an unset value from the label's case, else otherwise. The datarecord side is DEP 17. Not proposed.
  6. breakpoints: true on a dimension. A piecewise block's over must name one; an ordered numeric dtype is implied. Not proposed.
  7. result: true on constraints and expressions. Marks a dual or value a consumer stores. mathspec gives it no meaning. Not proposed.
  8. Keys with no math meaning. partial, meta and traits at the top level, within on a dimension, unit on dimensions, parameters, variables, properties and expressions. Validated for shape, carried, otherwise ignored. unit is asked for in mathspec#836, open, with no pull request; the rest not proposed.
  9. A public model of the file. Spec is what datarecord parses with, so its fields, the ones above included, are part of mathspec's public API. On main: mathspec.spec is public since mathspec#878; the new fields join it.
  10. A version bump. version: 1, since relations goes and dtype spellings change. Not proposed.
  11. The PyPSA spec over one entity dim. See one entity dim. Not proposed; mathspec#843, open, discusses deriving datarecord's schema from mathspec's PyPSA files.

docs.title: PyPSA: one entity dim
docs.text:
PyPSA's components are labels of one entity dim, categorized by entity.component, as datarecord's PyPSA tool has them since DEP 13. mathspec's PyPSA spec moves to that shape; the tool does not move to mathspec's.

mathspec's PyPSA spec today becomes dims generator, link, line, store, … one dim entity; component: {enum: [...]}; entity.component Generator_p_nom, Link_p_nom p_nom: {dims: [entity]} Link_bus0, Link_output_bus, Line_bus0, … the multi-dim connection over (entity, bus), with connection.role link_output and its two relations connection, role: output Link_efficiency over link_output efficiency: {dims: [connection]} a per-type sum, sum(Link_p, over=link, …) sum(p, over=entity, …) in a constraint with where: "entity.component == 'Link'" a name one type has, Store_e_nom e_nom: {dims: [entity]}, carried by stores only through a trait
  • A name shared by types is one parameter. Its fill may differ per type through a per-category missing; which types may carry it is a trait, and a where after DEP 19.
  • A per-type constraint is filtered, not indexed. Each constraint over a type's dim becomes one over entity with a where on entity.component. The math is the same; the index set is wider and filtered.
  • This is the largest change in the list. The PyPSA spec is about 4600 lines, and every name, dim and relation in it is touched.

docs.title: What changes in datarecord
docs.text:
• attributes and results as manifest keys are replaced by parameters, variables and result: true.
  • default becomes missing, in DEP 17's shape, gaining refused and absent; dtypes take the shared spellings.
  • breakpoints moves from the attribute to the dimension.
  • Schema is built from mathspec.to_spec, and mathspec becomes a core dependency.
  • version goes to 2.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
One file, not a spec embedded in a manifest. Embedding the spec under a math key with datarecord's annotations beside it needs nothing from mathspec, and leaves two places that name every parameter. Aligning the languages costs a list of upstream changes once and removes the second place for good.

Properties, not relations. After DEP 13 the single-coordinate relation is a property in datarecord, stored as one column of its subject's row. mathspec spelling it as a separate table with a prefixed name (Link_carrier) is the namespace spelled into the name that DEP 13 rejected.

mathspec's words where they differ. parameters, variables and missing are what a modeller reads; missing also carries refused and absent, which default cannot say. Datarecord is pre-1.0 and its manifests are rewritten either way.

What breaks:

  • Every manifest is rewritten, and every record re-exported: attributes/results to parameters/variables, default to missing, dtypes respelled.
  • Core gains a dependency on mathspec, agreed for this DEP; CONTRIBUTING.md's list of core dependencies changes with it.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Building a record's schema from the PyPSA spec fragments:

spec = mathspec.merge(["pypsa/network.yaml", "pypsa/generator.yaml", "pypsa/link.yaml"])
ws.write(root(Schema(spec)), uri)

Reading the spec back from a record:

record = Workspace.at(uri).record
record.schema.spec.program.parameters["p_nom"].dims  # ("entity",)
record.attributes["p_nom"]  # its data

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Raise the mathspec issues for each item in Changes in mathspec, and agree the shared spellings there.
  2. Land DEP 15, DEP 16 and DEP 17, which need nothing from mathspec.
  3. Parse with mathspec. Schema wraps mathspec.Spec; attributes, results, properties, dimensions derived; shared spellings; version 2.
  4. The PyPSA tool reads mathspec's PyPSA spec once it is over one entity dim, instead of building a schema from PyPSA's registry.

Checks that hold once built:

  • One file validates in both: mathspec.to_spec(path) and Schema(mathspec.to_spec(path)) both accept the PyPSA manifest.
  • A schema round-trips through manifest.json, and its spec equals what it was built from.
  • Removing a parameter from the spec removes the attribute.
  • Every trait test passes with traits read from the mathspec-parsed manifest.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text:
The spec embedded under a math key, with datarecord's annotations in sibling sections. Needs no mathspec change, and keeps two places naming every parameter. The first draft of this DEP proposed it.

An extension slot in mathspec (x-datarecord: per block). Two vocabularies in one file, one of them opaque to the other.

Properties nested in their dimension's entry (bus: {dtype: str, properties: {x: …}}). Keeps a dim self-contained, but makes dimensions hold two kinds of entry body and departs from the per-subject section DEP 12 settled; a top-level properties sits beside parameters as the other kind of value.

One dim per PyPSA component, as mathspec's PyPSA spec has it. Every name is prefixed with its type, a name two types share is two parameters, and a record could not add a component type without a schema per type. Datarecord's tool already has one entity dim.

docs.title: Properties in the math
docs.text: Whether a non-into property is readable in expressions, or only in where and by=. bus.x as a parameter over [bus] blurs the property/attribute line for the math, while datarecord keeps it for storage.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: Which constraints and expressions are results. result: true is explicit. Every constraint's dual being one would be shorter and store data nobody reads.

docs.title: Upstream
docs.text:
• mathspec#915 is open. If it merges under another key or shape, DEP 16 and this DEP take its spelling. If it does not merge, change 4 grows to propose enum itself.
  • Most of the changes in mathspec are not proposed yet. Each one mathspec declines leaves its key datarecord's alone: listed beside partial for mathspec to carry unread, or kept out of the shared file. One declined broadly (properties, dotted addressing) leaves this DEP as the embedded spec it rejects.

docs.title: DEP 19: conditions replace traits
docs.text: DEP 19 Title conditions replace traits Author Bryn Pickering Status Draft Requires DEP 17, DEP 18 Created 2026-10-21 Replaces DEP 3

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: Traits go. Which labels may carry a parameter becomes a where on the parameter, in mathspec's condition grammar, and a rule over values becomes one of mathspec's assumptions. Datarecord checks both, a where when a value is staged and an assumption when a layer is written, so removing traits removes no refusal. This settles #60.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
A manifest that is a mathspec (DEP 18) says which labels carry what twice. traits is a key only datarecord reads; a constraint's where on entity.component says the same thing to the math. A trait renamed in one and not the other drifts.

A trait cannot state a rule over values. p_max_pu within [0, 1] is checked nowhere. mathspec's assumptions state it, and leave the check to the consumer attaching data.

A switch cannot vary. DEP 3 left open a switch that differs by period. A condition reading a parameter varies as the parameter does.

docs.title: What a trait said is a condition
docs.text:
A trait narrows: p_max_pu is carried by generators and links only. That is a where on the parameter, in mathspec's condition grammar. A rule over values rather than labels is an assumption.

trait after DEP 17 becomes on: {by: entity.component, cases: [Generator, Link]}, attributes: [p_max_pu] p_max_pu: {where: "entity.component == 'Generator' OR entity.component == 'Link'"} an attribute no trait claims, carried by every label a parameter with no where switch: p_nom_extendable (DEP 3) p_nom_max: {where: "p_nom_extendable"}, a condition on a boolean parameter Schema.attributes_for(dim, **categories) the same call, evaluating each where against the given categories set refusing an attribute the category does not carry set refusing a label its where excludes 
parameters:
  p_max_pu:
    dims: [entity, snapshot]
    missing: 1
    where: "entity.component == 'Generator' OR entity.component == 'Link'"

assumptions:
  p_max_pu_is_a_fraction: "p_max_pu >= 0 AND p_max_pu <= 1"

A parameter's where is not on mathspec main, where only variables and constraints take one (changes in mathspec).

docs.title: When each is checked
docs.text:
A where is checked per label, when a value is staged. set, add and the writer evaluate it against the label's properties and parameters as staged, and refuse a value for a label it excludes, naming the condition. A NULL broadcast reaches only the labels the where admits.

An assumption is checked per write, against the folded record. It may relate several values a caller stages one at a time, so it is evaluated when a layer is written, not on each set. A failing entry refuses the write with mathspec.program.assumption_message, the message mathspec defines for it. The assumptions mathspec adds for a piecewise block are on Program.assumptions beside the file's, and are checked the same way.

Datarecord evaluates the condition mathspec parses. mathspec exposes each parsed condition on the program as a typed tree (program.Mask, Assumption.holds); datarecord compiles it to a narwhals expression over the folded frames. A condition using a construct datarecord cannot compile is refused at schema load, not skipped.

A category in a condition is checked at load once mathspec#915, open, merges and reaches properties (DEP 18, change 4): where: "entity.component == 'Genrator'" is then refused. Until then a misspelt category excludes every label.

docs.title: What goes
docs.text: traits, Trait, Schema.traits, switch and _carried go, and traits leaves DEP 18's list of keys only datarecord reads.

docs.title: Changes in mathspec
docs.text:
Status is as of mathspec main on 2026-10-21.

  1. where on parameters. A parameter's where says which labels may hold a value, in the condition grammar, checked by the consumer that attaches data as assumptions are. On the program it is a Mask, as a variable's is. Not proposed.
  2. Conditions as public trees. On main: program.Mask and program.Assumption are public, and assumption_message with them. Nothing to change.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
One mechanism, mathspec's. A trait and a where both say which labels carry a value; one keyed on PyPSA's component types and read only by datarecord, the other in a grammar the math already reads. Keeping the second removes the first.

Staged versus written. A where reads one label's own properties and parameters, which a set has in hand. An assumption may relate values staged by separate calls, so only the written layer can be checked.

What breaks:

  • Every trait in a manifest is rewritten as a where.
  • A write can now fail on an assumption over values, which no trait could state. A record written before this DEP may not pass them.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
w.set(
    "p_max_pu", 0.8, entity="load1"
)  # refused: `entity.component == 'Generator' OR ...` excludes it
schema.attributes_for("entity", component="Store")  # evaluates each `where`

docs.title: Implementation notes
docs.text:
1. Compile mathspec's condition trees to narwhals.
  2. Check a parameter's where in set, add and the writer, and assumptions on write.
  3. Rebuild attributes_for on where.
  4. Port each PyPSA trait to a where; then drop Trait.

Checks that hold once built:

  • Every refusal a trait made, a where makes: the trait tests pass with each trait rewritten as a where.
  • A failing assumption refuses the write, with mathspec's message, and a passing record writes unchanged.

docs.title: Rejected Ideas
docs.text: Keeping traits beside assumptions. Two mechanisms for which labels carry which values, one keyed on PyPSA's component types.

docs.title: Open Issues
docs.text:
• What an assumption check costs on a large record. It is evaluated against the folded record on each write. Scoping it to the values a layer touches would be cheaper and needs the fold to say which those are.
  • Which conditions datarecord compiles. The grammar has comparisons, AND, OR, NOT and presence; anything a later mathspec adds must be compiled or refused at load.
  • mathspec may not take a parameter's where. If it declines, where on a parameter joins traits as a key mathspec carries unread, and the math does not see it. If it takes another shape, this DEP follows that spelling.
  • mathspec#915 is open. If it does not merge, or does not reach properties, a misspelt category in a where is not caught at load, and datarecord checks it against the enum itself.

docs.text:

Keep it under about 2,000 words. State each rule once, in the section it belongs to, and cut what restates it, narrates how the design was found, or tours internals the reader can look up.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install datarecord           # core
pip install datarecord[pypsa]    # with the PyPSA tool

Or with conda/mamba, from conda-forge:

conda install -c conda-forge datarecord

docs.title: Workspaces and stores
docs.text:
A Workspace holds the DuckDB database and reaches files; a Store is one location — its schema, its revisions, its layers — on a workspace several stores share (design).

from datarecord import Workspace

ws = Workspace()  # ":memory:" by default
store = ws.store("/data/my-record")  # absolute; never empty
record = ws.at("out/")  # a standalone directory

ws.con is the calling thread's DuckDB cursor, so one workspace serves every thread; a frame belongs to the thread that built it.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: page what it covers Reading a record the Record protocol, properties, flags The schema declaring dims, properties and attributes Layers revisions, branching, materialising Editing WorkingRecord: set, add, edits Writing store.root, rev.child, ws.write Tools consuming a record from a modelling framework

docs.title: Editing
docs.text:
WorkingRecord is a record plus pending edits, held in memory and not yet written anywhere. It satisfies Record, so what it reads is the data with its pending edits applied — an edit can be read back, or the record handed to something that only knows how to read, without writing it (design).

from datarecord import WorkingRecord

w = WorkingRecord(root.record)

docs.title: set
docs.text:
w.set("p_nom", 150.0, entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # broadcast
w.set("p_nom", [150.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])  # per label, positional
w.set("p_nom", {"wind1": 150.0, "wind2": 80.0})  # per label, keyed
w.set("p_max_pu", frame, entity=["wind1"])  # a long frame
w.set("p_max_pu", series.rename_axis("snapshot"), entity="wind1")  # a series
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.9)  # every label carrying it, now and later
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, component="Generator", carrier="wind")  # the ones there are now
w.set("efficiency", 0.9, entity="dc", bus="north")  # a connection
w.set("p_nom", 200.0, entity="wind1", scenario="high")  # scoped to one scenario
w.set("p_nom", nw.col("value") * 1.1, entity=["wind1"])  # derived
w.set("entity.carrier", "solar", entity="g2")  # a property, by its subject
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # not `x`, an attribute of its own
w.set("p", solved_frame, kind="outputs")  # a result

Every coordinate is a keyword, a group's fields included — bus="north" with entity="dc" addresses one connection, from=/to= one corridor. A coordinate no keyword names is NULL, which means "every label of it": on a categorized dim, every label whose categories carry the attribute, including ones added later. A group's fields must all be given or none, since a group value is a whole tuple (design).

A property as a keyword selects labels at call time: a keyword is bare, a coordinate of the attribute first, else any property of a dim it reaches, so component="Generator", carrier="wind" stages one row per label matching both on the record as staged. A label added later is not reached; a plain NULL is how a value reaches those. A name several reached dims declare a property of is refused: set it per dim.

A mapping's keys or a series' index are labels of the one coordinate no keyword names, unless the series' index is named after a coordinate; where neither says, the call is refused rather than guessed.

set writes properties too, a category included, each named by its subject: set("entity.component", "Load", entity="g1") patches one column of g1's axis row. A plain name is an attribute or result; set("carrier", ...) with only properties so called is refused, suggesting bus.carrier and entity.carrier.

An nw.Expr value is a function of the current value: it reads the resolved value including earlier pending edits, so two such calls compose, and what gets staged is the result rather than the expression (design). A named target that resolves to no row raises — the caller asked for those rows to take a new value and there is nothing to compute one from.

docs.title: add / remove / add_group / remove_group
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

w.add("carrier", ["wind"])
w.add("bus", ["north", "south"])
w.add("entity", ["wind1", "wind2"], component="Generator", carrier="wind")
w.add("entity", ["dc"], component="Link")
w.set("p_nom", [100.0, 80.0], entity=["wind1", "wind2"])

w.remove("entity", ["old_coal"])

w.add_group(
    "connection",
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "connection": [
                {"entity": "dc", "bus": "north"},
                {"entity": "dc", "bus": "south"},
            ],
            "role": ["bus0", "bus1"],
        }
    ),
)
w.remove_group("connection", [("dc", "south")])

add(dim, labels, **columns) works on any dim. The keywords are the axis file's other columns — the dim's properties, bare, and a nested dim's parent keys — each a scalar or a sequence aligned to labels. An attribute keyword is refused: attributes go through set, whatever their dims (design). A label exists by virtue of its axis row, so add is not a sequence of set calls: adding a bus with no properties makes the point.

remove(dim, labels) stages a tombstone per label, with no dim scope — a label exists or it does not. It need not enumerate what it deletes: the fold applies it to every value keyed by the label, and remove also tombstones every group tuple naming one (design). It is refused while a property into the dim still names one of the labels — entity.carrier naming gas — since that row is its subject's and outlives the label: set it to another label or None first (design).

add_group/remove_group stage a group's tuples, as one struct column named for the group with the group's properties beside it. Every group is reached the same way — connection has no call of its own, being one group among however many the schema declares.

docs.title: Inspecting and rolling back
docs.text:
w.attributes["p_nom"]  # the edit applied, over the base's rows
w.properties["entity"]  # additions in, removals out
w.rollback()  # discard everything staged

What you staged is read back from the record itself, which satisfies Record and answers with the edits applied (design). Staged rows live in DuckDB tables on the record's connection, so they vanish with it and never touch disk (design).

docs.title: Writing the edits
docs.text:
A WorkingRecord does not write. Nothing touches the record until you hand its edits to a writer (design):

new = root.child(w.edits)  # a patch layer under a new child of the base
ws.write(w, "out/")  # a standalone record, flattened
w.rollback()  # clear the staging area, if you are done

w.edits is only the edits, and the fold resolves the rest from the parent. w itself is the resolved result — what is staged plus what the record already reads — which is what a standalone directory needs, there being no parent to resolve against.

The edits are a delta against the revision w was built over, so child raises if you write them under another one. The layer lands in the child, never in the node you branched from — layers are write-once (design) — so it is the returned node that reads the edits back:

new.record.attributes["p_nom"].collect()

Writing clears nothing: a WorkingRecord still holding its edits reads exactly what it did before, until rollback().

An edit replaces the rows it names, so restating a coordinate overwrites it and the last write is what stands. A remove after a set wins regardless of order — a deleted label has no values — and an add after a remove brings the label back, without its group tuples.

Neither write carries a base's results across: an edit changes the inputs a result was computed from. What it does carry is results staged into this record through set(..., kind="outputs"), which were computed against these pending inputs (design).

Edit-level mistakes are caught when the edit is staged, not at write, so a typo is reported at the line that typed it (design).

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
A Revision is a node in a tree of layers. Each node adds one layer; what it resolves to is that layer over its ancestors', last-writer-wins (design).

from datarecord import Workspace

store = Workspace().store("/data/my-record")

root = store.root(source)  # a new node, with `source` as its layer
child = root.child(patch)  # branch off it, with `patch` as its layer
record = child.record  # the resolved overlay, as a `Record`

There is no empty revision: a revision exists by writing its layer.

Each revision is a file under revisions/ beside layers/, so a location alone is enough to find the tree, and a Revision serialises as its id, its parent and its store's location (design).

A layer's data is write-once, so any node may be a parent and no cache ever needs invalidating (design). Branching is several children sharing a parent by pointing at it, not by duplication.

docs.title: Materialising
docs.text:
materialise() writes a node's owner map and resolved dims under layers/<id>/resolved/, so descendants' reads stop there instead of walking to the root. Purely additive — a policy, not a lifecycle step, changing no answer, only how many layers a read touches (design):

child.materialise()

docs.title: Navigating
docs.text:
revision = store.revision(uuid)  # load one by id
store.revisions()  # every revision, unordered
revision.ancestry()  # the root→node path
store.layer(uuid)  # one layer read alone

docs.title: The Record protocol
docs.text:
Everything a consumer codes against. It is read-only, and structural — a plain directory, a hundred-layer overlay, a record with pending edits and a framework's own object all satisfy it, and a consumer cannot tell which it holds (design).

record.schema  # what may exist: the axes, the properties, the attributes
record.dims["entity"]  # axis labels, keyed by dim
record.properties["entity"]  # stored property values, keyed by dim or group
record.groups["connection"]  # group rows, keyed by group — one frame each
record.attributes["p_max_pu"]  # long input frames, keyed by attribute
record.outputs["p"]  # long result frames, keyed by attribute
record.flags(component="Generator")  # which axes each attribute actually uses

Every frame is a narwhals.LazyFrame — a plan, not data. Nothing is read until you .collect(), and listing the keys reads nothing at all (design).

entities = record.properties["entity"]
gens = entities.filter(nw.col("component") == "Generator").collect().to_pandas()

docs.title: Labels and properties
docs.text:
dims[dim] is the axis's key columns only — the labels, and a nested dim's parent keys — in axis order.

properties[subject] is a dim's or a group's key with every property declared for it, as stored: a NULL is a value no layer wrote.

One category's labels are properties[dim] filtered on a categorizing property — an Enum property of a partial dim. Which properties they carry is Schema.properties_for(dim, **categories), and an unset one's default, default_by per category included, is Schema.default_for("entity.sign", **categories) — a property named by its subject, the categories by their plain names, as the frame's columns are (design).

docs.title: Wide and long
docs.text:
dims, properties and groups are wide — one row per label or tuple. attributes and outputs are long — one row per value:

<coordinate> ... | attribute | breakpoint | value

attributes holds every attribute, whatever its dims — p_nom over entity alone is long rows just like p_max_pu. The coordinates are the attribute's own — entity for p_nom, one connection struct column for a connection attribute like efficiency, and no entity column at all for one addressed by another axis alone (design).

A NULL dim column means "all values of that dim", not that the attribute lacks the axis: a constant p_max_pu is one row with timestep = NULL, a varying one is a row per timestep (design). entity broadcasts like any dim; on a categorized dim a NULL reaches only the labels whose categories carry the attribute, so one p_max_pu row with entity = NULL reaches every generator and no load. A group column broadcasts the same way, a NULL connection meaning every connection. breakpoint carries the abscissa of a piecewise-linear value.

attributes shows stored rows only: a coordinate no row covers takes the attribute's default, which Schema.default_for(name, **categories) answers per category.

No property is a column of an attribute row — attributes["p_max_pu"] holds every entity's rows together. To scope to one category, join properties["entity"], filtered on the category, on entity.

docs.title: flags
docs.text:
flags() answers which axes each attribute's rows actually use, across the record in one query, so a consumer can plan its reads without opening a file. flags(**categories) answers for one category of one dim, counting only rows reaching a matching label and only attributes those labels carry:

flags = record.flags(component="Generator")
set(flags)  # which attributes generators have at all
"timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].varies  # some row sets it
"timestep" in flags["p_max_pu"].broadcast  # some row leaves it NULL
flags["marginal_cost"].breakpoints  # some row carries a curve

The two sets are not complements: a dim in both means the labels disagree — some carry a per-timestep series, others a single constant row — which is the instruction to use both containers, not an ambiguity (design).

docs.title: Reading a directory
docs.text:
A parquet directory is a record. Nothing about layers is involved:

from datarecord import Workspace

ws = Workspace()
record = ws.at("s3://bucket/my-record/")
record.attributes["p_nom"].collect()

The layout is the whole format (design):

record/
├── manifest.json            # the schema, and the record's id
├── dims/<dim>.parquet       # one axis per declared dim: labels and their properties
├── groups/<group>.parquet   # which tuples of the group exist, and their properties
├── inputs/<attr>.parquet    # one input attribute per file, whatever its dims
└── outputs/<attr>.parquet   # one result attribute per file

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
One schema per record, written down as manifest.json (design).

import narwhals as nw
from datarecord import Schema, Dimension, AttributeSpec, PropertySpec, Group, Trait

schema = Schema(
    version=1,
    dimensions={
        "entity": Dimension(dtype=nw.String()),
        "bus": Dimension(dtype=nw.String()),
        "carrier": Dimension(dtype=nw.String()),
        "country": Dimension(dtype=nw.String()),
        "scenario": Dimension(dtype=nw.String()),
        "timestep": Dimension(dtype=nw.Datetime()),
    },
    properties={
        "entity": {
            "component": PropertySpec(
                dtype=nw.Enum(["Generator", "Link", "Load", "StorageUnit"])
            ),
            "carrier": PropertySpec(into="carrier"),
            "sign": PropertySpec(
                dtype=nw.Float64(),
                default=1.0,
                default_by={"entity.component": {"Load": -1.0}},
            ),
        },
        "bus": {
            "carrier": PropertySpec(into="carrier", default="AC"),
            "x": PropertySpec(dtype=nw.Float64(), default=0.0),
            "country": PropertySpec(into="country"),
        },
        "connection": {"role": PropertySpec(dtype=nw.String())},
    },
    groups={"connection": Group(over={"entity": "entity", "bus": "bus"})},
    attributes={
        "p_nom": AttributeSpec(
            dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"entity"}, default=0.0, unit="MW"
        ),
        "x": AttributeSpec(dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"entity"}, default=0.0),
        "co2_emissions": AttributeSpec(
            dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"carrier"}, default=0.0
        ),
        "p_max_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"entity", "scenario", "timestep"}, default=1.0
        ),
        "p_min_pu": AttributeSpec(
            dtype=nw.Float64(),
            dims={"entity", "timestep"},
            default=0.0,
            default_by={"entity.component": {"StorageUnit": -1.0}},
        ),
        "efficiency": AttributeSpec(
            dtype=nw.Float64(), dims={"connection", "timestep"}, default=1.0
        ),
    },
    traits={
        "dispatchable": Trait(
            attributes={"p_max_pu", "p_min_pu"},
            on={"entity.component": {"Generator", "StorageUnit"}},
        )
    },
    partial={"entity", "bus", "scenario", "connection"},
)
  • Dimension declares one axis: its dtype (a narwhals dtype, translated to its DuckDB name — a DuckDB type name works too, for a type narwhals does not spell) and within for an axis whose labels identify a point only inside another's — multi-period time being the case (design). entity is a dim like any other.
  • properties is metadata: per subject — a dim or a group — the values that identify, classify or describe one of its labels, one value per label and never varying along another axis. Each is a column of the subject's own file, dims/entity.parquet or groups/connection.parquet, so its name is the subject's alone and it is addressed as subject.name — entity.carrier, bus.carrier, connection.role (design). A property may share its name with an attribute, a dim or another subject's property: bus.x is not the attribute x, nor entity.carrier the dim carrier; one named like its subject's key, or a group's coordinate, is refused.
  • A property may be into a dim: its values are that dim's labels, its dtype the dim's. entity.carrier and bus.carrier above name labels of carrier, bus.country one of country; set and add refuse one the record lacks, NULL meaning none, and remove("country", ...) is refused while a bus still names the label. It never categorizes: a category is a declared Enum, a label is data (design).
w.add("country", ["DE"])
w.add("bus", ["north"], country="DE")
w.set("bus.country", "FR", bus="north")  # refused: no `country` label FR
  • An Enum property of a partial dim categorizes it: its values are the dim's categories, which traits and default_by key on by its dotted name. component above is one; a dim may have several, and no name is special. Schema.categorizing("entity") lists them (design).
  • default_by overrides default per category, on properties and attributes alike: the first key listing the label's category wins. Schema.default_for("p_min_pu", component="StorageUnit") answers -1.0 (design).
  • attributes is data, and flat — one name, one spec, record-wide, across attributes and results; a property may share an attribute's name, Schema.resolve telling x from bus.x. A Trait narrows attributes (and properties) to the labels whose category its on names. One no trait claims is carried by every label its dims can address, so p_nom above reaches every entity while p_max_pu reaches only generators and storage units. Schema.attributes_for("entity", component="Generator") and Schema.properties_for(...) resolve what a category carries (design).
  • AttributeSpec.dims is the only addressing mechanism, naming dims and groups alike — efficiency is a connection attribute because its dims name the group, carried as one struct column (design). It is what makes a scenario-varying p_nom a violation rather than data. Every attribute lands in inputs/, whatever its dims, so widening one is a compatible change that moves no file.
  • Group declares which tuples over several dims exist, mapping coordinate name → dim; a list is sugar where the two coincide. connection over (entity, bus) is the one every network has. Adding into declares the group functional into that dim — each over tuple carrying exactly one of its labels — which is a constraint checkable on write; it needs two coordinates or more, one being a property into the dim (design).
  • partial is the layering granularity — which dims and groups a layer may patch value by value, and the fold key. entity in it lets a layer patch one entity, and is required for its categories to key traits and defaults. bus and scenario are patchable, carrier restated whole, a few rows; timestep is not patchable, so a patch to one hour restates that entity's whole series rather than leaving a curve resolved across two layers with a hole in it (design). A group is the same: with connection in it a layer patches one connection's efficiency, without it the layer restates every connection's.
  • unit and description are stored and never interpreted — no conversion, no dimensional analysis. None is undeclared, "" genuinely dimensionless (design).

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
schema.compatible_with(other) answers whether layers written under other still read under self, returning one reason per incompatibility and an empty list when the change is compatible (design).

reasons = new_schema.compatible_with(old_schema)
if reasons:
    raise ValueError("\n".join(reasons))

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
A tool is one modelling framework's view of a record. Tools live under datarecord/tools/, are reached by importing them (no registry), and nothing in the core imports one — so importing the record layer pulls in no framework (design, module layout).

from datarecord.tools.pypsa import PyPSA

missing = PyPSA.verify(record)
if missing:
    raise RuntimeError(missing.describe())

n = PyPSA.build(record)  # a pypsa.Network
n.optimize()

record_back = PyPSA.to_datarecord(n, ws.con)  # the inverse; a `Record`
results = PyPSA.results(n, ws.con)  # Frames, in the long schema

to_datarecord and results plan their frames on the connection they are handed — the workspace's that writes them, or the record's they are set on — so they reach the write path without a copy; build reads record.con itself.

verify catches what the record layer cannot — an entity type the framework has no registry entry for, a connection role it cannot place, a partial set that breaks its constant-versus-varying split — and returns a falsy Requirements when the record is usable. build raises UnsupportedRecordError rather than producing a partial model.

docs.title: Buses and carriers
docs.text:
PyPSA's buses and carriers are dims, not entity types: a bus is a label of bus, a carrier a label of carrier, and what PyPSA stores on either is a property of the label or an attribute over the dim, every name PyPSA's (design).

record.dims["carrier"]  # carrier
record.properties["bus"]  # bus | carrier | type | x | y | unit | location
record.properties["entity"]  # entity | component | carrier | sign | type
record.attributes["v_nom"]  # bus | attribute | breakpoint | value
record.outputs["marginal_price"]  # bus | snapshot | scenario | ...

A property is named by its subject, so x is a line's reactance and bus.x a bus's coordinate. entity.carrier and bus.carrier are into carrier, naming its labels:

w.add("carrier", ["H2"], color="#f0f")
w.add("bus", ["north H2"], carrier="H2", x=10.1, y=52.0)  # bare: the dim's own
w.set("v_nom", 380.0, bus="north")
w.set("bus.x", 10.2, bus="north")  # `x` alone is a Line's reactance
w.set("entity.component", "Load", entity="g1")
w.set("entity.carrier", "coal", entity="g1")  # refused: no label `coal`
w.set("carrier", "AC")  # refused, naming `bus.carrier` and `entity.carrier`
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, component="Generator")  # selector: `entity.component`
w.remove("bus", ["south"])  # and every connection at it
w.remove("carrier", ["gas"])  # refused while a carrier names it

A bus and a load may share a name, being labels of two dims. to_datarecord adds every carrier a component or bus names but n.carriers does not list, and stores PyPSA's "" carrier as NULL. verify reports an entity attached to no bus.

docs.title: Solving and writing results back
docs.text:
results returns the same Frames type Record.outputs presents, so a solve's output goes straight back:

w = WorkingRecord(rev.record)
w.set("p_max_pu", 0.8, entity=["wind1"])
n = PyPSA.build(w)  # a WorkingRecord is a Record
n.optimize()
for attr, frame in PyPSA.results(n, w.con).items():
    w.set(attr, frame, kind="outputs")
rev.child(w.edits)  # one layer, inputs and results together

A result is checked against the schema's results, its name and its dims, but its labels need not resolve — a solve may produce rows for labels it derived rather than read (design).

docs.title: Writing a whole record
docs.text:
root = store.root(source)  # a new root revision with this layer
child = root.child(source)  # a new child of root with this layer
record = ws.write(source, "out/")  # a standalone directory, read back

source is anything satisfying Record — including a framework object presenting itself as one, which is what puts read and write on a single seam. An existing layer directory is an error rather than an overwrite: frames are staged into a sibling path and renamed on success, so a source that fails validation leaves no layer rather than half of one (design).

A revision's file is written after its layer and the manifest, so a write that fails leaves no revision behind; a standalone directory's manifest is written last for the same reason (design).

Every column the schema declares a type for is cast to it on the way out, so a record's files carry the schema's types and a reader can trust them. Validation is structural — a long frame carries the format's columns, and an entity frame carries every dim it is keyed by.
